journey.prep:
Focus on your CGPA. During our time, many compa nies had a minimum CGPA criteria of 7.5, which led 
to a large number of students being filtered out even before getting the opportunity to sit for the company. It 
really hurts when you don’t even get the chance to appear despite having the skills. 
Placements are a tiring yet humbling process. I had reached the HR rounds of InCred and Quantiphi before 
this opportunity, and both interviews went really well, but I couldn’t make it to the final shortlist. That’s when 
I truly realised how important factors like CGPA and luck can be in the placement journey. Sometimes, even 
after giving your best, things don’t work out—but they prepare you for the opportunity that’s meant for you. 
My personal suggestion would be during your 6th semester, shut out the noise around you and just believe 
in your hard work  . When your day finally comes, everything will start to make sense  ,you’ll realise why 
you weren’t selected earlier and how it was all just a testing phase before something bigger.Having your family 
and supportive friends around you trule encourages you to not get carried away by rejections and prepare for 
upcoming companies. 
Study everything that’s commonly asked  in interviews. In placements, being a  jack of all trades  often 
works better than excelling in just one domain. Practicing DSA is important, of course, but relying only on it 
won’t help much—only 4–5 companies are heavily DSA-focused and I realized it much much later. The rest 
mostly have doable coding questions in their online assessments and give high importance to aptitude, which 
most students tend to ignore. 
For interviews,  know your resume inside out —every project, every line.  SQL is the underdog  in 
placements, so make sure to practice it thoroughly beforehand. 
When it comes to projects, having a simple project that you understand deeply is far better than having an 
overly complex one that you can’t explain properly. Lastly, know your OS, CN, and DBMS concepts really 
well—many companies ask questions from these subjects. End-moment preparation won’t help much here, so 
start early. I’d recommend watching  CodeHelp’s OS playlist , which is around 30 hours long —it’s a time 
investment that’s truly worth it. 
 
All the very best for your placements! Give your best, trust the process, and have faith in your hard work. 
Everything will fall into place when it’s meant to.God does have a plan for all

1. [Aptitude Round] [All students from Comps,AIML,DS and having minor in computers from EXTC 
were eligible for the process] 
The Aptitude Round consisted of 100 questions covering Quantitative Aptitude, Geometry, Verbal 
Ability, and Logical Reasoning to be solved in 1 hour. The quantitative section included problems on 
percentages, ratios, time and work, and geometry-based questions. The verbal section tested grammar, 
reading comprehension, and vocabulary, while the reasoning section focused on analytical thinking. In 
addition to these, there were a few behavioral and situational questions such as “If your team member 
isn’t contributing effectively, what would you do?” to assess decision-making and teamwork skills. 
Overall, the round focused on both technical and behavorial assessment. 
 
This round followed a +4 -1 marking scheme so make sure to attempt the questions you are fully sure 
about, I managed to solve 94 questions. Since navigation was allowed,I quickly solved logical verbal and 
behavorial questions in the first 20 minutes and then proceeded to do the aptitude questions. 
 
I practiced Quantitative, Logical, and Verbal Aptitude questions from IndiaBix, and most 
importantly taking their timed tests greatly helped me improve my speed and time management skills, 
which play a crucial role in performing well in aptitude exams. 
 
2.     [Coding Round] [ 72 candidates were shortlisted for this round] 
Round 2 consisted of two sections – the first focused on basic Python MCQs, while the second included 
easy-level coding questions similar to those found on LeetCode. The only programming language allowed 
was Python. I was able to solve all the coding questions and pa ss all the test cases, along with answering 
almost all the MCQs correctly. This round was quite doable, and the key differentiator turned out to be 
time . Candidates who managed to solve almost all questions accurately and submitted their test about 15 
minutes early were the ones who proceeded to the next round. 
 
but since only allowed programming language was python and my primary language was Java,I practiced 
some basic questions from this youtube channel. 
https://youtu.be/78FsbjYSWIU?si=ehBIXHc3uNnGOLEF  
This has around 100 coding questions which will give you a strong grasp of the basics 
For other DSA rounds,Practice Striver’s sheet being well versed wit h it will help you clear DSA coding 
rounds of almost all the companies. 
I practiced python mcqs from Sanfoundry(It has 1000 mcqs but to be able to be quick with mcqs that much 
of practice will really be worth it as you would have seen or solved all the questions in the past). 
 
3.    [Group Discussion Roud] [25 candidates were shortlisted for this round] 
The topic given to us was “Technology: Boon or Bane.” Candidates who expressed their points in a clear, 
concise, and professional manner, speaking confidently and with good articulation, were the ones selected 
for the next round. 
 
4.  [Technical Interveiw] [11 students were selected for this round] 
The interview was primarily focused on Python and Machine Lea rning. The interviewer was very particular 
about the answers and often went into detailed discussions. He began by asking me to introduce myself. Since 
I had researched Mahindra Finance beforehand, I knew that one of its key sectors deals with loan approva l, 
which aligned well with my credit risk modelling project. I mentioned this connection during my introduction, 
which led him to ask several project-related questions. 
He asked which algorithm I had used, and since I had applied SMOTE during preprocessing , he asked me to 
explain SMOTE along with its advantages and disadvantages. He then asked me to draw and explain the 
working of Random Forest and justify why it performed better than XGBoost in my case. 
Next, he moved on to questions about my dataset. My project involved two datasets that I had merged, so he 
asked me to write the pandas query for merging them using the ID column as the key. He further asked detailed 
questions about the types of columns in my dataset and their relevance. 
The discussion then shifted to model evaluation metrics, where he asked me to explain precision, recall, and 
accuracy, and to justify which metric mattered the most in my project context. 
After that, he presented a case study scenario: “If Uber ride prices suddenly increase from ₹400 to ₹800 within 
10 minutes in the same location, how would you identify and fix the bug in your ML model?” He asked me 
to describe the parameters and features I would use in such a model. He then gave another scenario: “If all 
drivers in a certain area stop accepting Uber rides and instead take private trips, how would your model detect 
such behavior?” I explained my approach, mentioning that one of the parameters would be peak-hour timings. 
He further asked how I would determine peak hours without having an existing dataset. 
The interview concluded with me asking him three questions about Mahindra Finance’s advancements in 
Machine Learning and how the company is integrating AI into its operations. Overall, it was a highly engaging 
and technical discussion that tested both conceptual understanding and practical problem-solving. 
 
 
 
 
 
5.[HR Round] 
The HR round surprisingly lasted for around 45 minutes, during which the HR was noting down my 
answers carefully. The discussion mainly revolved around situational and behavio ral questions. I was 
given several case-based scenarios such as how I would handle a situation where a team member is not 
contributing effectively, or how I would respond if I witnessed something wrong happening around me. 
The HR wanted to understand my th ought process, decision -making, and ability to handle real -life 
workplace challenges. Overall, it was a situational round focused on assessing attitude, ethics, and 
teamwork rather than technical knowledge. 
 
Finally 5 students were selected :)

journey.howSecured:
1.     Online Assessment [ Students with >=7 CGPA ] 
The first stage was an online assessment consisting of a single DSA question + 4 logic/Aptitude questions. 
The DSA question was mainly based on mathematical reasoning rather than complex data structures. 
After this round, 24 students were shortlisted. 
2.     Predictive Index Assessment [ 24 students ] 
The shortlisted candidates were asked to complete a Predictive Index assessment the following day. This 
assessment was focused more on behavioural and personality evaluation rather than technical skills. 
After this stage, 13 candidates were shortlisted for the interview process. 
 
3.    Technical Interview Round 1 (Online) [ 13 students ] 
 
The first technical round was conducted online on a coding platform called Meetl. 
 
The interview focused on: 
• Core Java fundamentals 
• Java Collections Framework 
• Object-Oriented Programming concepts 
• DBMS basics 
• Data Structures and Algorithms 
I was given two DSA problems: 
• One was Leetcode easy level.  
• The second problem was of medium difficulty (roughly LeetCode medium level). 
 
I had to write the code for both problems and explain the logic clearly. 
After this round, 3 out of the 13 candidates were shortlisted for the next round. 
 
 
4. Technical Interview Round 2 (Onsite) [3 students] 
 
This round was conducted onsite at the company office and was a pen-and-paper coding round. 
This interview again focused heavily on OOP concepts and Java fundamentals. 
Some of the questions included: 
• Explanation of Parent p = new Child() and Child c = new Parent() along with reasoning. 
• Typecasting in objects. 
• Lambda functions in Java. 
• Streams in Java. 
• Serializable interface. 
• Questions about my hackathon experiences and projects. 
After this , the interviewer asked 4 DSA questions  
1. Linked List 
Delete a node in a singly linked list in constant time. 
2. Array Problem 
Find the second maximum element in an array using one pass and constant space. 
3. Integer Stream Problem 
The interviewer described a scenario where  a large stream of integers flows into a queue throughout 
the day, with the constraint that the difference between consecutive numbers is always 1. 
At the end of the day, we need to answer  q queries asking whether a specific number x appeared in 
the stream, and the requirement was to answer queries in constant time and constant space. 
4. Array Partition 
Given an array, divide the elements into  two arrays such that the difference between their sums is 
minimum . ( time complexity of order 1 )  
The problems themselves were not difficult but were slightly tricky and required reasoning/proof .  
I wrote code for all four problems and explained the logic clearly. The interviewer seemed satisfied with 
both my OOP explanations and DSA solutions. 
The next day I received a call from HR saying that  the feedback was positive, and I was invited for the 
next round.  
 
5. Technical Interview Round 3 (Senior Engineering Manager) [ 2 students ] 
 
This round was again conducted onsite and a pen-and-paper round .  
The interviewer was an Engineering Manager who had been with the company for around 11 years. 
The round began with questions on the  Java Collections Framework , after which the discussion went 
deep into HashMap internals. 
I had to explain: 
• How key-value pairs are stored 
• Load factor 
• Rehashing 
• Collision handling 
• How collision handling worked before Java 8 and after Java 8 
After this discussion, I was asked to write a Student class with attributes: 
• name 
• id 
• marks 
I wrote the class and implemented the constructor. 
Then the interviewer asked whether we could directly use this class as a key in a HashMap. 
This question was meant to check my understanding of equals() and hashCode(). 
I explained: 
• The default implementations provided by the Object class 
• How they compare memory references 
• Why overriding them is necessary for logical equality 
I then implemented: 
• equals() using student id 
• hashCode() accordingly 
I also explained what would happen if we did not override these methods. 
Next we discussed: 
• Comparable vs Comparator 
 
• Writing a Comparable implementation 
• Writing a Comparator for a different custom sorting strategy  
• What the return values -1, 0, and 1 represent 
The interviewer then moved to JDBC, which I had not worked with before, so I honestly mentioned that 
I had not used JDBC. 
We then discussed SQL concepts, including: 
• Different types of joins 
• Database indexing 
• Data structures used in indexing (B-Trees) 
Finally, the interviewer asked two logical puzzles: 
Puzzle 1: 25 Horses and 5 Tracks 
Find the top three fastest horses. 
Puzzle 2: 2 Eggs and 100 Floors 
Determine the highest floor from which an egg can be dropped without breaking. 
The interviewer was mainly evaluating  how I approached the problems and broke them down 
logically, rather than expecting an immediate answer. 
I struggled a bit with the horses puzzle, but with some hints I eventually arrived at the solution. 
I had mixed feelings after this round because the puzzle part did not go perfectly. 
 
6. Technical Interview Round 4 ( Online )  [ 2 students ] 
After about a week, HR informed us that there would be one final technical round. 
This round was conducted virtually and had two interviewers: 
• One senior engineering leader from the US 
• One engineer from the Mumbai office ( if selected , he/she will be your manager ) 
This round was more conversational compared to previous rounds. 
We started with a discussion about my projects and hackathon experiences. I was asked about the most 
challenging aspects of my projects and how I approached solving them. 
One interesting question was about  a product in the market that I admire or would like to work on , 
and I spoke about a technology product I had seen on Shark Tank India. 
 
The discussion then moved into database concepts, including: 
• Relational vs Non-relational databases 
• MongoDB 
• Redis ( Since I had used in my project )  
• Why Redis, despite being very fast, is usually not used as a primary database for large systems 
I was also given a  probability puzzle involving 50 black balls and 50 white balls distributed across 
two bags, where the goal was to maximize the probability of drawing a black ball. 
I initially took some time to reason about the problem, and with a hint from the interviewer I arrived at the 
correct solution. Towards the end of the interview, the discussion became more open-ended. I asked about 
a concept the interviewer mentioned called the S2 geometry data structure, which is used for geospatial 
indexing in systems like Google Maps. 
I also asked what areas a new engineer should focus on during the first few months after joining. 
Overall I was able to answer all questions in this round , but again felt dumb because I took a lot more 
time than required on that simple probability puzzle , brain felt saturated at that moment and stopped 
thinking, but with one hint from interviewer , arrived at the ans . 
After this round, there was a long silence from the company for around 14–17 days. During this time, 
another candidate who was interviewing along with me received a call from HR for the HR discussion 
round, while I did not receive any update.  
Naturally, I felt that my process might have ended there. However, after around two weeks, I unexpectedly 
received a call from HR informing me that my profile had been moved to a different team  internally, 
and because of that, I would have to go through two additional technical &/ team rounds which were 
scheduled immediately on the next day .  
 
7. Technical Interview Round 5 ( Online )  
The fifth round was conducted by a manager from the Mumbai office with around 7 years of experience. 
The interview was relatively short and focused mainly on Java fundamentals and problem solving. 
 He first asked me about the internal working of HashMap, where I explained buckets, key-value 
storage, hashCode(), equals() , collisions, collision handling, etc. 
Then he moved to a DSA problem similar to the “Search Suggestions System” problem on LeetCode. 
Similar to : Leetcode Search Suggestions  
I came up with a sorting + string prefix matching based solution.  O(n^2) and coded the approach and 
output was correct. 
 
Although the problem had a more optimized binary search based approach possible, he did not ask me to 
optimize further once the logic and output were correct  . The round ended after he asked whether I had 
any questions for him.   
8. Technical Interview Round 6 ( Online )  
The sixth and final technical round was with a senior engineer from the US team who had around 15 years 
of experience. This round was very different from the previous ones.  
It was not focused on coding or rapid -fire technical questions. Instead, it was more of a deep two -way 
discussion about the team, their domains, systems, and the type of work they do. He spent a significant 
amount of time explaining the team structure and the backend systems they work on.  
I asked a few thoughtful questions regarding the domain and one specific question that he appreciated a 
lot during the discussion. I also asked him what I should focus on learning before joining so that I could 
reduce the amount of training effort required from the team side once I joined. He seemed to like that 
question as well, and the overall interaction was very positive and eng aging. The conversation lasted for 
around one hour. 
 
After these rounds, I received a call from HR stating that all interviewer feedback was positive and that 
the final HR discussion round was scheduled.  
The HR round mainly covered resume overview, family background, relocation, future plans, joining 
timeline, and compensation discussion. 
Toward the end of the HR round, I was also introduced to the manager(same person who took my second 
last interview) of the team I would potentially join, and we discussed the team goals and what I should 
focus on before joining. 
After the HR round, there was another waiting period because the profile had to go through final approval 
from the US side. Around a month later, I finally received the official confirmation and offer from the 
company for the role of Junior Software Engineer.

1.

Shortlisting

The

resume

shortlisting

round

was

conducted

through

a

Google

in

which

candidates

were

required

to

fill

in

details

about

their

previous

experiences,

including

committee

involvement,

internships,

and

key

learnings.

Shortlisting

was

done

based

on

the

relevance

of

these

experiences

to

the

role,

clarity

of

interest,

and

overall

consistency

in

the

candidate’s

profile.

This

round

focused

more

on

understanding

practical

exposure

and

motivation

rather

than

just

academic

performance,

and

the

selected

candidates

were

invited

for

the

interview

rounds.

2.

Online

Interview

The

second

round

was

an

online

interview

conducted

by

Adhik,

the

founder

himself.

This

round

was

more

conversational

in

nature

and

aimed

at

understanding

my

background,

motivation,

and

alignment

with

the

company

and

the

role.

The

interview

began

with

my

self-introduction,

after

which

the

founder

explained

the

product

in

detail

along

with

its

target

market.

This

helped

set

the

context

for

the

discussion

and

allowed

me

to

understand

the

business

side

of

the

company

better.

Following

this,

I

was

asked

why

I

was

opting

for

a

non-technical

role

and

what

I

had

learned

from

my

previous

internship

experience,

which

I

had

mentioned

in

the

resume

shortlisting

form.

Since

my

internship

was

in

the

marketing

domain,

I

explained

how

it

sparked

my

interest

in

business

development

and

sales,

and

how

I

enjoyed

working

closer

to

customers

and

strategy.

The

founder

seemed

satisfied

with

my

clarity

and

reasoning.

Towards

the

end

of

the

interview,

I

was

asked

about

my

place

of

stay

and

when

I

would

be

able

to

join

if

selected.

The

entire

interview

lasted

around

20–25

minutes.

A

few

minutes

after

the

interview

concluded,

I

received

a

message

informing

me

that

there

would

be

another

round

scheduled

offline

the

following

day.

3.

Offline

Interview

[

No

of

candidates

who

appeared

for

this

round

-

2

]

The

third

round

was

an

offline

interview

and

was

more

in-depth

and

practical

compared

to

the

previous

rounds.

It

focused

on

understanding

how

I

handle

pressure,

manage

multiple

responsibilities,

and

perform

in

a

sales-oriented

role.

The

discussion

initially

revolved

around

my

previous

experiences,

especially

how

I

balanced

my

internship

alongside

committee

work.

I

answered

honestly,

mentioning

that

managing

both

did

disturb

my

schedule

initially,

but

over

time

I

learned

to

prioritize

tasks

better

and

stay

focused

despite

pressure.

Since

the

role

involved

business

and

sales,

I

was

asked

to

pitch

the

company’s

product

to

the

founder

as

if

I

were

convincing

a

potential

client.

I

approached

the

pitch

from

a

day-to-day

usage

perspective,

explaining

how

the

product

could

be

seamlessly

integrated

into

everyday

life

while

being

both

beneficial

and

time-saving

for

users.

I

focused

on

practical

use

cases

rather

than

just

features,

which

helped

demonstrate

the

product’s

real-world

value.

The

founder

appreciated

this

approach

and

was

satisfied

with

how

I

positioned

the

product.

Towards

the

end

of

the

interview,

I

was

asked

if

I

had

any

questions.

I

used

this

opportunity

to

ask

about

his

thoughts

on

expanding

the

product

into

a

B2C

model,

especially

targeting

students

as

potential

long-term

users.

He

appreciated

this

forward-thinking

approach

and

showed

interest

in

my

perspective.

After

the

interview,

I

asked

for

feedback

and

received

a

very

positive

response

overall,

with

one

suggestion

that

I

could

have

shown

slightly

more

energy

during

the

interaction.

The

interview

lasted

around

25–30

minutes.

This

was

the

second

time

Lombard

visited

the

campus.

There

were

4

rounds

for

this

process.

It

was

announced

that

the

recruitment

process

would

include:

1.

Online

Assessment

(OA).

2.

2

Technical

Interviews.

3.

HR

Interview

1.

Aptitude

and

Technical

Test

[90

mins]:

The

first

round

was

a

comprehensive

test

that

included

aptitude,

technical

multiple-choice

questions

(MCQs),

and

coding.

It

was

divided

into

7

sections,

and

the

total

duration

was

90

minutes.

The

first

section

was

a

coding

question

(DP)

which

was

to

be

completed

in

30

minutes.

The

other

6

sections

were

MCQ

questions.

The

aptitude

section

was

timed

and

non-navigable,

meaning

you

can

navigate

between

questions

but

once

you

exited

this

section,

you

couldn't

return

to

it.

The

remaining

6

sections

covered

topics

like

Database

Management

Systems

(DBMS),

Data

Structures

(DS),

Computer

Networks

(CN),

Object

Oriented

Programming

(OOPS),

Operating

System

(OS)

and

Aptitude.

2.

Technical

Interview

1

[50-60

mins]:

This

round

was

one

of

the

main

rounds

of

the

interview

process,

lasting

approximately

40–45

minutes.

It

primarily

focused

on

my

resume,

core

technical

knowledge,

and

problem-solving

approach.

a.

Introduction

&

Resume

Discussion

The

interview

began

with

a

brief

self-introduction,

followed

by

an

in-depth

discussion

of

my

resume.

The

interviewers

focused

on

a

project

where

I

had

implemented

multi

AI-agents.

I

was

asked

questions

related

to:

●

What

AI

agents

are

●

Their

implementation

●

Their

working

mechanism

●

The

overall

architecture

and

design

decisions

b.

System

Architecture,

AWS,

Docker

&

Kafka

Since

AWS,

Kafka,

and

Docker

were

mentioned

in

one

of

my

projects,

the

interviewers

explored

these

topics

in

detail.

●

I

was

asked

to

explain

the

complete

architecture

of

the

project.

●

One

of

the

interviewers

then

asked

me

to

list

and

explain

the

AWS

S3

and

Docker

commands

I

was

familiar

with.

●

I

was

asked

about

the

working

of

AWS

Glue

and

AWS

Athena,

including

how

they

are

used

for

data

crawling

and

querying.

●

I

was

asked

whether

MongoDB

can

be

set

up

using

Docker,

to

which

I

answered

yes.

●

Following

this,

I

was

asked

to

explain

all

the

commands

required

to

set

up

MongoDB

from

scratch

inside

a

Docker

container,

including

container

creation

and

configuration.

c.

Authentication

&

Security

(JWT)

The

discussion

then

moved

to

authentication

concepts,

specifically:

●

What

is

JWT?

●

Access

Tokens

and

Refresh

Token

●

Edge

cases

related

to

access

and

refresh

token

handling

●

Differences

between

JWT-based

authentication

and

session-based

authentication

d.

Object-Oriented

Programming

(OOPS)

Next,

I

was

asked

questions

related

to

OOPS

fundamentals,

including:

●

The

four

pillars

of

OOPS

●

SOLID

principles

●

Inheritance

and

its

different

types

e.

SQL

&

Database

Concepts

The

interviewers

then

covered

basic

SQL

concepts,

which

included:

●

Types

of

joins

in

SQL

●

ACID

properties

●

Order

of

execution

in

SQL

queries

●

Writing

a

SQL

query

to

filter

duplicate

rows

from

a

table

f.

Overall

Experience

Overall,

this

was

a

relatively

easy

and

well-structured

round.

The

key

takeaway

is

to:

●

Be

confident

while

explaining

your

projects

and

technical

concepts

●

Stay

calm

during

problem-solving

●

Clearly

communicate

your

thought

process,

as

the

interviewers

were

more

interested

in

understanding

how

I

approach

problems

rather

than

just

the

final

answer

3.

Technical

Round

2

[15-20

mins]:

a.

Project

Discussion

This

was

the

easiest

interview.

The

interviewer

asked

me

to

choose

any

one

project

that

would

impress

him

with

my

skills

and

explain

it

thoroughly.

Then

he

asked

follow-up

questions

on

that,

which

also

included

a

few

questions

on

the

tech

stack

mentioned

for

each

project.

b.

Internship

&

Achievements

He

then

moved

on

to

the

Internship

section

and

Achievements .

He

asked

about

hackathons,

including

which

project

I

made

in

which

hackathon,

what

problems

I

faced,

and

how

I

tackled

them.

For

this

round,

you

must

have

to

know

each

and

every

feature

of

the

project

that

you

have

mentioned,

along

with

the

tech

stack

you

have

mentioned.

4.

HR

Round

[10-15

mins]:

The

final

round

was

a

10–15

minute

interview.

Make

sure

you

are

well

prepared

for

generic

HR

questions.

The

interviewer

started

with

questions

such

as:

●

Where

do

I

belong

from

●

Where

do

I

currently

stay

●

How

many

family

members

I

have

and

what

they

do

●

Why

I

am

interested

in

an

insurance

firm

He

then

picked

one

of

my

projects

and

asked

me

to

consider

a

scenario

where

users

are

ghosting

the

platform

and

how

I

would

expand

the

business

across

geographies.

It

was

more

of

a

conversation-based

round

aimed

at

assessing

my

mindset,

thought

process,

and

long-term

goals.

5

students

were

offered

the

role

and

I

was

one

of

them

!!!

Dhruv Deshpande 
CSE-DS 
  The superset application for AuxoAI  was opened for us on 4th September 2025. The eligibility criteria for 
applying was CGPA>=7. There were 5 rounds in total: 
1. Resume shortlisting . 
2. Online Assessment 
3. Technical Round 1 
4. Culture Fit Round (Basically a techno-HR round) 
5. HR round 
 Before you read further, I want to inform you that this experience is focused on a Machine Learning (ML) 
role, not a SDE role. For SDE-specific experiences, I recommend referring to the experiences shared by my 
peers who were placed in SDE roles.  
  
      1.Resuming Shortlisting :  ( I think around 90-100 students appeared ) 
 In the resume shortlisting round, we were evaluated on our resumes based on the job description provided 
by the company. Around 50 students were selected  after this round .While  I cannot exactly pinpoint the 
formula to succeed, a good way to increase your probability of succeeding would be to include the skills 
and languages mentioned in the JD in your resume. 
 
  Resume Tips: 
     1.Since this is an AIML role, I would suggest that you should have all the projects in the field of 
AIML. Please try not to include development projects (if possible). All the 3 projects mentioned on my 
resume were based on machine learning. 
    2. I would recommend including 1–2 projects on your resume where you have developed machine 
learning models from scratch. These projects highlight your ability to code from scratch and 
demonstrate a strong fundamental understanding of  concepts. 
  3. Work experience is always appreciated. Try to have an internship before the placement season 
starts. I did not have any experience and thus was a bit tensed about my chances for this round . 
 
 
2. Online Assessment ( Around 50 students appeared for the test): 
 
  The test was conducted on campus in the afternoon ( around 4pm). The duration of the test was 60 
minutes,and there were 2 sections : 1. Aptitude section (20 questions) ,2. Coding section ( 4 questions). 
  Navigation was strict(once you visited a question , you could not visit it again). The aptitude section 
consisted mainly of topics like speed-time problems , simple interest-compound interest, trigonometry 
and ratios. The coding section consisted of the following questions: 
1. A basic string traversal question 
2. A question similar to Rotate Array - LeetCode. 
 
3. A question on finding previous smaller element ( Can be implemented using a stack). 
4. Implementing Logistic regression from scratch. 
 
For some reason , Java was not included in the list of available languages. Since I used Java , I was 
worried. So , I quickly changed my strategy and instead tried to solve all the questions of aptitude. 
I completed around 18 -19 questions correctly in around 45 minutes and then in the 15 minutes left , 
tried to solve the coding questions, With some basic knowledge and some common sense , I passed some test 
cases of all the questions(In 1 question , I passed 50 percent cases and in the others 20 30 percent  ) and thus 
the test concluded. 
 
 
Tips:  
  1.Try to have C++ or Python as your primary language and then study OOPS in Java for a well-
rounded knowledge base. Even though I knew to solve the coding questions and would have solved all of 
them collectively in less than 10 minutes(but in Java), my rigidity with Java would have resulted in a costly 
fumble. 
  2.The aptitude section for AuxoAI was of a moderate to high difficulty level  .I personally used my 
strong intuition of mathematics to solve the questions.While I had all the time in the world to solve the 
questions , it won’t always be the same .I solved 18-19 questions . 
 
Resources: This video is a goldmine for probability. PROBABILITY in 1 Shot | From Zero to Hero | JEE 
Main & Advanced   
 
Overall 10 students were selected for the interviews and I was glad  to be among them.  
 
    
3. [Technical Round 1]:  ( 10 Students appeared for this round)  
  
The results for the OA were declared around 12 in the night and the interviews were scheduled from 11 in 
the morning.There were 2 interviewers in each panel.I introduced myself to the panel and then they asked 
me  to select a  project on which a deep dive could be possible .  I chose the first project on my resume(It was 
a  LSTM+ XGBOOST hybrid model ) , where I explained in detail the methodology of the  project  .They 
proceeded by asking the information about the columns used and why only those were selected, the source of 
the data , the number of rows present , and related questions. They then asked me to tell the metrics of the 
model (R2_SCORE and the MSE error) and inquired about the mathematical formulas of the metrics 
and the intuition behind them.(Some questions such as “explain R2_score to a layman” were also asked. 
Then I was asked in detail (bohot depth me gaye) about XGBOOST and LSTM and the mathematical 
intuition behind them .I answered almost all the questions correctly and they were pleased with my 
fundamentals.They asked me about the gradient descent algorithm and how it works and its mathematical 
intricacies(fundamental understanding of coordinate geometry and curves is needed). Finally  I was asked a 
bit about GEN-AI . 
To wrap up the interview , I was asked  a simple DSA question.( Sieve of Eratosthenes) . The expectation 
was to write a working code  . I explained the brute force solution and then  explained in detail the optimal 
approach . I coded the solution (easy tha)          and they were pleased  by it(it seemed) .Next I was asked 
about the TC and  the SC  of the solution ,and I correctly answered it. The interview  concluded with me 
asking a question to the panel .  The round lasted around 40 minutes. 
 
Tips:    1. Have strong fundamentals of machine learning and  mathematics. 
            2. Be calm. 
             
 
4.Technical Round 2 :   (5 students appeared for this round) 
The interview started with my introduction to the panel and another discussion on my projects ensued. 
They asked many questions on the projects , the technical difficulties and the non technical difficulties which 
I faced (This was a group project). I was asked about gradient descent and was able to answer almost all 
the follow up questions on it . 
Following this, I was asked to design a chatbot for some application (I think this was to check the 
understanding of the software development cycle ). While I initially stumbled , I was able to rectify and 
refine my approach iteratively .  
Finally I was asked a guesstimate on the number of pizzas eaten on a Saturday night in India. The round 
lasted around 30 minutes. 
 
Tips: 1. In the guesstimate, I did all the calculations mentally , rather than on paper. This can help you . Also 
it is important to break the problem statement into smaller parts and then find the solution. 
2.Be calm. 
 
 
Round 5: HR ROUND (3 students appeared for this round): 
This was an informal round conducted by the MD of the company. It lasted around 10 minutes for me .It was 
just an informal chat wherein he asked me about my day , how do I feel about the situation and just some 
information on the company .  
Tips: 
1. A calm mind is the need of the hour .You might be put in unknown and extreme high pressure situations 
throughout the whole placement process and it is important to not lose your sense of reasoning . 
2. Prepare answers for standard HR questions beforehand (jot down the main points) and then try to relate all 
these points to weave a story . 
 
 
The interviews concluded by 7 pm on 12/09/25. After that, I departed for my home .But the results were not 
announced that night and also the following night .It was a really long wait and finally the results were 
announced on 15/09/25. I was selected finally. 
 
 
 
 
Resources: 
1.For Machine Learning and Deep Learning ,CampusX has the best playlist on YT. 
    1. Playlist name: 100 Days of Machine Learning 
    2. Playlist name:100 Days of Deep Learning  
    3.He is making some new playlists on advanced topics as well , do check it out . 
 
2.  3BLUE1BROWN (YT channel ) has some playlists on mathematics. Do check it out . 
3.For Puzzles: 
   Since this is a machine learning role , puzzles would be asked mostly on probability(like coins and cards),   
also you can refer to GFG for top 100 puzzles. 
4.DSA: Follow Striver’s sheet and then specifically pick some questions from a topic which can help you 
revise the entire topic. Just do those questions before the OA.(just a suggestion). 
 
 
 
General Tips and a small peek into my journey: 
 
1. My placement journey would not have been possible without the constant support of my 
parents and friends. Have a strong group of people around you who genuinely wish for your 
success. I feel blessed and lucky to have so many good people in my life. Also , be genuinely happy 
about others’ achievements. 
 
2. Believe in God’s plan.  
 
3. My placement journey lasted 78 days.I cleared the online assessments of General Mills (summer 
intern ) , PhonePE , ZETA , IDFC , BrowserStack ,  BlackRock , Mahindra and then finally AuxoAI. 
I was rejected in the initial rounds in General Mills ( was asked a NP hard problem) , PhonePE( I was 
not confident enough and thus underperformed ), IDFC (was asked about cloud, Springboot ( topics 
which I did not study) ), Browserstack. I reached the last round in ZETA  but was rejected. In 
BlackRock , I was not given a chance to  give an interview even after clearing the OA (was waitlisted 
). Throughout this process , I was not asked about any of the projects in even 1 of the interviews and 
then in AuxoAI , I was asked in detail about my projects(I honestly built the projects) . So , it was a 
bad streak of luck(for about 2 months) .The thing to note here is that it is fine to take a break of 1-
2 days after a rejection and then have a fresh start leaving everything behind . 
 
 
4. Patience is something which is quite underrated in this journey. While people around you might 
be in  a hurry to get placed, it is important to keep calm, think rationally, and then take any decision. 
  
5. Luck and the importance of timing cannot be understated in this journey. While consistently 
getting the toughest questions in OAs (randomized questions in OA)  broke me , I was really lucky 
that AuxoAI came for hiring. Luck evens out in the end (law of averages) but for luck to be on 
your side,  you should be ready to work really hard even in adversity. 
 
 
 
I sincerely hope that each one of you achieves more than what you dream of, finds great success, and be 
satisfied. May your batch perform even better than our batch.  
 
All the very best !! 
 
Feel free to contact me on WhatsApp : 8976801000 and LinkedIn: (19) Dhruv Deshpande | LinkedIn

Online Assessment Round: (36  Questions 120 minutes)
Technical Interview I
Technical Interview II
HR round

1) Online Assessment Round: The online test was conducted on the HackerRank platform and consisted of 36 questions, including 2 coding problems, several SQL queries, and questions on Operating Systems and Networking. This test was common for both the App Development and Associate Consultant roles, and candidates were shortlisted for the Associate Consultant interview based on their performance. The coding questions varied for each candidate; for me, one of the problems was the Valid Parentheses question, which can be easily solved using a Stack.

2) Technical Round I :   [27 students were selected for the technical interview]
The interview started after a PPT presentation from Oracle at around 12:00 PM.
It began with the question “Tell me something about yourself apart from your resume.”
 Be prepared for this in advance — try to include your strengths, hobbies, extracurricular activities, and any committee participation. Everything you mention should highlight how effective and valuable you can be for the company.After introducing myself, the interviewer asked me which programming language I was most proficient in. I said Java, as it’s my favorite language and I usually solve coding problems in it.
She then asked me a few OOPs questions — what is Abstraction, Polymorphism, why one should learn Java, and why Java is platform-independent.
 Since we had prepared well for topics like Collections Framework and Multithreading (as Oracle often asks these), I was confident. Next, she asked why I had chosen MongoDB for my projects. I had mentioned both MongoDB and MySQL in my resume, so I explained my choice based on schema flexibility and scalability, describing how MongoDB scales both horizontally and vertically.
 I also added that relational databases are equally important because they follow ACID properties, ensuring data integrity and security.  She seemed very happy with this answer.
She then asked about the machine learning algorithms I had used in my projects. One of the questions was to explain Naïve Bayes, which I had used during the initial phase of my project. I didn’t give a detailed example but explained how it works and why it’s effective.
Tip: If you’ve implemented any functionality, make sure you understand the high-level flow, how you implemented it, and how it actually works in the backend.
Later, she asked a few questions on Authorization and Authentication, including how JWT (JSON Web Token) works.
After that, she moved on to two basic DSA questions:
Swap two numbers without using a third variable.
Reverse a string.
For on-campus interviews, string-related questions are very common, so make sure to prepare linear data structures thoroughly.
Finally, she asked some basic SQL questions — definitions and the differences between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP commands. Some questions about View how does data in view table get updated even it does not support DML
After that, my interview concluded.

2) Technical Round 2:  [ around 20  students appeared for it]
Round 2 began with a quick greeting, and the interviewer immediately moved to a DSA question, asking for the solution in Java. The problem was: given an array of strings, convert all elements into camel case and then sort them based on the first character of each element. I wrote the complete solution, explained my approach, and he seemed satisfied with my explanation. After that, he asked two simple SQL questions — one on LEFT JOIN and another on a basic aggregate function. I solved both queries and also mentioned that if a similar question appeared, I could handle it using the GROUP BY clause.
Afterward, he reviewed my resume and asked me to elaborate on any one of my projects that I could explain well. I confidently replied that I could explain any of the three projects mentioned in my resume, so he asked me to choose one. I described the project in detail, and he didn’t interrupt or cross-question, indicating that my explanation was clear.
He then asked a few personal questions — where I was from and about my role as the Point of Contact for the Alumni and Mentorship Program at SPIT. My advice is to answer such non-technical questions smartly. You can add a touch of personality or humor to make the conversation more engaging and reduce nervousness. Interviewers usually appreciate candidates who are not only technically strong but also have good communication and interpersonal skills.
For me, this approach worked really well — the interviewer became more comfortable, and our interaction felt natural. We both enjoyed the conversation, and overall, the second round went very smoothly for me.
Round 3 : HR round : [ Around 12 students appeared for it]
The HR round was more of a formality. The HR asked a few basic questions such as my nationality, hobbies, and whether I was satisfied with the compensation offered. She also asked if I had any questions for her, to which I responded with two simple queries related to the company culture and growth opportunities.
After this round, there was a short waiting period of around 45 minutes while the panel discussed the results. Finally, the results were announced — 11 students were selected for the role, including 6 from MCA and 5 from B.Tech.

what

living,

about

It

to

to

personal

for

the

organization.

They

also

asked

me

how

my

interview

followed

up

with

questions

why

I

didn’t

continue

my

engineering

at

the

same

where

completed

my

diploma.

The

entire

10–15

Even

many

calm.

technical

skills.

●

Know

your

projects

well.

ready

to

explain

why

made

certain

decisions,

not

just

what

you

did.

should

be

able

to

defend

your

choices

confidently.

●

Think

out

loud.

go

completely

while

problems.

your

thought

process;

helps

keep

the

conversation

going

shows

how

you

approach

challenges.

●

Be

honest

if

you're

stuck.

It’s

okay

ask

for

a

hint

or

say

not

sure,

matters

is

how

you

handle

the

situation.

finalists).

To be honest I was struggling with HR rounds, and it was faith that they haven’t asked me anything in the HR round. I previously got rejected after HR rounds in Barclays too. So that was a setback for me. But UBS just saw my technical skills and was done. So it’s all luck. Don’t get discouraged, you have enough capabilities, to be honest I think maybe I could have cracked phonepay, jp morgan,etc. But due to discouragement of rejection at Barclays , i felt i cannot but that wasn’t true. My technical skills were good, the proof itself is that I haven’t given my 100% for this still got selected. So Believe in yourself and don’t get discouraged by small things and take the placement of your true capability not just what you are getting at the discouraged phase. journey.howSecured:
1. Online Assessment (OA) 
2. Technical Interview Round 
3. HR Interview Round 

1.     Online Assessment Round ( 197 Students ) ( 11/07/2025 ) 
UBS had a criteria of 7+ gpa till 3rd semester( I was in Summer breaks of 4th Sem to 5th Sem when the company came for internships).  So 226 Applicants Filled the google form but along with filling the google forms you also need to register on their website. Only 197 registered on their website and hence the rest were not eligible for OA round. Before OA round there were 2 assessments on their website 
UBS culture matching test 
Aptitude 
You can prepare for this just by searching about those on google/youtube ,etc. 

Next there was the OA round. 
It was a 90min Online Test on HackerRank. 
There were 15 java/dbms/data structure questions + 15 Aptitude questions + 1 DSA question 

Aptitude Questions included : 
Sets questions ( just revise the sets from 12th standard or DSGT)
Probability ( just revise class 12th probability) 
Basic graph interpretation ( class 10th graph knowledge would work)
Passage based questions  
For the passage based questions just remember to extract the relevant information only. Remember this is important. It will have a lot of irrelevant information and take a lot of time if you read it entirely. 

DSA Question:
They asked pretty easy questions. Just based on Arrays, HashMap, basic techniques like sliding window,prefix-suffix,etc. So just preparing for basics would also work, no need to go through DP on trees,etc. 
My question was: 
You will be given an array of size n. You need to divide the array in 2 parts such that the sum of the number of distinct elements from the left part and right part is maximum. You need to return that maximum sum.
constraints : 1<n<10e5 
Example : 3 1 4 1 5 
So here , if i partition them like 3 1 and 4 1 5 then no. of distinct elements of 3 1 is 2 and for 4 1 5 is 3 so sum is 5 , where as if i partition them like 3 and 1 4 1 5 then the no. of distinct elements would be 1 and for the 1 4 1 5 it would be 3 so sum is 4. But by partitioning 3 1 and  4 1 5 we got the sum as 5. So that is the maximum that we need to return. 

My Approach: 
So obviously brute force won’t work as constraints are 10e5, So what i want ? 
I want the left distinct +  right distinct as max. So , let’s think that i will try at every index that by partitioning at that index , what can be the sum and i will find the maximum among that. 
Ok , so it will take O(n) , now I need to find the no. of distinct elements from left and right in either O(1) or in O(n). So brute force is just finding the no. of distinct elements every time. What if we just precompute those. Yes, we will use the prefix and suffix approach and that’s it. We are good to go. 
You can check out the code at : https://pastebin.com/G7g3Pm2n 

So I advise that you focus on java and aptitude , dsa questions were pretty much doable. 
Just be chill, you can do it, don’t get too stressed, that’s the advice. 
2.     [Technical Interview ] [16 Students] 14/07/2025 
It was an offline face to face interview. 
So the first question they asked me was what’s your CGPA. I answered it, I guess I was the only one of
whom they wrote the GPA on the Resume. ( Maybe because it was  high(9.79)). Next they asked me about 
the Barclays minor as I was part of that. Next they asked me to introduce myself. 
Then the next question was what’s my strongest subject, what’s the subject that I don't like. 
Although I did say oops as my strongest subject they still asked only 3-4 theory questions and 1 written question. 
Next they moved on to the Data Structures, they asked me a lot of questions on this. And asked very basic algorithm questions. 
Then next they asked me 2 quizzes. One was on probability and other I avoided answering it. 
Then next they asked me some DBMS questions. Then they asked me about github, leetcode,codechef profiles. Then they moved on to some HR questions. Although it was technical round but still they asked me 
HR questions.(I don’t know whether other’s faced the same or not).Just make sure you attend the preplacement talk with them. That’s enough for the knowledge regarding the company. 
They also asked about my strengths, weaknesses, hobbies, extra-circular activities, where I live,what my parents do, etc all. Being a part of any committee and leading any position would work for extra circular activities. 

For OOPS :  java docs, Kunal Kushwaha, Durga Software Solutions and MOST IMP IS BY JUST RANDOMLY TRYING RANDOM CODES. I mean just write the random codes, what if i add static here , what if I add final here. 
For Data Structures : As i said java they asked how internally java Collections implement these Data Structures, So make sure you see the actual implementation. Next, preparing well for even Semester exams was ok(not sufficient) for this. Just have a curiosity while preparing for semester exams you will learn some 
Relevant things around the syllabus and that’s sufficient. 
For Algorithms : It was basic. Following any sheet might work. To be honest I didn't even refer to one. I just solved Random Questions. One of the key mentors is Sujal  Das  . Doing CP for this is extremely more than enough. 
For DBMS : Pretty Basic Questions on this. But College Syllabus is not enough for this, You have to prepare 
Well other than college syllabus. 

3.    [HR Round] [9 Students ] 14/07/2025 
     To be honest, for other people it was around 15-20 minutes grind. For me it was just 2 minutes of casual talk. They asked me where I live, what my parents do, from where I completed my 12th, why I didn't choose Walchand Sangli (I am from Solapur, I did my 12th from Walchand Solapur, They mis understood it as Sangli and hence asked). Also they asked what is Barclays Minor in my Resume. And that’s it, I have literally listed entire HR round questions. They just asked me these questions and for others it was literal grind. So if you do well in the technical round, HR will be just a formality. 
Finally 3 people got selected for Internships.

journey.prep:
Communication should be top notch; you don’t have to know everything in tech but can’t lack in 
communication and self-confidence. 
Get a good sleep one night before interview. In majority cases, OA shortlist is released one night before 
interview. I’d strongly suggest to get a good sleep rather than preparing all night for interview, I’ve regretted 
it every time.  
Finally, be patient. This was my 10th interview; I’ve failed 9 company interviews before ofss.  
I’ve seen people better than me getting into worse companies that came early, and also people less capable 
than me getting into better companies. 
There are a lot of uncertainties, and be prepared to handle them.  
And for OFSS,the HR literally told they have vacancy for everyone who came for interview, all we had to do 
is explain what we have done throughout our college, and be honest & confident. 
                               
Please feel free to connect and ask anything :LinkedIn

journey.howSecured:
Eligibility Criteria:   
     
 
1.OA [All unplaced,eligible btech & mtech students] 
On hackerrank platform. 
Had to be given from home due to heavy rains. 
95 minutes long test. 
3 sections:  Aptitude,Coding,Fundamentals 
 
Aptitude:[12 Questions] 
Question were easy to moderate 
Resource: Cocubes test series on testbook, https://testbook.com/cocubes 
 
Fundamentals:[20 Questions] 
They were on the tougher/advanced side. 
Topics: Cloud migration, Network layer(OSPF), DFS,etc. 
 
Coding:[2 Questions] 
Both were easy-moderate level, everyone had different questions. 
Q1. Request Rate Limiter 
• Given a list of requests with (userID, timestamp), determine whether each request should be allowed. 
• A request is allowed only if the user has made fewer than k requests in the last 1-minute window. 
Example: 
n = 3, user = [1, 1, 1], timestamp = [6, 10, 65], k = 2 
Output → [1, 1, 0] 
 
=>Implemented it using HashMap and deque. 

 
Q2.BFS(implemented using 3 hashsets(would recommend to use queue rather)). 
 
Last to last year when they came for same role,OA consisted of one rest api and one dsa problem but this time 
both were dsa. 
25 students were shortlisted. 
 
2.Tech(60%) +HR(40%) [25 students] 
Q.Introduce yourself. 
Q.Your Projects. 
Q.SQL vs NOSQL. 
Q.Stored procedure in sql(couldn’t answer it) 
Q.Update wherever name=adithya to adithya nair in sql (wasn’t really confident about my answer) 
Q.Primary key and forign key with examples,write it on paper 
Q.Write api’s in ur projects(wasn’t really confident about my answer) 
Q.C/C++? 
ME: “JAVA” 
Q.What are DTO?  
Me: “DTO In JAVAAAA??No idea,never heard bout it.” 
Q.Why ORACLE? 
Q.If you’ve all the resources on this planet what would you do? 
Me: “I would complete my major project” LOL 
Interviewer: “No something else” 
Me: “Oh okay since I have all the resources on this planet,would solve most important problem like building mechanism 
to utilize solar energy much more efficiently since there will be shortage of electric energy in future.” 
Q. How many 1cm side cubes can be fit in 9cm side cube? 
Q.Pillars of OOPS. 
Also while explaining my project “shit like that” slipped out of my mouth,I instantly apologized, she wasn’t 
looking happy about it. 
Overall techwise the round went terrible for me,I wasn’t expecting to be called for next round.Only thing that 
went well were hr questions and I was clear about what I knew and what I didn’t. 
 
3.Tech(25%) + HR(75%) [ I believe around 10-15 students were called] 
Q. Tell me your entire background, everything. 
Q.What went wrong with jee?(I had mentioned I couldn’t score well in jee) 
Q.About Projects, Hackathon. 
Q.Your project seems very basic, no ai, data ,or any buzzwords? 
Me: “I wanted to solve real life personal problems” 
Then for next 10 mins he was convincing me to join as a business analyst. 
Him: “I’ve 600 people working under me,400 developers and 200 B.A.’s, I respect B.A.’s more” 
I said tech excites me more than anything else, then eventually he asked me if I am willing to do DevSecOps, 
Without a second thought I agreed. He warned, it is super tough, barely any engineer under him completely 
understood K8s and if any problems occurs y’all are blamed first and fired. Then asked about anything I knew 
of devops,since I had taken cloud computing in last sem,I knew basics.  
Q.Explain docker, microservices,K8s 
Then he pulled out his phone, turned chatgpt on voice mode and asked me to learn about K8s right in front of 
him. The lady which took my first round came to the cabin as well. It felt weird, they both were sitting across 
the table and I was talking to gpt. 
Then asked about location preference and discussed bout why I prefer moving out ,and ended the round. 
Total 8 were selected.

1. Pre - Placement Talk: 24th June
2. Resume Screening: 27th June
3. Online Aptitude Test: 28th June
Further rounds took place offline on 2nd July
4. Group Discussion
5. Interview Round 1
6. Interview Round 2
7. HR Round
Resume Screening
Your resume is as very crucial a part of the entire selection process as any other. Building your
resume is a time consuming process, so allot enough time for it. Try to tailor your resume to the
role you are applying for.
All resumes are screened by an ATS (Applicant Tracking System), so you can check your score on
websites like “ResumeWorded”. My resume had a score of 72.
Key points regarding resumes -
They should be 1 page resumes as that’s what is expected from freshers.
Make single column resumes in Latex format.
Try to include all relevant coursework / competition / projects / internships in your resume.
Having 1-2 good finance projects on your resume helps.
Participate in case study competitions.
Do some finance certifications and add them onto your resume.
You can make minor changes to your resume that you are taking for your interviews. Results were
announced 1 day prior OA Test around 9. 
Online Assesment (67 Students were shortlisted)
The online test was conducted on campus. With a total of 45 marks, it consisted of 4
sections -
Finance & Accounting (10): This section contains mostly accounting and corporate finance
questions. I think it had 1 question about puttable bonds.
Market Awareness (10): This section contained quite a few economy questions and market
sentiment questions, I had something related to “ what is the exemption on taxes for investing
in government pension schemes”, so focus on market situations and terms, be aware of 
      current affairs just to be safe
Quantitative Aptitude (15): This section focused on permutations, probability, and algebra
questions. So this one is out and out mathematics.
Verbal Ability and Reading Comprehension (10): This is an English section, pretty simple if you
try to stick with the basics. 
The time given was 45 mins, so there is a time crunch as the quant section is tough, the VARC
section is easy but time consuming. So try to segregate the sections into time slots so you can
attempt as much as possible. 
The results for this round were announced a day before the final day i.e. 1st July. So don’t lose
heart in the process and be prepared.
Group Discussion  (37 students were shortlisted)
Group discussion Topic - “Central Banks' Diverging Paths Amid Geopolitical Stress - The Bank of
England maintains rates at 4.25% due to global uncertainty, while Norway and Switzerland have
opted for rate cuts. Explore how central banks should balance inflation control with growth risks,
particularly in the context of conflicts or trade wars.”
The moderators also introduced subtopics during the discussion. As far as I remember, these
included “Views on Forex reserves”, “What are the impacts of having different views and policy of
central banks”
Ensure you contribute at least 3–4 meaningful qualitative points.
Try to work as a team, acknowledge others points and add on to it.
Make sure you speak for 45 sec - 60 sec per point so the moderator takes note of you.
The discussion time was 20 mins and last 10 min were for summary
We had 3 panels for GD
Interview Round 1 (22 students were shortlisted)
The round consisted of accounting questions, Corporate Finance, puzzles, mental maths, market
awareness. The following are the questions that were asked to me. 
The change in depreciation and taxes and what are its effect on the financial statements.
Latest IPO and M&A
What is capital restructuring and why is it done.
I had made a DCF valuation project, so I was asked questions about it.
I was asked to calculate 57 × 63. Be sure to explain your approach.
Other people were also asked the values of roots i.e 2,3,10 etc.
I had done the forage investment banking simulation course, so a few questions on them.
The round lasted for 30-40 mins. I was last in panel but was called early which took me by shock.
If you are not able to answer anything don’t panic makes sure you tell the thought process and
approach for it. If you make a mistake or there is some misunderstanding in what you were
supposed to answer DO NOT PANIC, —your interview isn’t over. One or two mistakes are
acceptable so keep your head down and focus on answering the rest of the questions properly.
Once the GD is done you might receive the order of interview, but always be ready there can be
changes in last minute and you can be called anytime
Interview Round 2 (12-15 students were shortlisted)
This round was taken by the manager for CIB, the duration of this round was only 7-8 minutes. The
round consisted of 30-35 rapid fire questions. I was asked to explain the DCF valuation model I
had made. I was also asked questions on WACC, Beta, Financial Ratios, Talk about any stock for
30 seconds—its market capitalisation, stock value any and everything you know about it. I was
asked if I invested in stock, to which I answered no. I was able to answer all the questions correctly.
Make sure you are thorough with all the formulas.
My round 2 was scheduled a minute after my round 1 so be ready. Everything happens
simultaneously and can be chaotic, so be relaxed, focused and calm.
HR Interview (10 students were shortlisted)
This round was informal and relaxed, lasted for 10-15 mins. I was asked to briefly talk about my
resume and explain one of my leadership roles. I was asked about my family background. I was
asked did I know what exactly my job role is and how my past work and leadership experience can
help me to better in the internship.
10 students were selected for CIB banking role
Important Tips
1.The core essence of the process is not about how much you know but whatever you do,
how well-versed you are in it. So focus on learning things deeply rather than trying to do a lot
of things.
2.Resources
CFI courses - Accounting Fundamentals, Corporate Finance, Reading Financial Statements
Udemy - The complete investment banking 2025
Forage - Jp Morgan Investment banking job simulation
YouTube - DCF valuation, How are 3 financial statements linked, 2008 financial crisis, SVB
      bank collapse, what is SENSEX AND NIFTY, how is GDP calculated, Adani-Hindenburg saga,    
Puzzles - GFG 100 puzzles
Quants- IndiaBix.com
3. During interviews, always maintain proper posture, have a smile on your face, do not panic
even if you are unable to answer and at least let the interviewer know what approach you’re
thinking about.
4. The entire placement cycle is very hectic and stressful but it is important to stay in the present
and study without worrying about external factors like market situation, recession, etc. Believe
me, it never goes to waste. If you have prepared honestly, you will get opportunities.
5. If you have any questions,, I’ll be more than happy to help. You can reach out to me directly on
WhatsApp or Linkedin.
All the best

journey.howSecured: 1. Online Assessment [ 240 students appeared, 27 selected ] This was an online round, conducted offline at the college, with a duration of 1.5 hours. It consisted of 14 questions: 1 medium-level DSA coding question, 1 easy-level SQL query, and 12 MCQs. The MCQs focused on fundamental concepts of Java, OOPS, and DBMS. Make sure to review the core concepts of OOPS, DBMS, and basic SQL queries. For the coding question, submit your code even if it only passes partial test cases. 2. Technical Interview [ 27 students appeared, 15 were selected ] In this round, the interviewer focused mainly on my resume, and the interview lasted about 20 minutes. He began by asking me to share something about myself that wasn’t included in my resume. He then asked me to explain each project listed on my resume and the motivation behind them. I explained why I chose each project. I gave an overview of the features, frameworks/languages used, and the event flow for each project. He also asked in-depth questions about the keywords in my project section, like APIs and machine learning models. He asked, "What are APIs?", "What are API response codes?", "What is an API token and why is it important?", and "Have you built an API?" For the college recommendation app I worked on, I explained the ML model, even though it was handled by another team member, emphasizing the need to fully understand all aspects of a project. The interviewer pointed out flaws in my projects, and I explained my approach to fix them and why the issues occurred. For example, in a 24-hour hackathon, time constraints prevented full implementation. He also asked how I would implement security layers in each project. We discussed the Flutter framework and Firebase. He asked if I had experience with NoSQL databases, to which I responded that Firebase Realtime Database is a NoSQL database. When asked about AWS and Kafka, I admitted I had read about them but didn’t have in-depth knowledge. Lastly, he presented a scenario: if a transaction occurred in Mumbai at 11:20, followed by another in Pune 20 minutes later, how would I detect fraud? I acknowledged that I wasn't sure of the exact technology to use, but my approach would involve calculating the time difference and distance between the two locations to determine if the transaction was possible. For this round, it's important to answer honestly. You’re not expected to know everything, but relate what you do know to the topic. 3. HR Interview Round [ 15 students appeared, 13 were selected ] This round was mainly HR-focused, but the interviewer also asked some basic technical questions. It lasted about 20-25 minutes. He began by asking which programming languages I’ve worked with. I mentioned that my primary language is C++, but I also have knowledge of Java, Python, and Dart. Then he asked me to explain Object-Oriented Programming, what polymorphism is, where I’ve implemented it, and the difference between the two types of polymorphism. After that, the HR questions started. He asked what challenges I faced during my internship. I explained that I encountered issues deploying the app on the Play Store due to Google policy conflicts, and I described how I resolved those issues. Next, he asked why I chose Barclays and followed up with a few more questions based on my response. He then presented a hypothetical situation: What would I do if a superior said something rude to me in a meeting? He also asked how I would handle it if a junior told me I had spoken rudely to them, and how I would manage two team members arguing during a meeting if I were the team leader. For these questions, ensure your answers align with the company's values. He also asked me to describe a situation where I experienced conflict with teammates and to share an experience where I led a team. I described my experience as the Mudra domain head here. For HR questions, it's important to understand the company’s values and tailor your answers accordingly. 13 students were offered the Summer Internship.

1.   	Technical Test (240 students appeared, 27 selected)
During my technical test, which lasted 1.5 hours, I encountered questions across SQL, Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA), and Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) concepts. The test was a mix of multiple-choice questions (MCQs), which asked for the output of given programs, and theory-based questions. There were also some specific questions about inheritance, exploring the fundamentals of OOP.
One of the SQL tasks required me to write a query that extracted the month from a date column and filtered the results to show only those where the month was October. This combination of theoretical and practical questions tested both my conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills in real-time.
Additionally, the technical test featured a high-weightage DSA question where points were awarded based on the number of test cases passed. The problem was quite challenging, with 8 hidden test cases and 2 visible ones. The task required constructing the lexicographically smallest string of length m+n−1, given two input strings of length m and n. The second string contained only 'T' and 'F', and wherever there was a 'T', I had to copy the entire first string from the start. For positions marked by 'F', the substring starting from that character in the result needed to be unequal to the first string. The solution had to return -1 if it was impossible to construct such a string. This problem tested my understanding of string manipulation and logic-based problem-solving.

2.     Technical Interview Round (27 students appeared, 15 selected)
I was first asked to introduce myself, after which the focus shifted to DBMS JOINS. I had to draw Venn diagrams representing the different types of joins and write queries for each. The interviewer provided two tables, "employee" and "department," and asked me to explain the different joins—inner, left, right, and full—and how they differ.
We also discussed my projects, and I was asked to write basic for and while loops. The interviewer then posed an interesting question about the while loop: whether incrementing the loop variable before or after the statements inside the loop would make a difference.


3.    HR Round (15 appeared, 13 selected)
In my HR round, the interviewer started by asking me to introduce myself and talk about my projects. Then, I was presented with a few scenarios.
In one scenario, I was part of a team of six, and both I and another person were assigned the same task by the line manager, who was supposed to distribute different tasks to everyone. The other person completed the task first and received appreciation. I responded that I would review their work and aim to improve it from my perspective.
Another scenario involved working in a team of two, where my teammate had no knowledge of the required tech stack, and we had a deadline. I explained that I would provide resources, help them learn the necessary concepts, and work together to meet the deadline.
Finally, I was asked to explain and differentiate between machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, data analytics, and supervised learning.

[ 13 students were offered the job ]

1. Technical Round 
• For this round, I would recommend refreshing all the CS core subjects you have studied in 
earlier sems. Most common questions were regarding OOPs, DBMS, DS, CCN, etc.  Regarding 
the interview itself, first the interviewer will ask you to introduce yourself. Its crucial to 
prepare a good introduction for yourself and to present it confidently. Ideally, it would 
include your academic background, achievements, and something personal like your 
hobbies. They might ask a few questions about your hobbies, so be prepared to answer the 
same. 
• Next, they might ask you about the CS fundamentals in different subjects. You need to 
answer these confidently, and seek no validation from the interviewer. My interviewer gave 
no reaction at all beyond a ‘yes’ or an ‘okay’ to all my answers, which slightly threw me off. I 
later found out that this is just something they do to test the confidence of the candidates, 
so do not panic if your interviewer does the same. 
• You might also be asked some questions pertaining to your particular skill set. Since I had 
mentioned my Competitive Programming profiles on my resume, my interviewer asked me 
about my favourite problem that I had solved. 
• Next, I was asked to explain some of the projects on my resume. Make sure to review all your 
projects before going, as they do ask some very intricate questions regarding those. Try to 
convey as much information as possible in your answers, and for the umpteenth time, be 
confident. Depending on how specialized your project is, the interviewer may not know 
about the technologies in detail, so you can get away with making some statements that are 
not entirely true, if you are confident enough. 
  
 
 
 
2. Techno-HR Round (15 candidates appeared for this round) 
 
• This round was purely HR for some, and was a mix of techno-HR for others. The technical 
questions were not too different from what were asked in the first round, but some of the 
HR questions were very tricky. 
• In my case, no matter how I answered, the interviewer seemed to dislike my answer, and 
would try to debate with me about it. You don’t have to agree with the interviewer on every 
single point they raise, but be polite if you want to express that you disagree.  
• If you did well on the technical questions in the round, you should mostly be fine even if the 
HR section was not that great.

Online Assessment 
The process began with an online assessment that covered Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), SQL, and Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA). This round lasted approximately 1.5 hours and was conducted online. Out of an initial pool of 200 applicants, 27 were selected for this round. The criteria for selection were based on knowledge of OOPS, DSA, SQL i.e the score of the online assessment.
I prepared for this round revising the basic and advanced concepts of OOPS and DSA. Solved problems on platforms like LeetCode and practiced timed coding sessions to improve speed and accuracy. I didn’t prepare for SQL but anyways we had it in our semester so I retained certain syntax and concepts when encountering SQL-related questions during the assessment.
Technical Round
This face-to-face interview lasted about 20 mins. Of the 200 candidates from the online assessment, 27 were selected for this round. The selection criteria included performance in JAVA, CS fundamentals and relevant project experience.
The technical interview was both challenging and comprehensive, designed to assess various aspects of my programming knowledge and problem-solving skills. The interviewer began by probing my motivation with a direct question: "Do you even want to be a programmer and why?" Following this, the focus shifted to my projects, where the interviewer meticulously examined my work, pointing out potential loopholes and challenging me to defend my design decisions. They were particularly interested in the bugs I had encountered and resolved during my project development. Then I was presented with three Java code snippets and asked to predict their outputs. The scope broadened to include questions about UNIX, though the specific queries escape my recollection. Finally, the interviewer asked about RESTful APIs.
I should’ve read about UNIX/OS fundamentals thoroughly as I was unable to answer those questions. Secondly I should’ve already thought about the loopholes my projects have.
HR Round
This final round lasted about 45 minutes. Out of the 27 candidates from the technical round, 15 were selected for this stage. The main criteria were technical proficiency and cultural fit. 
It began with a standard request to introduce myself, followed by an inquiry into why I chose Barclays specifically. The interviewer then took an unexpected turn, leveraging my earlier mention of stock investing to test my financial acumen by asking me to derive the Fixed Deposit (FD) formula. This led to a discussion on risk management, where I was asked to differentiate between risk and loss, including strategies for risk mitigation. The focus then shifted to my career aspirations, with questions about my professional goals and the timeline I envisioned to achieve them. The interview concluded with a situational question that assessed my ability to handle a delicate professional scenario: how to address concerns about a senior manager's plan during a conference meeting while maintaining professionalism.
In this round, the focus is on highlighting my non-technical skills. Alongside my technical expertise, I have actively engaged in various extracurricular activities. I smartly mentioned all the extra curricular activities I have participated in and made the interviewer understand that I am a perfect fit for the company and I am ready to adapt all the technology and values followed in that company.

2.     Technical Interview (Out of 27 students who appeared, 15 were selected for next round) 
This round lasted for about 25-30 minutes. The process began with the interviewer asking me to introduce 
myself, followed by a few questions related to my resume. Since I'm from Jammu and currently studying 
in Mumbai, they asked why I chose to come so far for my education. They also inquired about my interest 
in the IT sector and whether I genuinely wanted to pursue a career in this field. This was a brief 
conversation before the technical questions started. 
Next, I was asked to explain one of the projects I had listed on my resume. I selected a project and went 
into detail about it. The interviewer asked why I chose specific technologies for the project (e.g., "Why 
did you use Next.js instead of React?"). The y also wanted to understand the relevance of the project: 
whether it had any real-life application and if it was solving a real-world problem. 
After that, we moved on to questions related to computer science fundamentals. I was given real -life 
scenarios and asked how I would solve certain problems. One question I remember was about withdrawing 
money from an ATM. The question was: If money is debited from your account but not dispensed by the 
ATM, what could be the issue and how would you resolve it? 
Another technical question involved synchronizing two APIs: If the result of the first API is used as input 
for the second, how would you avoid any errors or overlaps during this process? . Then, the interviewer 
asked few questions on OOPS and DBMS. 
 
To clear this round, it’s important to be thoroughly prepared with your resume  and solid in your 
understanding of computer science fundamentals. 
 
2. HR [Out of 15 students who appeared, 13 were selected] 
The interview started with the typical question: “Introduce yourself.” After that, I was asked a series of 
behavioral and personal questions, including: 
• When did you take a position of responsibility? What challenges did you face, and how did you 
overcome them? 
• How many members are there in your family? Do you often have conflicts with your siblings? 
• Can you share an experience where you worked in a team, and there were differences in opinions? 
How did you resolve the conflict or handle clashes between your views and those of your team 
members? 
The interviewer also wanted to assess my general awareness and asked for my opinion on the current 
situation in Gaza and the Israel conflict. This round lasted around 20-25 minutes. 
I wasn’t fully prepared for this type of questioning, but I stayed honest and answered each question 
based on the STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) approach. It’s crucial to stay calm and composed. 
Even if you don’t have an immediate answer, take a moment to think it through and respond confidently.  
That said, it’s always a good idea to practice these types of questions beforehand with friends or family 
through mock interviews. This helps you prepare and handle such rounds more smoothly.
