journey.howSecured: 1. Technical Round (27 candidates appeared for this round) There were Questions about OOP, Databases, Docker, AWS majority of which were used in my projects that i mentioned. To Prepare for this round i had gone through all of my projects even ones not listed in my resume but uploaded on my github. I have also Covered my basics of OOP, Python, API, AWS Cloud basics(EC2, S3 Bucket),Docker (API Specifically used in my Docker monitoring tool), Databases (Structured & Non Structured). Also some Situational based Questions that i had prepared form online forums and Websites like GeekForGeek, Javatpoint, etc 2. HR Round (15 candidates appeared for this round) In this round Situational and Technical Questions were asked as for technical questions i had already prepared for round 1 it same process was repeated and as for the Situational based questions they had to be answered honestly as they were based on what was my personal Opinion/Action that i would have taken or will take in case xyz Situation happened. Some Questions were also related to companies like what are the Values of Barclays (RISES) these had to be studied from the official website & Wikipedia of Barclays. Example Questions: 1. What are values of Barclays(RISES) 2. Why Barclays ? 3. When did I lose my Integrity in any situation? 4. What is Risk ? 5. What if Risk is going to cost us loss? What will be my action ? 6. If there are 2 ropes burning uneven thickness taking 1 hr to burn from start to end i had to measure the 45 min mark.

Placement Process 
This company is very approachable if you have a strong command of C++. 
After not receiving a PPO from my internship at Barclays, I hadn't prepared much for the final placements as
journey.prep:
This company is a great fit for you if you know C++ well. In addition to DSA, you should focus on 
advanced C++ concepts: 
• OOPs principles (especially the internal working of virtual functions). 
• Templates 
• Multithreading (e.g., spinlocks) 
• Smart Pointers (unique_ptr, shared_ptr)  
• Implementing your own string and vector classes. 
For these topics, I highly recommend the YouTube playlist by Keerti Purswani. 
In my opinion, the most challenging part of the process is the OA because you need to know basic Python 
for the coding question. I learned the required Python syntax in 4-5 days by solving problems on 
HackerRank. 
Overall, I would say this is a very achievable company to crack. Even though I was unprepared after my 
internship at Barclays, I was able to cover all the necessary topics in about a week. Another plus is that they 
never ask about your projects.

journey.howSecured:
This company is very approachable if you have a strong command of C++. 
After not receiving a PPO from my internship at Barclays, I hadn't prepared much for the final placements as 
I had been fully focused on my internship. I consider myself lucky because Dolat Capital had already visited 
the campus once while I was interning, but they returned for a second round of hiring. This time, students 
who had applied previously were not eligible, which created a new opportunity for people like me. 
 
Online Assessment (OA) 
For the OA, only 20 students were shortlisted, mostly from MCA/M.Tech programs and those who hadn't 
applied during the company's first visit. The assessment consisted of five sections. 
1. C++ MCQs: The questions were quite tricky. Some were based on concepts like the static and 
volatile keywords. 
one question  was like  
class Person{ 
string name; 
Person(string name){ 
name=name;     //what will happened here  
}  
}; 
 
 
 
Int main(){ 
Person p1(“sumit”); 
Printf(“my name is %s”, p1.name);// so basically when constructor is called without this  
//As compiler in person class do not know about which name is used it just assigned its value to itself 
//and does not touches the class data member basically in constructor this was required; 
 
} 
 
2. Python MCQs: I had never coded much in Python, but the questions were manageable if you 
understood basic syntax like for loops and array slicing (e.g., arr[:-1]). 
3. Python Coding Question: The task was to remove outliers from a given array. An outlier was

o upper = mean + standard_deviation 
o lower = mean - standard_deviation I used NumPy's standard functions, np.mean() and 
np.std(), to solve this. There seemed to be a compiler issue on the platform; the same code 
that compiled once failed on a subsequent submission. I made sure to submit my working 
code and not touch it again, and I reported the incident to the placement cell. 
4. C++ Coding Question: I was asked to design a parking system, which I felt was the most difficult 
question among all the candidates. The pricing logic was as follows: 
o If 1 vehicle is in the parking lot, the charge is ₹100 per car. 
o If 2 vehicles are present, the charge is ₹200 per car. 
o If 3 or more vehicles are present, the charge is ₹300 per car. 
The input consisted of a car's name, start time, and end time. You had to implement a Parking class 
to calculate the total cost for each car. 
Input: 
A 10 20 
B 10 20 
A 15 20 
A 30 40 
Output: 
Cost for A is 400  // (100 for 10-15) + (200 for 15-20) + (100 for 30-40) 
Cost for B is 100 
As a competitive programmer (subtle flex, lol), this was quite easy for me. While it could have been 
solved with a brute-force approach, I had seen this problem before and implemented an optimal 
solution using a sweep line algorithm. 
5. Aptitude: The questions were a mix of easy and tough problems. 
      OA Tip: To clear the assessment, focus on the Python and C++ coding questions. The test cases seemed 
limited, so even a brute-force solution could potentially pass. 
 
After the OA, 5 students were shortlisted for interviews. 
 
Interview Round 1 (In-Office) 
This round was held at their office and covered technical and quantitative topics. 
Technical & DSA Questions 
1. What is abstraction? I was asked to explain the concept and provide a code example, detailing how 
virtual functions work internally. 
2. Difference between struct and class in C++ 
struct Node { 
    int data; 
    Node* next; 
}; 
Then, I explained the difference between a struct and a class in C++. Many people confuse C 
structs with C++ structs. I knew the key difference is that members of a struct are public by 
default, whereas members of a class are private by default. The interviewer seemed impressed, and 
at that moment, I felt confident I would clear the technical round. 
3. Linked List Reordering: I was asked a common LeetCode problem: reorder a linked list to connect 
the i-th node to the (n-i)-th node. 
o Input: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 
o Output: 1 -> 4 -> 2 -> 3 I didn't need to pretend to think about it. I immediately gave the 
optimal solution: find the middle of the list using a slow and fast pointer, reverse the second 
half, and then merge the two halves. I wrote the full code on paper, which took almost two 
pages, ensuring it was clean and modular with separate functions for each step. 
Probability & Statistics Questions 
The next interviewer started with quantitative questions. 
1. Expected value of a fair six-sided die? (Answer: 3.5) 
2. Expected number of rolls to get a 6? (Answer: 6) 
3. He then asked me to write a recurrence relation for the expected number of rolls to get a 5 followed 
immediately by a 6. I wasn't sure how to formulate the exact recurrence relation, so I wrote down the 
basic recursion logic, and he was satisfied with that. 
4. Distributions: I was asked to name some common distributions. I mentioned Binomial, Normal, 
and Uniform distributions. He followed up by asking for the PDF (Probability Density Function) 
and CDF (Cumulative Distribution Function) of each, which I knew. 
5. Sum of Normal Distributions: The final question was how to derive the distribution of 
N_3=N_1+N_2, where N_1 and N_2 are independent normal distributions. I didn't know the exact 
proof but tried to formulate an approach using variable transformations to show that I don't give up 
easily. 
 
 
HR Interview 
The HR interview was more of a formality. The questions were standard: 
• Tell me about yourself. 
• What is your CGPA? 
• Tell me about your family background. 
• What are 3 of your greatest strengths and 3 of your weaknesses? 
 
Interview Round 3 (Online C++ Round)(confirmatory round which was online) 
Two students were shortlisted for this final online round, which took place the next day. 
1. Implement a Data Structure: I was asked to implement a class with the following functionalities: 
o add(a): Adds a number to a stream. 
o avg(): Returns the average of the last k numbers added. I immediately proposed an 
optimized approach using a queue. We can push elements into the queue. If the queue size 
exceeds k, we pop from the front. This maintains a window of the last k elements. 
He then added a follow-up: 
o update(new_k): The value of k can be changed. For this, I suggested using a std::vector 
and a prefix sum array. With a prefix sum array, we can find the sum of the last k elements 
in O(1) time. He then asked if it was possible to implement it without the extra space of the 
prefix sum array. I thought about it for a bit, and he said it was okay and moved to the next 
question. 
2. Delete a Node in a Doubly Linked List: This was a straightforward question. First, he asked me to 
write the struct for a doubly linked list node. 
C++ 
struct Node { 
    int data; 
    Node* next; 
    Node* prev; 
}; 
Then, he asked me to write a function to delete a node given only a pointer to that node. This is my 
implementation: 
C++ 
void deleteNode(Node* ptr) { 
    if (ptr == nullptr) { 
        return; 
    } 
 
    // If the node to be deleted is not the head 
    if (ptr->prev != nullptr) { 
        ptr->prev->next = ptr->next; 
    } 
 
 
    // If the node to be deleted is not the tail 
    if (ptr->next != nullptr) { 
        ptr->next->prev = ptr->prev; 
    } 
 
    // Free the memory to avoid a memory leak 
    delete ptr; 
} 
After I wrote the code, he asked me what a memory leak is. I was prepared for this and explained it 
thoroughly. This is a very common interview question, so it's good to practice it. My code was 
exactly what he was looking for, and I was confident I would be selected. 
In the end, I was the only one selected from this round. Previously, they had hired two others, bringing the 
total to three students.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
This company is a great fit for you if you know C++ well. In addition to DSA, you should focus on 
advanced C++ concepts: 
• OOPs principles (especially the internal working of virtual functions). 
• Templates 
• Multithreading (e.g., spinlocks) 
• Smart Pointers (unique_ptr, shared_ptr)  
• Implementing your own string and vector classes. 
For these topics, I highly recommend the YouTube playlist by Keerti Purswani. 
In my opinion, the most challenging part of the process is the OA because you need to know basic Python 
for the coding question. I learned the required Python syntax in 4-5 days by solving problems on 
HackerRank. 
Overall, I would say this is a very achievable company to crack. Even though I was unprepared after my 
internship at Barclays, I was able to cover all the necessary topics in about a week. Another plus is that they 
never ask about your projects.

journey.howSecured:
1. Online Assessment [219 candidates had applied] 
Platform: DoSelect || Questions: 4 || Time: 1hr 30mins 
 
I would advise you to skim through all the questions first and start with the one which seems familiar/ 
easy. I started with Q3, which I solved in 7–8 minutes. Then I moved to Q1, got stuck on an edge 
case due to limited debugging options, but managed to solve it in 20 minutes. I spent the rest of the 
time on Q2, implemented a recursive solution, and passed a few test cases. 
 
 
1) You were given n people and 2 array A and B of size m, where each pair (A[i], B[i]) means that 
A[i] is a friend of B[i]. Also, friendships are transitive, so if x is a friend of y and y is friend of z, 
x is also friend of z.   You were told to find the minimum no of new friendship  such that 
everyone is friend is each other.  
Approach: The question can be easily solved by counting the no of components. I used DSU to 
find the no of co nnected components and return it -1, A DFS or BFS approach would have 
worked too. 
 
2) You were given an array A which represented the laddoos given to n employees. Each person 
must receive atleast 1 and atmost m laddoos. You had to assign laddoos to employed who had 
received 0 laddoos such that the absolute difference between two employees is not more than k. 
And finally, you had to print the no of valid ways distributions.  
Approach: I thought of writing a recursi ve sol ution first and then  optimizing it using  
memoization, but was only able to solve 5 test case . Thought of debugging it but the platform 
didn’t allow to see  print statements  (tho after  the test I got to know that you can see print 
statements via custom inputs). Gave approx. 45 mins to this problem but was not able to solve it 
completely 
 
3) You had to find the count of unordered pair such that their sum is s and the total of set bits in both 
the number is <=k 
 
Approach: As the constraint was small enough for O(N2) to work but I solved it in O(N) as it 
was quite similar to the famo us 2 sum problem . So used a map to store numbers and if the 
complement (s-a[i]) is present in the map checked for the set bit condition.   
 
4) The question didn’t specify the no of edges so didn’t even look at this question as I had no practice 
on how to take input of this kind. However, as the question only needed to print possible or not 
possible and each test case having only one result so just printing possible was enough to get 6/8 
testcase right. And further as one of the wrong testcase was the sample one so hard coded it and 
got 7/8 right.  Well, they did mention that code quality was being considered but taking  into 
consideration that no one was able to solve this optimally and almost everyone printed possible, 
this question may as well have not been considered for the selection. 
 
I solved 2 problems completely and 2 partially which was enough for being selected for the next round.  
 
2. [Technical Round 1] [ 30 students appeared] 
All the 30 students were divided into 3 panels of 10 each. I was part of the 1st panel. 
 
The interviewer introduced himself and ask for mine as well. I ke pt my into short as I wanted more 
time for the 2 problems. 
 
Question 1: Find the peak element in a  2d matrix. Where peak element is defined as the element 
which is greater than its 4 adjacent neighbors. 
 
Before starting the question, I made to fully understand the problem by clarified the constraints, is it 
4-directional or 8-directional adjacency. I started with the brute force solution which was to iterate 
and see if the condition is met. 
 
Then I showed him how monotonicity is maintained in a 1d array  for finding the peak element  and 
how we can use binary search to implement it. Thought of flattening the 2d array and applying binary 
search on it. However soon found out that it does not work. With the help of some hints from the 
interviewer, found the optimal solution which involved binary search with the search space as the 
range of rows/cols. He then asked me to code the solution of paper. 
 
Question 2: You were given a tree and q queries . Each query had a start node, an end node and a 
destination. The task was to find the node which is at a minimum distance from destination while 
also being on the path from start to end node. 
 
Ex: Consider the n-ary tree  
And the query [2,5,7]. 
 
The path from 2 to 5 would be 2->1->3->5 and out of all the node the node 3 is at minimum distance 
from 7 so the answer is 3. 
 
It started by saying that we can precompute the distance between all pair of nodes (MSSP algorithm) 
by using Floyd -Warshall algorithm and then for each query find the path using dfs/bfs while also 
maintaining a parent array to track the path. And using the parent array to trace the path we see which 
node has the minimum distance from destination.  
 
However, as the distance matrix takes O(N 3) time to compute, it wasn’t optimal so the interviewer 
asked me look the answer in terms of LCA  (Lowest common ancestor) . I tried to find some 
observations from the testcase  and found that the answer can be one of the LCA  (start, end), LCA 
(start, destination) and LCA (end, destination). Once these 3 nodes are  found we can calculate the 
minimum distance from the destination. However, it was not optimal and time was up so left it there. 
 
The interviewer then asked for any questions for him. I had researched about it and asked him. 
 
 
I was not able to solve both the question however don’t let it demotivate you. The interviewer is more 
interested on how you approach the question so be open to hi m and read out your thoughts out loud 
and ask him for any hints if needed. 
 
To save some time, from each panel 3 were fast-tracked to give the HR round before 2nd tech round.  
 
 
3. [Technical Round 2] [ 14 students appeared] 
My 2nd tech round happened after my HR round. And similar to 1st tech round we were asked to solve 
2 questions. I was not asked for my intro this time. 
 
Problem 1: Given a matrix of size m*n, each element had a heat value which I gained if I landed on 
it, I had to return the minimum heat with which I could reach bottom right corner from top left corner 
under the following constraints: 
1. I could move left, right, bottom or top. 

 
2. I could not retrace my path at any point. 
3. I couldn’t move the same direction more than 3 times. 
 
I initially approached the problem using BFS, but since we’re trying to minimize a cumulative cost 
(heat), I pointed out that Dijkstra’s algorithm would be more suitable here. 
 
I took 5 state s in my heap as heat, x, y, prevDirection, countOfPrevDirection and implemented the 
standard Dijkstra with the constraint on the paper while considering the code quality as well . I was 
asked a follow up that what if I had to move k steps before changing direction. I handled that as well 
 
Problem 2: The exact problem from leetcode 
I started with a greedy solution which as expected didn’t work on a few cases. Then I thought about 
dp to which the interviewer said  I was on the right track. I was able to find the state which is quite 
similar to 0/1 Knapsack but the interviewer was not satisfied. I then dry runed the test cases given by 
him and my solution worked. He was satisfied by m y answer till the end of interview I then asked 
him what would the optimal solution be . He opened the  leetcode question itself and showed the  
editorial. The editorial had the same solution as mine. He then shook hands with me and said “Well 
Done”.   
 
  
4. [Hiring Manager Round] [ 11 students appeared] 
 
PhonePe’s HR round isn’t a typical HR round; it revolves more around the resume so be have good 
projects on it and (internship if any). 
 
The interviewer was the engineer manager at PhonePe. He started by asking me to walkthrough my 
projects. Since two of them were hackathon-winning projects, I had a clear strategy on how to present 
them: I first explained the problem or need, then walked him through how I approached and solved 
it, which helped build curiosity around the tech stack I had used. He asked me about jwt and RSA 
algorithm. I was not sure about the e xact implementation of it but gave  a rough idea to him. In one 
of the projects, I had worked on the entire software development lifecycle , and I made sure to 
highlight that experience specifically. 
 
I also made sure to explain him about a devOps experiment that I had done which wasn’t mentioned 
on my resume. He was quite impressed by this. 
 
He then asked me about my favorite app and its most used feature and I answered with reddit. 
He went forward to ask me to implement the post feature  from the DB selection to the schema and 
optimizations (Pagination, caching, etc.). 
 
He then followed with typical HR question. I gave honest and diplomatic answers to him  using real 
life examples. 
 
 
 
 
 
I was one of the first to have concluded with all the rounds so had to wait 4 hours for the results t o 
be announced  
 
7 students received the offer.

journey.prep:
1. For OA prepare all the topics. Should know all the common patterns and able to solve 
LeetCode medium- hard problems. 
2. Can follow Striver’s series but I also recommend to do  blind 75 questions 
https://leetcode.com/studyplan/leetcode-75/ - for clearing up basics before proceeding to the 
advance topics. 
3. Stay calm and confident during Interview. Think out loud during the technical interviews. 
Even while coding it out keep on explaining and discussing the approach.  
4. Interviewers are helpful in case if not able to proceed they can give hints, after hints try to 
think on them as they give idea about how to proceed to a particular problem. 
5. Doing CP (Competitive Programming)  is highly recommended as this year CP topics were 
asked. Participating in contests on platforms like Codeforces can significantly enhance your 
problem-solving skills and help you get accustomed to the pressure of live contests. 
All the Best for your placements 
 
Feel free to reach out for any doubts and guidance, 
 https://www.linkedin.com/in/venisha-kalola-997756258/

journey.howSecured:
1. OA ( Coding Round) [All those who applied (200+)] 
Patform : DoSelect || 90 minutes || 4 Questions 
Each Question has 100 points (Total 400 points)  
1. 1. There are some n friends and needed to find components, as soon as I read the question I 
understood it was a DSU (Disjoint Set Union) or Union-Find question so I wrote the DisJoint 
Class and was able to solve this question within 10-15 minutes. It was simple just had to count 
the total components. 
I was able to pass all test cases (12/12 testcases). 
2. You are given an array of length n representing the number of laddoos distributed to n 
people standing in a line. Each person must receive at least 1 and at most m laddoos. Some 
people have already been assigned laddoos (represented as numbers between 1 and m), 
while others are yet to be assigned and are marked with a 0 in the array. 
Your task is to assign laddoos to the unassigned positions (i.e., the 0s in the array) such that 
the final array satisfies the condition: for every pair of adjacent people, the absolute 
difference between the number of laddoos they receive is less than or equal to k. You need 
to determine the total number of valid ways to make these assignments such that all 
constraints are satisfied. 
 
For Example :  n=3, m=5, k=3.    Array = [5 3 0] 
Expected Output : 5 
 
Solution : So for the last person as we can assign (1 to m i.e. 5 laddoos) as the adjacent 
element is 3 the condition of <=k holds so here I have 5 different ways  
( [5 3 1], [5 3 2],..,  [5 3 5]) 
My Approach : I was able to solve it partially I used recursion , it could also be further 
memorized for all testcases to pass. 
 
 
 
3. Given an Array of n elements have to find 2 elements whose sum is equal to m and the bit 
addition is <=k. Suppose sum should be 10 and I have elements 6 (110 in binary) and 4 (100 
in binary) 
So for 6( the bit sum will be 2 + 1 = 3) and for 4 (2) 
The total sum 3+2 =5 and if it is not more than k it will be considered. 
 
My Approach : I had sorted the array (Time Complexity : nlogn) so that I can use 2 pointer 
concept to find sum = m, and if the sum condition holds then I check the bit condition . 
For checking bit condition ran loop to all bit position from 0->31  
Suppose we have             0 1 0 1 0 1  ( left is msb while right is lsb) 
position :  5 4 3 2 1 0 
sum :          4 + 2 + 0 = 6 (so this way easily can just add the positions of 1) 
I was able to solve this question fully (8/8 testcases) 
 
4. Sorting Hat : You are given n students and m, the maximum number of students allowed per 
house. There are four houses: Slytherin, Gryffindor, Hufflepuff, and Ravenclaw. Each student 
has a list of preferred houses they can be assigned to. Additionally, some pairs of students are 
friends and must be placed in different houses. Assign each student to one of their preferred 
houses such that no house exceeds capacity m and no friends share the same house. Determine 
if such an assignment is possible. 
Solution : It can be solved using backtracking as can assign in a particular friend group n try 
different ways and in end if all get assigned can print “Possible” else “Not Possible” 
I was able to solve it partially. 
 
Tip : When the number of friend relations is not specified in the input, using Scanner in Java 
is not ideal, as it relies on knowing how many inputs to read. In such cases, BufferedReader 
is preferred since it allows reading input line by line until the end. This makes it important to 
understand how to handle different input formats across programming languages. 
In total I was able to solve 2 questions fully while other 2 partially. I had solved question 1 and then 
jumped to question 3 n then proceeded to solve it completely. I think had around 50 minutes to try 
ques 2 and 4 and was able to do that both partially. Total 30 candidates were selected for next round.  
Tip : Don’t waste time on 1 question first try the questions which are able to solve and even if able 
to solve partially some question its ok, Partial Marking does helps so try to increase the number of 
total testcases passed across all problems. 
 
2.     Technical Interview 1 [ 30 students appeared this round ] 
This was offline interview, there were total 10 panels so the round happened in 3 batches a there 
were total 30 students. My Technical Round 1 happened in first batch. It was a 1 hour round 
where 2 Coding questions are asked.  
My Interviewer didn’t asked me for a Intro and told me he will be giving 2 questions and he 
expects to have 1 coding question with proper optimized code on paper with complexities and the 
 
 
2nd problem if not able to code out completely atleast properly discussed optimized solution and 
having written something on paper to even stand a chance to reach to the next round. 
 
1. Given a NxM matrix have to find the peak element 
Example : [ 1 2 3 
        2 1 5 
             3 1 2 ].  
Solution : Here Peak Element is 5 as 5 is greater than all its adjacent numbers in all 4 
directions ( if a number is on boundary assume out of boundary all elements have a negative 
infinity ) 
We had to return any peak element from the matrix 
 
My Approach : I first explained the obvious brute force solution which would be check for 
each number if peak n when find peak return. It would take time complexity of O(n^2) . 
As we wanted any peak element for each row we can perform binary search space , in normal 
binary search we need the array to be sorted but here binary space search would work as just 
need any element. 
I explained with example if we have 1 4 3 5 4 3 2 6 1 here middle element would be 4 we see 
on left of 4 we have 5 which is >4 so now right boundary mid -1  
So search space : 1 4 3 5  middle = 4 which is greater than both left and right so its peak 
elemnt for a particular row. 
So my approach included for every row find the peak element n then just need to check for 
the above and below row if its peak element and can return. 
Time Complexity : O(nlogm)     Space Complexity : O(1) 
Interviewer was looking for a n(logm) solution and he told my approach was correct and I 
proceeded to code out the whole solution on paper. 
 
2. The second question was based on n-ary tree  
Example :             1  level 0 
            /   \ 
           2     3   level 1 
         /      /  |  \ 
       4     5   6   7  level 2 
 
Q queries will be given : [startnode, endnode, node] 
Example if q [ 2,5,7] 
If path of 2-> 5 includes nodes 2,1,3,5.   From node 7 – node 3 is the nearest which is also 
present in path. It was a LCA ( lowest Common Ancestor) Question and a Competitive 
programming concept Binary Lifting can be used for most optimal solution. 
 
My Approach : As the question was been explained I understood it had something to do with 
LCA and I told LCA and the Interviewer smiled as I was able to guess the type of question 
very quickly.  
For  startnode and endnode first find LCA so for node 2 and 5 it would be 1 and then I told I 
can run a dfs for the node and find nearest node from the path, he told me I can optimize more 
and don’t need a dfs so was able to come up with the solution where using parent node 
 
 
information and the depth the traversal was not needed. I coded out the solution on paper , 
also implemented the LCA function. 
Interviewer was satisfied , we had also discussed time and space complexity for every 
approach. 
He asked me do I have any Competitive Programming Experience I Told yes as I had given 
contests on codeforces and codechef along with Leetcode. Interviewer was satisfied as I did 
further optimizations in the LCA Approach. It was a binary lifting question where can find 
using logn and its most optimized approach, interviewer was ok if not able to code binary 
lifting in my case as I was able to achieve a similar optimized approach and had wrote code 
for it. 
He asked do I have any questions for him- 
I asked him about NPCI and the system design for UPI payments in general, we had a discussion on 
NPCI and his work experience and his role in company. 
 
3.    Technical Interview 2 [ Around 14 students appeared] 
My Technical Round 2 took place after the HR round. 
For some students, the HR round happened before Technical Round 2. This might have been 
done to speed up the process or to save time. 
Technical Round 2 was similar to Round 1 - we were asked to solve two coding questions on 
paper. I gave a quick introduction before starting the questions. 
 
1. Given an array [ “abc”, “or”, “xyxcba”, “cba”, “xz”] 
Check if a palindromic string exists after concatenation of 2 strings. 
For above example : we have abc + cba = abccba OR  abc + xyxcba = abxcyxcba 
There might exist many palindromic string can return any 1. 
 
My Approach : First discussed the brute force where for every pair check if palindrome and 
then the optimized version included usage of Trie , in trie can store the reverse string suppose 
in trie abc is already stored in reverse as cba and for string cba later can see c exists and a 
word exists so can return , now for a case like xyxcba also forms palindrome with abc right 
so now see that xyx is itself a palindrome so from the rest it forms palindrome so it will form 
a palindrome. 
It had TC : O(n*k*k) n= length of array , k=length of a string 
I asked is there any further optimized approach and interviewer said no and I proceeded to 
code out the Trie solution. 
 
 
2. It was the exact question from Codeforces with Rating 2700 which is around International 
Grandmaster (IGM) level - https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1270/G  
My Approach : Explained the brute force and the Interviewer gave hint to focus on the 
constarints 𝑖−𝑛 ≤ 𝑎𝑖 ≤ 𝑖−1 and separate the dependent variables  
 
 
I was able to derive that i-ai lies between (1 to n ) and it was 1-indexed array so even I lied 
from (1 to n) 
Drew edges from i to i-ai and saw it formed a cycle, I understood that the sum will be 0 where 
there will be cycle. He asked to explain why the cycle leads to 0. 
This was a question No student in any panel was able to come to optimized solution on its 
own. I think this particular question was asked to see thinking process and if can reach to 
solution with help of hints maybe. I dry ran the approach of cycle, didn’t completely wrote 
the code as time was up but the basic idea I wrote on paper. 
Interviewer asked if I had any questions –  
We had a discussion on overall experience also in PPT they had mentioned they used T -store 
internally in PhonePe I asked about it and had a discussion over same. Also how UPI payments 
can be made using SMS service too. 
 
3. Hiring Manager Round [ Around 11 students appeared] 
During the interview, I began by greeting the interviewer with a “Good Afternoon.” He asked me 
to start with my internship experiences, where I explained both roles, my responsibilities, and key 
learnings. We then moved on to the projects on my resume - two web projects and one mobile 
application. I had the app on my phone and offered to demonstrate it, which he agreed to. The app 
included an ML model, leading to a discussion on how the model was integrated and called from 
the backend. He appreciated the design of the app. He then asked if I had worked on any team 
projects. I shared a project that contributed to my team winning an international hackathon 
featuring participants from over 10 countries. 
Since I had mentioned teaching experience on my resume, he asked how I got that opportunity 
and what I taught. I explained that I had taught 11th and 12th-grade students, helping them with 
computer science and clearing doubts in other subjects for college entrance exams. I also spoke 
about my volunteering experience with an NGO, where I taught 7th and 8th graders. The NGO 
had on learning about my prior teaching background asked me to help students prepare for 
Olympiad topics. Following that, we discussed one of my major projects in detail, including the 
system architecture. I explained the flow using paper diagrams and covered topics like 
authentication, how OAuth works, OTP-based verification, and how API calls are made. 
Toward the end, the interviewer asked about my most-used application, and I said YouTube. He 
then asked me to design a system for YouTube Shorts. I drew a high-level system design on paper 
and explained various components, including how the system dynamically adapts video quality 
based on network bandwidth. We also discussed why I am pursuing a minor in management from 
SP Jain, and wrapped up with a few HR-type questions - one of which was how I handled conflict. 
I shared an example from the JPMC Code for Good Hackathon, explaining how our team resolved 
a disagreement.  
This round primarily tested knowledge of my resume and understanding of system design. 
When Interviewer asked do I have any questions – I asked 1-2 questions and discussed topics 
related to it. We also had discussion over if in future payments can be done using facial 
recognition and the challenges and how it can be misused. 
 
 
A total of 7 students received the offer, and I was one of them.

journey.prep:
1. Placement preparation should start 3–4 months prior to the placement season. You can do it during your 5th 
semester. Preparing 1 month before placements will create huge pressure and stress. You will get no time to 
learn before OA or Interview Day. Ultimately, it depends on you how you manage your time. 
2. If preparing for non-tech, do not fully rely on non-tech roles, as only 10% of roles are non-tech and 90% of 
jobs on our campus are tech roles (a mix of SDE and data roles). Always have a backup and prepare for the 
tech side by side. Read my story below to avoid this mistake. 
3. Practice DSA and Aptitude and be well-versed before the placement season begins. It cannot be done one 
night prior or one week prior. And DSA & Aptitude done one night prior cannot help you clear OAs easily. 
4. Once the OA-related part is cleared, focus on practicing for interviews. Try to give mocks to friends or try to 
improve communication skills in front of a mirror. 
5. Prepare an approximate 2–3 minute introduction talking about your academics, internship/work experience 
details (showing its significance and what impactful work you have done), academic achievements (if any), 
and your interest in the role offered. This is the starting punch in which the interviewer understands you as a 
whole, analyzes the candidate, and prepares the next consecutive questions. 
6. Always have a smile on your face and try to connect with the interviewer instead of just answering questions 
like a robot. Do not panic or be nervous, try to handle the situation. 
7. Always ask effective questions to the interviewer at the end. Frame questions that can impress the 
interviewer and leave a lasting impression. Asking questions also shows that you are curious about the 
company. Do not ask vague or very basic questions. 
8. Be very well-versed with the projects you prepare or put in your resume. You can expect deep questions 
about them. Diversify your projects, which will help you apply for various roles. 
9. Usually, people say “do not compare yourself with others,” and that’s true—comparing yourself with others 
will always put you under stress and pressure. But what I would suggest is just keep a short analysis of your 
competitions, so that you know you need to perform better to clear tests & interviews. 
10. Balance your preparation. Do not focus on only one skill. For eg. Do not do ONLY DSA & no Dev and Similarly 
do not do ONLY Dev & no DSA. Balance both things, plus additional CS Fundamentals and AIML concepts. 
11. Do not get depressed by rejections. Rejection is a part of placements, and every rejection gives a learning. 
You should not give up and should keep trying again and again. Switch ON your beast mode and never settle 
until it is achieved. Trust on God’s plan. Even God takes our exam before giving results.  
12. Always remember, placement is the joint result of hard work and luck. Luck is not in our control, but hard 
work is in our control. And Hard work increases the probability of Luck favouring you. You need to put in all 
your efforts to stand out from the crowd. AND if you are lazy and unambitious, then trust me you are already 
behind in the race.  
 
 
Back Story – 
My story is that I was purely preparing for JPMC non-tech roles during my third year, and I was not focusing much on 
tech roles. I was confident enough and took a risk that I would prepare for JPMC ONLY and get selected there. But 
things became uncertain, my resume didn’t even get shortlisted for JPMC. I had thoroughly prepared for the OA, GD, 
interviews, and many more, but I was not even able to cross the initial step, i.e., resume shortlisting. That was a 
depressing night for me. 
After that, I was unable to clear tech role OAs (because I was less prepared) and kept getting rejected. So, I decided 
to give my best at that moment and started very hard preparation for tech roles. Meanwhile, by that time, I already 
had an inclination towards data-related roles because I was also interested in machine learning and data science. So 
next, I purely focused on clearing OAs. I prepared all the stuff that is required for OAs and practiced aptitude. 
Companies were coming, I was getting rejected, companies were running out, but parallelly I was preparing harder. 
After much efforts, the time came when I was finally able to clear my first OA, which was BlackRock, and I was 
confident enough for the interview (not overconfident) that I could be able to impress Interviewer. Interview is 
nothing but selling yourself. I prepared all the stuff related to the data role (as I was shortlisted for Aladdin Data) and 
prepared each and everything about my resume, my projects and technical concepts. I gave the interview 
confidently. Later, the results came out, and I was able to enjoy the fruit of my hard work. 
 
General Advice – 
Decide what you want to pursue Tech or Non tech. Tech people need not worry much because there will be a greater 
number of opportunities. But for Non tech people, kindly note that opportunities for Non tech are fewer and limited. 
So if preparing for Non Tech, then also prepare for Tech side by side as a backup. Luck plays a very vital role and you 
never know what is the next move of your luck. The only thing you can do is be an ideal person who has knowledge 
of all skills and be ready for every kind of job. At the end, you are the captain of your own destiny.  
Placement Observations – 
Below are the observations that I found during placements, and these can help you note down things in advance. 
THIS IS JUST an observation, do not rely completely on it.  
1. The average hiring ratio is 5:1. Example – if 30 students shortlisted for interviews, then on avg 5-6 students 
will be selected. The number can be higher or lower as well, but averagely its 5:1. 
2. Copying can be very risky. If found, you might not be able to sit for next 2-3 companies (which may be good 
companies). 
3. Students with ONLY DSA skills were unable to answer web development questions in interviews, and 
students with ONLY development skills were unable to answer DSA questions in interviews. You need to 
prepare both.  
4. There’s no fix date or time of any company. Anybody can come anytime. Or even may not come. 
5. Communication skills matter most in interviews and GDs. Even if you are intelligent but unable to convey 
your answers, you might not move forward. 
6. You might see your friends or peers getting placed, but you should not take that as depression. Depression 
will slow down your productivity and willingness. Instead, you should learn from your mistakes, learn from 
your peers, put in more efforts, do not give up and achieve your goal. 
7. Things to consider about Bad Luck – 
- You might not get selected in your dream company. 
- Your resume might not get shortlisted even being perfect. 
- Your server may crash during test and you are out. 
- You might get hard/strict panel for interview. 
- Your interview might get scheduled in the last slot. By the time your slot comes, the company may have 
already made decisions. 
- Undeserving students might get shortlisted. 
8. About Good Luck - it will come surprisingly. 
Resources: 
These are general resources for both roles. You can also refer individual company interview experience sheet and 
previous year sheets for more detailed prep. 
Tech and Data Roles - 
1. DSA/Coding – Striver’s A to Z sheet. If not able to complete full sheet then atleast try to cover concepts from 
each topic from the sheet. Problem solving on Leetcode, HackerRank etc platform. For SQL you can do basics 
on https://sqlbolt.com/ and advance on SQL 50 on Leetcode. For OOPS and CS Fundamentals like DBMS, OS, 
CCN you can refer any resources of your own. 
2. Projects – hackathon project or any impactful project which can impress interviewer. For data roles, you can 
do analytics or machine learning project.  
3. Aptitude – Indiabix, GFG. Refer each topic of indiabix individually from YT or any other resource. Practice 
aptitude as much as possible because practice only can help you solve questions in OA quickly, with fast 
calculation, saving time, completing all questions and build confidence for even selecting tukka option.  
4. Puzzles – refer GFG puzzles.  
5. For data roles, make sure to do machine learning concepts and implement models for better understanding.  
Non tech Roles – 
1. Aptitude – same as like mentioned above. Also do current affairs, market awareness of last 1 year. 
2. Finance, Case Study, Guesstimate – Best resource sheet prepared by my senior. Refer this. 
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Nwf3VM4tBb92TxsgUxDtghXyLeSLHU_v/view?usp=s 
3. Additional resources –  
- This is all-in-one course for Finance. No other course required - 
https://www.coursera.org/specializations/finance-and-financial-markets 
- Note that only JPMC requires Finance knowledge. Rest other Non Tech roles require knowledge of 
Consulting, Marketing, Supply Chain, Markets & Economics etc. So you can practice Case Studies of 
various non tech fields.  
- For puzzles refer GFG top 20, top 50 etc. and for guesstimates you can refer this YT - 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g7nvHCYzXQE&list=PL-q2MNxDekiSFUNcwCI-Q4-QqHWe5K42p 
-  You can learn Finance from Valuation School YT Channel. You can also do courses on Financial Risk 
Management (which is required for JPMC CR). 
Check your resume score on – resumeworded site. Try to keep above 65-70.  
It has limited no. of attempts, so use attempts wisely.  
 
All the Best to everyone!  
Be honest with your struggles and give your best.  
 
You can connect me - 
Email – vinay.marathe23@spit.ac.in 
Contact - 7796160414 
LinkedIn - www.linkedin.com/in/vinay-marathe

journey.howSecured:
The process consisted of 3 rounds 1 Test and 2 technical rounds. The Entire process including interviews was online. 
OA on 22/8/2025 
Interviews 2 rounds on 28/8/2025. 
Eligibility criteria was 7.5+ CGPA. I would recommend to maintain CGPA of 8 which is eligible for almost all companies 
except for few. 
Preplacement Talk was conducted on 20/08/25. And this was a Pool Campus Recruitment Drive. 
 
1.     OA Round [100+ Candidates] 
Test was conducted on eLitmus platform and it was camera proctored. Duration was 1.5 hrs consisting 3 sections. 
Since BlackRock visited our campus for the first time, we didn’t had any previous interview experience so I searched 
on Web and Interview experience in YT to prepare and understand the pattern. The actual test pattern was similar to 
what I researched. 
1. Aptitude section. 
- It consisted of Quantitative Aptitude, Data interpretation and Logical Reasoning. 
- The key point here is that calculators were not allowed, so you need to be fast with your mental maths 
and logic. 
- Practising various questions and giving mock aptitude test on any online platform will help you to 
develop quick maths skill. 
- Also prepare all types of aptitude topics because which type of question can come you never know. 
2. Technical/Programming. 
- This was not a coding section, but an MCQ based on coding/programming questions. It consisted of 2 
types: Flowchart and Pseudocodes. 
- Guess the output of code snippet and guess the output of flowchart were asked. Flowchart were not 
easy for sure. They were complicated and require practice to tackle such kind of questions. Some 
questions were fill in the blanks in flow chart.  
- Pseudocodes were on Data Structure operations mostly related to Trees.  
3. SQL Section – 
- It consisted of SQL Code snippets. It was actually Oracle SQL which has slightly different syntax but 
overall logics were same.  
- I suggest cover every topic of SQL right from basics, joints, subqueries etc. In MCQ, options are very 
closely differentiated from each other, so firm remembrance of syntax and logic is important for time-
based questions. 
Overall, Test was moderate level and balanced. Time management is very important, you need to be very fast in 
identifying the logic, calculating the maths for quant questions, imagining the outputs and understanding the code 
snippets. Practicing such questions beforehand boosts confidence and improves critical thinking ability.  
 
2.     Technical Interview Round 1 (Online) [25 to 30 were shortlisted (including waitlisted students)] 
My first interview round began with a polite greeting and a brief introduction about myself. I prepared my 
introduction which aligned with the role offered, matching my skill set with the role and showed that I am interested 
in this role. Then a follow-up question was asked based on my work experience, what skills I gained, and what were 
my learnings there. Then the conversation moved on to the projects in my resume. Imp pointer – Always put the 
project which you are very confident about in the first place. I was asked for an overview of all projects mentioned in 
my resume and a detailed explanation of the first project. In-depth questions were asked regarding the project. It 
was an ML project, so questions related to Python, which library was used, which model was used, why that model, 
what were the results, what were the challenges, how the dataset was formed, etc., everything in depth was asked. 
Also, they asked twisted questions like if dataset columns are changed or a new column is added, then how the 
model will react. Then what was the outcome of the project, what problem does it solve, etc. Make sure to know the 
in-and-out of your project (also about the coding part) so that you can answer confidently. I was asked to explain a 
function of my project code. 
Next, the interviewer jumped to the coding part and asked me to open an online compiler and gave a question to 
code in Python. I was familiar with CPP , so I asked him and coded the solution in CPP . He then changed the input 
array and asked me to print the solution. Then he asked about time and space complexity, then how I can optimize it, 
and so on. The question was easy – print the frequency of each element.  
At last, the interviewer asked me about what BlackRock does and why I wanted to join BlackRock. Then he asked me 
how I stay updated about Finance and AI. Luckily, I used to read the news, so I was able to answer. He asked for any 
latest news regarding AI, and I answered him with three news. Then the interview ended, and I was given an 
opportunity to ask them any questions. So I asked them two appropriate questions. Overall, the interview went very 
well. My preparation helped me to answer confidently in the interview.  
 
3.    Technical Interview Round 2 (Online) [15-16 students approx] 
My second round was a little bit stricter than the previous round. The interviewer directly asked me for my 
introduction and straightaway asked me a DSA question. He asked me which language I code in and to name the data 
structures of that language. Then he asked me some micro questions which then layer by layer ended up asking the 
“Kth largest element” question and its optimization. Then he asked scenario-based questions which were based on 
HashMaps. Then he asked OOPS concepts. Then again, I was grilled on the first project mentioned in the resume. 
Similarly, in round 2 also, the interviewer manipulated my project inputs and project dataset and asked how my 
project would perform on manipulated data. This conveys that you should know each and every function, code, 
input-output scenario, and limitation of your project. Overall, the interview went medium (according to me). But 
answering confidently and being transparent would have impressed the interviewer even though he was strict. 
Also, always keep a smiling face and do not show your anxiety or fear. A happy and good conversation between you 
and the interviewer always results well.   
 
 
 
4. Temporary Round [10 students] 
On the interview day, i.e., 28 Aug, all results were already announced to the TPO. However, an AI copy-case incident 
happened during our interview rounds. The company caught some candidates using AI, which was very clearly 
evident to them. So, they decided to cancel the recruitment from SPIT. We all were tensed and anxious because, due 
to some candidates, everybody would have to suffer. 
So, the next day, Sikka Sir called 10 students for the next round, and Sikka Sir took an HR kind-of interview of us. 
Later, they discussed the copy-case incident and how they convinced the company not to cancel recruitment from 
SPIT, as BlackRock was visiting SPIT for the first time. After a stressful situation, Sikka Sir finally announced the names 
of the selected candidates, and we were very happy. The ones who copied using AI were straightaway rejected from 
the process. 
[ Total 10 selected students –> 6 for SDE + 2 Aladdin Data + 2 Global Marketing]

journey.prep:
• Don’t lose confidence even if you face multiple rejections. I interviewed in 8 companies before 
BlackRock, and though I often felt demotivated, I eventually realized that things fall into place at 
the right time. 
• Even if you feel others less deserving are getting placed, remember that your journey is unique. I 
had won multiple hackathons but wasn’t placed initially — yet I ended up in a top MNC like 
BlackRock, which I never even dreamed of. 
• Stay confident and keep a smile throughout your interview. It creates a positive impression and 
shows your enthusiasm. 
• Always interact with the interviewers. Don’t stay quiet — even if you don’t know the exact 
answer, explain your thought process. Many times, they are more interested in how you approach 
the problem rather than just the final solution. 
• Practice explaining your projects clearly in bullet points (features, technologies, and real-world 
impact). This not only shows clarity but also highlights your problem-solving ability. 
• Know your resume inside out. HR and technical rounds can both heavily focus on what you’ve 
mentioned, so be prepared to discuss every detail confidently. 
• Prepare both technical and behavioral aspects. While DSA and technical knowledge are crucial, 
soft skills, communication, and genuine interest in the company matter equally. 
• Ask questions at the end. Always have 2–3 role- or company-related questions ready. This shows 
curiosity and genuine interest in the company. 
• Be consistent in preparation. Whether it’s aptitude, SQL, or programming, practicing regularly 
(LeetCode, mock tests, etc.) makes a big difference. 
• Network smartly. Connect with seniors, peers, or professionals on LinkedIn to get insights into the 
process. Sometimes even small tips can give you an edge. 
• And most importantly, trust the process. If one door closes, another one will open with an even 
better opportunity. 
If you have any further doubts, feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn :)

1. Online Assessment Round [100 + candidates appeared] 
During the placement process, one of the key eligibility criteria was maintaining a CGPA of 7.5 or above . 
This benchmark served as the initial shortlisting factor and emphasized the importance of consistent academic 
performance. Apart from academics, the resume played a vital role in getting shortlisted. Having a properly 
formatted resume — preferably in Jake’s template style — added a professional touch. What mattered more, 
however, was the project section of the resume. A strong resume required at least one major project with 
unique features  that stood out from the rest, supported by a couple of smaller personal projects  that 
showcased fundamental skills and hands -on experience. The project descriptions had to be written in bullet 
points, focusing on the specific features, outcomes, and technologies used. I also realized the importance of 
arranging projects in an order where the most impactful or “sellable” project was listed first, as it immediately 
captured the recruiter’s attention. 
The online assessment test was conducted on the eLitmus platform and was fully proctored. Since this was 
BlackRock’s first visit to our campus , there were no prior student experiences to rely on. To prepare 
effectively, I searched extensively on the web for insights into the test pattern and previous questions. 
Fortunately, the test format I came across online turned out to be largely consistent  with the one that was 
actually conducted. The test duration was 1.5 hours, and it was divided into three major sections: Aptitude, 
Programming, and SQL. 
1. Aptitude Section 
The aptitude section was divided into three subsections — Quantitative Aptitude, Data 
Checking/Data Accuracy, and Logical Reasoning. 
o The Quantitative Aptitude  questions revolved around standard topics such as arithmetic, 
percentages, ratios, and number systems, requiring both accuracy and speed. 
 
o The Data Checking/Data Accuracy part was relatively straightforward and easy to solve. It 
primarily tested one’s ability to identify inconsistencies or errors within datasets quickly. 
o The Logical Reasoning  subsection was interesting, involving questions on pattern 
recognition, sequences, and puzzles . The key here was to attempt as many questions as 
possible without spending too much time on a single problem. Proper time management was 
crucial in maximizing the score in this section. 
Imp Links (Aptitude): IndiaBix, CodeHelp  
2. Programming Section 
The programming part was unique compared to typical coding assessments, as it was split into two 
subsections: Flowcharts and Pseudocodes. 
o In the Flowchart subsection , two flowcharts based on basic programming problems were 
provided. Each flowchart contained around 5–6 blanks that we had to fill in. The questions 
were objective (MCQ-based), where the correct option had to be chosen for each blank. One 
of the flowcharts was related to a string-matching algorithm, while the other was relatively 
simple and could be solved with a clear understanding of flow control. 
o The Pseudocode subsection contained three MCQs based on different algorithms and data 
structures. Two of them were focused on Binary Trees/BSTs  (covering fundamental 
operations like insertion, deletion, traversal, and calculating depth). The third question was 
based on AVL trees , specifically testing knowledge of rotateLeft and rotateRight 
operations (LL, LR, RL, RR) . Since I had prepared these topics in advance, I was able to 
approach this section with confidence and accuracy. 
3. SQL Section

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
• Don’t lose confidence even if you face multiple rejections. I interviewed in 8 companies before 
BlackRock, and though I often felt demotivated, I eventually realized that things fall into place at 
the right time. 
• Even if you feel others less deserving are getting placed, remember that your journey is unique. I 
had won multiple hackathons but wasn’t placed initially — yet I ended up in a top MNC like 
BlackRock, which I never even dreamed of. 
• Stay confident and keep a smile throughout your interview. It creates a positive impression and 
shows your enthusiasm. 
• Always interact with the interviewers. Don’t stay quiet — even if you don’t know the exact 
answer, explain your thought process. Many times, they are more interested in how you approach 
the problem rather than just the final solution. 
• Practice explaining your projects clearly in bullet points (features, technologies, and real-world 
impact). This not only shows clarity but also highlights your problem-solving ability. 
• Know your resume inside out. HR and technical rounds can both heavily focus on what you’ve 
mentioned, so be prepared to discuss every detail confidently. 
• Prepare both technical and behavioral aspects. While DSA and technical knowledge are crucial, 
soft skills, communication, and genuine interest in the company matter equally. 
• Ask questions at the end. Always have 2–3 role- or company-related questions ready. This shows 
curiosity and genuine interest in the company.

journey.howSecured:
1. Round 1 Online Assessment [All who registered] 
The First round (60 Questions) was the online assessment having 3 sections (No Negative Marking): 
Section 1: 15 Minutes, 15 Questions  
About: Logical based thinking. Questions were asked on patterns and reasoning. 
Useful Tip: Questions might appear tricky. Since this will be the first section you will be attempting -
the key part here is to balance your time as 15 minutes is less for this section. Go through all the 
questions and solve according to easiest to difficult strategy.  
Section 2: 15 Minutes, 15 Questions 
About: English Language based. Questions were asked on grammar, arranging the sentences in the 
chronological order , comprehension etc.  
Useful Tip: Section is straight forward with the basic level of English you will be able to crack this 
easily. Time is not an issue here, just have to think calmy. 
Section 3: 40 Minutes, 30 Questions 
About: Technical Based. Questions were ranging from the topics of Object Oriented Programming, 
Database Management Systems, Computer Communication Networks, Data Structures and 
Algorithms etc. 
Useful Tip: Questions here were of easy to moderate level. A key part here is to take the smart guess 
when not sure. Some of them are objective based theory while some will be solving according to a 
data structure or so. 
 
2. Round 2: Technical Interview Round [18 Candidates appeared for this round]  
 
 
This round will last for about 45 minutes to 1 hour. The best tip would be to remain calm and smile 
in this situation. The interviewer is judging you on the depth of you r knowledge and the way you 
explain which highlights your communication. 
 
As any interview would start, the first question asked was – Introduce yourself. The key part here is 
to spend a bit more time and highlight the aspects that you want the interviewer to ask you . This is 
 
going to form the base of your interview. I talked about my internship experience and current projects 
in web development and also the brownie points that I had won multiple hack athons and worked at 
NGO. Consequently, the first half shifted on my projects and work experience where I was asked to 
explain about it in depth and then further was asked situational based quest ions – Were these 
collaborative projects? If yes and a conflict arose then how would you manage it? (Another question) 
If some of your team mates were not on the same page then what would you do? (Another one) How 
would you approach people when you had to bu ild a project on a tech stack th at you don’t know?   
The way I answered these questions was that I took examples of the projects and explained each one 
of them highlighting that I have been in these situations and have leadership qualities.  
 
Then the next part of the interview was on the aspects they had mentioned in their job description  – 
Data Analytics and Cloud Computing. (Questions li ke – What is cloud computing?) They don’t 
expect me to have in depth knowledge on them but I gave an overview on them and they were happy 
about it.  
 
The third phase of this interview spanned on the DBMS. I was asked about SQL and what I knew 
about it. Then I was asked to design a schema for a School. I used the “Thinking Out Loud” method 
– which is essentially whatever I wrote I spoke about why I wrote it and then added the constraints 
(NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY). I did this so that the interviewer know 
the process in which I am thinking. After this I was asked to explain the Schema. The interview then 
asked me SQL Queries on the same. The queries were related to the Schema I made, and one of the 
questions on which the interviewer emphasized was the difference between the HAVING and the 
WHERE clause. 
 
Since I had an interesting resume, they again came back to my work e xperience and then ended the 
interview by asking – Why choose General Mills? Researching about the company helps here. Overall 
the round was based on resume and you should know it thoroughly anticipating the questions that can 
arise. 
 
9 Candidates went to the next round. 
3.    Round 3 – HR Based Round [9 Candidates Appeared for this Round] 
This was a purely HR based round with common questions . Mine was the shortest one lasting about 
20 minutes. There were two people in the pan el. They were looking at how you are going to tackle 
these questions.  It started by walking them through your resume. This similar was as in the Technical 
Round but here my focus was on the fact that I worked at NGO which resonates w ith the company 
policy of giving back to society. Some of the questions were:  
• Where do you see yourself in 5 years? 
• If not engineering then what will you be doing? And why? 
• One impression – good and bad that your friends will have about you? Why would they have 
that? 
• What do you know about General Mills? 
• Why choose General Mills? 
 
The answers that you give can lead to follow up questions on that. The key is to keep calm and have a 
smile on your face and then give the reply to best of your ability. Highlighting points relevant to the 
company is always beneficial as they see that your goals align with theirs.  
In the end 4 people got the internship offer.

journey.prep: ● Know your basic concepts: Be well-versed in the fundamentals of CCN (Computer Communication Networks), OS (Operating Systems), DBMS (Database Management Systems), and Data Structures. ● Aptitude practice: Practice sequences, patterns, and work-related problems on various aptitude websites to sharpen your problem-solving skills. ● Focus on DBMS: Pay special attention to normalization in DBMS as it is a key concept often discussed. ● Prepare for technical rounds: Be thorough with the projects mentioned in your resume and be ready to explain them in detail. ● Master the basics: Ensure you have a strong understanding of core concepts, even in areas outside your projects. ● Curiosity matters: If you're unsure about an answer, show curiosity and eagerness to learn more about it. This reflects a positive attitude towards learning. ● Be engaged and eager: Show genuine interest in whatever the interviewers explain and ask thoughtful follow-up questions. ● Stay confident: Maintain confidence throughout the interview, as it can leave a lasting impression.

journey.howSecured: 1. Round 1 Online Assessment [All who registered] The online assessment round consisted of 60 questions and had a duration of 1 hour and 10 minutes.There were three sections: logical reasoning, language proficiency and technical questions. Logical reasoning: This section was of 15 minutes(15 questions) and it contained basic questions related to math, patterns, sequences. The 15 minutes time was less for this section. Language proficiency: This section was of 15 minutes(15 questions) and it contained questions related to basic English. The time was sufficient for solving this section. Technical questions: This section was of 40 minutes(30 questions).It contained questions ranging from topics of Database Management System, Computer Communication and Networks,Object Oriented Programming,Operating Systems and Data Structures and Algorithms. 2. Technical Round [ 18 students were shortlisted for this round] This round lasted for 45 mins to 1 hour . The interviewer began by asking which subject excites me the most and I chose App development. I was given a case study to design an app. The task began with me asking relevant questions to understand the requirements thoroughly. I had to consider factors like the app's functionality, user experience, and the overall system architecture. Once I had enough information, I proposed a design that detailed both the frontend and backend components, explaining how they would interact. A key focus was on scaling the app from 3,000 to 30,000 users, and I discussed strategies like efficient data storage, user management, and backend optimization to handle the increased load. The interviewer tested my ability to break down the problem, gather requirements, and present a robust, scalable solution. Following this, I was asked about storing large amounts of data using Firebase, which had been a core part of my previous app development experience. The interviewer wanted to understand if I knew how to handle scalability issues in Firebase, especially with large databases. I explained Firebase's strengths in handling real-time data but also discussed its limitations when it comes to scaling beyond certain thresholds. This led to a deeper conversation about database management, where I was quizzed on concepts like BCNF and normalization. I answered these questions, elaborating on whether normalization is needed for small databases. While I wasn’t very familiar with microservices, the interviewer was helpful in explaining key concepts, and I picked up the basics quickly, which allowed me to respond to further questions. Toward the end of the interview, the case study was revealed to be based on an app the interviewer had already developed, providing a real-world context to the task. I asked how they had solved the scalability problem in their app and was curious about their experience at General Mills. The interview tested my ability to think critically, learn on the go and apply theoretical knowledge to practical challenges. It wasn’t just about technical expertise but also about showing my problem-solving skills and willingness to engage with new concepts and feedback. Overall, it was an insightful experience that showcased my strengths and highlighted areas where I could continue to grow. 3. HR- Based Round [ 10 students were shortlisted for this round] In my HR interview, the panel consisted of two interviewers who started by asking me to introduce myself and share a bit about my family background. After that, they posed an interesting question—if I hadn’t chosen to pursue engineering, what other career path would I have taken. They then moved on to ask where I see myself in the next five years and how my friends would describe me, giving me a chance to reflect on both my professional goals and my personal traits. The interview then touched on some of the major decisions I’ve made, as they asked me about the easiest and most difficult decisions I’ve taken so far in life.I was also asked to explain about one of my projects in brief. Finally, I was asked why I wanted to join General Mills, which allowed me to express my interest in the company. At the end of the interview, I had the opportunity to ask them questions. The key is to stay calm and maintain a friendly smile throughout the process. Answer the questions confidently and ensure that your responses reflect genuine interest while aligning with the company’s values and goals. 4 students were offered internships after this round.

customSections.content: ● Know your basic concepts: Be well-versed in the fundamentals of CCN (Computer Communication Networks), OS (Operating Systems), DBMS (Database Management Systems), and Data Structures. ● Aptitude practice: Practice sequences, patterns, and work-related problems on various aptitude websites to sharpen your problem-solving skills. ● Focus on DBMS: Pay special attention to normalization in DBMS as it is a key concept often discussed. ● Prepare for technical rounds: Be thorough with the projects mentioned in your resume and be ready to explain them in detail. ● Master the basics: Ensure you have a strong understanding of core concepts, even in areas outside your projects. ● Curiosity matters: If you're unsure about an answer, show curiosity and eagerness to learn more about it. This reflects a positive attitude towards learning. ● Be engaged and eager: Show genuine interest in whatever the interviewers explain and ask thoughtful follow-up questions. ● Stay confident: Maintain confidence throughout the interview, as it can leave a lasting impression.

journey.prep: To succeed in this selection process, focus on your core computer science fundamentals such as computer networks, object-oriented programming, operating systems, SQL, and aptitude. These areas are crucial to clearing the online assessment round. For the technical interviews, ensure that you know your projects and internships thoroughly. Be prepared to discuss your contributions, the tech stack you used, and your reasoning behind specific choices. SQL and DBMS will often be revisited, so make sure to revise those topics, along with basic data structures and algorithms (DSA). It’s important to be confident but also take your time to think through the questions before answering. When it comes to the HR round, honesty, clarity, and genuineness go a long way. Research the company extensively before the interview so you’re ready to talk about it, and make sure you're prepared to discuss your interests outside of academics. This will help you navigate the more personal questions.
journey.projects: Core projects and domain architectures discussed in interview rounds.
journey.howSecured: 1. Online Assessment [Around 150 candidates appeared for this round ] The online assessment round consisted of 60 questions and had a duration of 1 hour and 10 minutes. There were three sections: logical reasoning, language proficiency, and technical questions. The aptitude section consisted of 15 basic questions on topics like time-work problems and general math, to be completed in 20 minutes, where balancing speed and accuracy was critical. The language proficiency section consisted of 15 questions in 15 minutes, focusing on grammar, vocabulary, sentence structure, and comprehension. It was straightforward but required quick thinking and good command of the English language to finish within the limited time. Lastly, the technical section included questions on object-oriented programming, computer networks, operating systems, SQL, and DBMS, emphasizing the importance of having a strong grasp of core computer science concepts. Out of the 150 that appeared, 18 were shortlisted for the next round. 2. Technical Interview [ 18 candidates appeared for this round] .The technical interview lasted 50 minutes to an hour, focusing heavily on my internship experience and projects, particularly in machine learning and web development. The interviewer began by asking which domain I preferred working in, and I chose machine learning. I was then asked to elaborate on why I found it interesting, followed by detailed questions about my experience in that field. I discussed the machine learning projects I had worked on and the contributions I made during my internship. These discussions led to further cross-questions, testing my in-depth knowledge of the work I had done. It became clear that having a thorough understanding of my projects and past experiences was crucial for this round. In addition, I was presented with a case study that lacked many details, and I was expected to ask relevant questions to gather more information. This part of the interview aimed to assess my critical thinking, problem-solving skills, and how I approach complex, vague scenarios, especially from a machine learning perspective. I had to explain my thought process and steps I would take to tackle the problem. The technical portion covered a range of topics: I was questioned about database choices, including the rationale behind selecting certain types and the differences between them. I discussed machine learning algorithms I had used, the reasons for choosing them, and the insights gained from their results. The interview also included specific SQL questions, and I was asked about neural networks—such as their different types, applications, and why they are used in particular scenarios. Additionally, I was asked which programming languages I used most frequently and received questions specific to those languages. The interviewer inquired about my favorite college subjects, with both theoretical and practical questions aimed at gauging my depth of understanding. Overall, the interview was smooth but had tricky moments, particularly when delving into complex technical details. Having a strong grasp of my fundamentals, being well-versed in everything on my resume, and being able to clearly articulate my thought process helped me navigate the questions confidently. Out of the 18 that appeared, 10 were shortlisted for the next round. 3. HR Interview [ 10 candidates appeared for this round] In my HR round, I was primarily asked personal questions, with a focus on my interests and experiences outside of academics. One of the more unique questions was when they asked me to "sell" General Mills to them, which tested my knowledge of the company and the research I had done beforehand. There was also considerable attention on the committees and extracurricular activities I had been part of over the past two years, and they asked me to discuss both the positive and negative aspects of these experiences. They were curious about my interests beyond my degree, and I was asked what I enjoy doing that isn’t related to academics. They also inquired about my future aspirations, asking where I see myself when I’m 35 or 40. Another question focused on my reading habits, asking about the most recent book I had read and to discuss it. Additionally, I was asked how my friends perceive me, both in terms of strengths and weaknesses.Overall, it was a smooth and comfortable round where the main focus was on being authentic and honest in my responses. Out of the 10 that appeared in the last round, 4 candidates were selected.

and products. 
3. You should know your resume in and out and should be able to explain everything in it. 
4. Many factors work except your performance so don’t overthink much just give your best , one day it will pay
