journey.howSecured:
1.     Online Assessment [ 191 applied on unstop and 133 shortlisted for test ] 
The test was held on campus on unstop with rigorous proctoring. It contained 3 sections – Aptitude, Technical 
MCQ, and coding. Each section had a  sectional timer. 
Aptitude(40 questions in 35 mins) – questions were very easy and you need to only score good in this setion 
for further calls for business analyst role. I was able to solve 30+ questions correctly but cutoff was too low 
because 60 students were called for business analyst gd. 
Technical MCQ (33 questions in 25 mins)  – questions were from various topics like html, css , javascript, 
java , oop, dbms and os. This section was of a moderate level and I was able to score decent enough questions 
correctly. 
Coding( 3 questions in 30  mins) – There were 3 coding questions I don’t remember all 3 but 1 was on graph 
traversal . Remember it was not like leetcode question solving where you are already given driver code and 
you just have to write the function and return the expected value. You have to write input and output coding 
statements also. 
2.     Group Discussion (Only for business Analyst role) [ 60 students appeared ] 
There were 6 groups of 10 each . Topic was given on the spot and every group got a different topic. Our 
topic was – The role of social media in shaping consumer trends. 
3 students were selected out of 10 from my panel and I was one of them. Here are some of the tips from 
my side - 
1. Always start the gd – I started the gd addressing the group clearly channelised the whole flow and told 
the topics that would be discussed. 
I spoke 4-5 times clearly and loudly and explained my point with many real life examples and 
experiences 
Out of the 6 groups , around 24 candidates were shortlisted for interview round 1. 
 
 
 
2. Technical Interview – Round 1 [ 24 candidates appeared ] 
 
My interview started with a basic introduction and he got very interested in asking about my startup 
that I worked on during my 2 nd and 3 rd year. He asked many follow-up questions and I was able to 
answer all of them clearly. Then he asked about my ml project that I have worked on in one of the 
hackathons. I explained it well and he asked related questions and kept asking levelling up the 
difficulty. He gave me many situation based questions that the deadline of a project is 2 weeks but tech 
team is not working efficiently what will you do?? Then he moved to a guesstimate question to tell the 
number of users you can get of your turf booking app (my startup) in the first quarter in kolkata. I 
explained him my approach and he was very convinced. He asked me why Quantiphi. When I 
expressed my interest he dropped the bomb by asking tell me 3 projects quantiphi is working on right 
now. It was really awkward because I didn’t knew about it but he said its okay that’s for your time. 
After a longggggg wait of 3 hours I got mail from unstop that my 2nd round is scheduled at 6pm. 
 
3. Technical Interview – Round 2 [ 12 candidates appeared ] 
This round was online and it was to be held at 6 but further delayed to 7pm. It was pretty chill he 
started by asking my introduction and he was also interested in my startup work ( that impressed 
everyone ngl ). Then he asked tell me what does quantiphi do and 3 projects ( same questwion again 
haha but this time I prepared it well). Then he asked many questions related to python . He also gave 
2-3 situational based questions ans waas happy after my answers. He gave feedback that he liked my 
communication skills and I can really handle client side of sales and analysis well. Within 5 minutes 
of round 2 I got message of my hr round scheduled after 5 minutes 
 
4. HR Round [ 6 candidates appeared ] 
 
It was not a typical hr round . many management case based questions and guesstimates were also 
asked (yeah every round was testing you in these things). He started by asking me where I live and my 
family background . Then he gave me a situation that how will you pitch our insurance automation 
tool to a law firm . He then asked a guesstimate question to guess number of ev vehicles in india. He 
asked many  behavioural related questions and finally all my rounds were concluded at 9pm in the 
night.

entirely.

around

and

seating.

aptitude

very

nice

The

real

challenge

came

in

the

coding

section.

We

had

3

questions

to

solve

in

just

30

minutes.

One

was

the

House

Robber

problem ,

I

tried

search.

My

logic

and

functions

worked

fine

when

input,

a

with

input

and

array

initialization

in

the

given

environment.

Even

the

enhanced

for-each

loop

wasn’t

working

as

ended

up

trying

3

different

variations,

but

none

passed

due

to

these

input

issues.

Because

of

that,

I

couldn’t

solve

any

coding

problem,

was

very

disappointing

the

part

was

actually

clear

to

On

the

aptitude

prep

side,

I

realized

that

platforms

like

are

no

longer

enough.

after

solving

everything

on

got

rejected

in

companies

,

level

was

higher.

prep,

strongly

recommend

through

Aggarwal’s

book ,

are

raising

the

bar

year

by

year.

OA

results

out,

found

myself

shortlisted

for

the

Business

Analyst

(BA)

role .

I

wasn’t

very

interested

in

BA

and

had

only

planned

to

attend

to

avoid

any

demerits.

The

next

morning,

I

got

to

know

that

candidates

could

apply

for

a

role

change ,

but

it

required

HR

approval

and

would

be

considered

purely

on

the

basis

of

the

resume.

The

catch

was:

before

applying

for

any

other

role

(like

Framework

Engineer

or

MLE),

all

BA-shortlisted

candidates

first

had

to

clear

the

Group

Discussion

(GD)

round.

If

you

failed

the

BA

GD,

you

were

out

of

all

roles .

There

were

about

60

students

shortlisted

for

BA ,

divided

into

6

groups

of

10

each.

For

the

GD,

we

were

given

1.5

minutes

to

jot

down

points

and

structure

our

thoughts.

My

group’s

topic

was:

“9-to-5

Job

vs

Startup.”

The

discussion

went

really

well

for

me.

I

didn’t

start

or

conclude,

yet

I

still

made

it

to

the

next

round.

This

made

me

realize

an

important

point:

it’s

not

always

mandatory

to

be

the

first

or

last

speaker

to

get

noticed.

What

really

matters

is

how

meaningful

and

relevant

your

contributions

are

during

the

discussion.

3.

BA

Round

1

The

interview

started

with

the

classic

“Introduce

yourself,”

where

I

briefly

covered

my

projects,

achievements,

and

interests.

The

interviewer

immediately

pointed

out,

with

a

smile,

that

my

resume

didn’t

have

a

single

mention

of

the

word

“business”

—

and

we

both

laughed

at

that.

He

then

picked

up

on

my

Profit

View

project

(Virtual

Trading

System)

since

he

himself

was

very

interested

in

the

stock

market.

He

asked

me

to

explain

it

in

detail,

which

I

did

confidently.

The

follow-up

questions

were

challenging:

●

“Suppose

you

have

8

billion

customers

next

day

—

how

would

you

handle

scaling,

and

what

would

be

your

revenue

model?”

●

“What

is

the

highest

stock

in

the

Indian

stock

market?”

●

“Why

did

you

integrate

AI

into

this

project?”

●

“Which

is

better:

AI

or

human

intelligence?”

I

answered

these

from

a

market

perspective,

staying

practical

and

confident.

He

also

tested

me

on

current

market

knowledge:

“The

market

is

bad

right

now,

which

sectors

would

you

invest

in?”

Another

situational

question

was:

“If

you’re

in

a

3-member

team

(1

stock

market

expert,

2

developers),

and

the

industry

stakeholder

wants

a

new

feature

X

that

clashes

with

your

ideas

—

whom

will

you

listen

to?”

Then,

he

switched

to

my

Legal

AI

project .

He

grilled

me

on

technical

details

—

models

like

BERT,

PEFT,

Microsoft

Phi-2,

and

why

I

chose

them.

He

also

asked:

“ How

many

cases

are

filed

daily

in

the

Mumbai

High

Court? ”

(a

guesstimate

question

linked

to

my

project

domain).

Towards

the

end,

he

challenged

me

on

role

alignment:

“ Why

join

Quantiphi

as

a

BA

when

your

resume

shows

you’re

a

developer? ”

I

explained

my

reasoning,

and

he

also

asked

me

about

Quantiphi’s

competitors.

Finally,

he

pressed

me

multiple

times

on

my

preference

—

BA

or

FE.

I

stayed

consistent

and

confidently

said

Framework

Engineer

every

time,

despite

the

follow-up

trick

questions.

The

interview

lasted

around

40–50

minutes ,

and

it

was

intense

but

engaging.

Before

wrapping

up,

I

asked

him

if

he

was

personally

interested

in

stock

markets.

He

smiled

and

said

yes

—

he

actively

invests

too.

That

made

for

a

nice

ending

to

the

discussion.

4.

FE

Round

1

After

being

promoted

to

the

Framework

Engineer

role

(based

on

my

resume),

my

interview

started

with

the

usual

introduction.

The

interviewer

then

moved

into

some

basic

technical

questions,

like

the

difference

between

C++

and

Java .

From

there,

the

focus

shifted

to

my

projects.

●

On

Profit

View ,

he

asked

me

about

the

working

of

the

system,

why

I

chose

specific

technologies,

and

the

role

of

message

queues

and

Redis

caching .

●

Next,

we

moved

to

Mark

Me .

I

explained

for

2–3

minutes

straight,

covering

why

I

chose

the

project,

the

problems

we

faced,

and

how

we

solved

them.

●

Chronologically,

he

then

asked

about

Legal

AI .

Specifically,

he

wanted

me

to

explain

what

RAG

is.

I

gave

a

detailed

2–3

minute

explanation

of

my

pipeline

—

including

saving

data

in

Astra

DB

and

the

flow

of

the

retrieval

process.

He

seemed

quite

impressed

with

this

project.

●

Since

my

primary

language

is

Java,

I

expected

some

heavy

DSA

questions,

but

surprisingly,

he

only

asked

very

basic

ones.

For

example:

●

“Given

the

area

of

a

circle,

find

its

radius.”

●

A

couple

of

easy

SQL

questions

—

one

on

filtering

(like

names

ending

with

"YADAV")

and

one

on

simple

joins.

The

entire

interview

lasted

40–45

minutes .

Key

Takeaways:

1.

The

interviewer

was

more

interested

in

my

projects

because

they

had

practical

use

cases

and

impact.

2.

For

one

of

my

friends,

the

interviewer

asked

a

much

tougher

question:

“ Write

code

to

fetch

live

coordinates

of

the

user

without

using

any

reference

docs

”

So

the

difficulty

can

vary

a

lot.

4.

FE

Round

2

My

second

interview

was

quite

short

and

casual,

lasting

only

about

15–20

minutes .

It

began

with

a

simple

“Introduce

yourself,”

and

I

kept

my

introduction

brief

and

to

the

point.

The

interviewer

mainly

focused

on

my

projects:

●

He

first

asked

about

Profit

View

(Stock

Market

Project) .

●

Then

he

moved

to

Mark

Me .

Since

I

mentioned

that

I

am

a

follower

of

ISKCON,

he

lightly

questioned

me

on

how

I

manage

to

work

on

stock

market

projects,

considering

it’s

not

typically

encouraged.

This

part

felt

more

like

a

conversation

than

a

formal

interview.

After

that,

he

asked

about

the

databases

I

knew

and

a

couple

of

very

basic

questions

on

the

difference

between

SQL

and

NoSQL .

He

also

asked

about

the

backend

technologies

I’m

familiar

with,

but

only

at

an

informational

level

—

there

was

no

deep

cross-questioning.

Towards

the

end,

he

asked

the

standard

“ Why

Quantiphi?

Who

are

Quantiphi’s

competitors? ”

and

reminded

me

that

the

Pre-Placement

Talk

(PPT)

is

very

important,

as

it

helps

us

understand

the

company

better

before

interviews.

Overall,

it

was

a

light

and

comfortable

interview

—

more

of

a

discussion

than

a

grilling

session

—

and

the

interviewer

seemed

satisfied

with

my

answers.

5.

HR

Round

Unlike

a

typical

HR

round,

this

one

focused

on

management

and

stakeholder

questions .

The

panel

began

by

asking

me

to

introduce

myself

—

but

specifically

told

me

not

to

mention

any

projects.

They

then

asked

several

situational

questions

like:

●

“If

your

team

members

are

not

working,

how

would

you

tackle

them?”

●

“How

would

you

convince

stakeholders

to

buy

your

product?”

At

one

point

they

said:

“You

are

linking

each

question

to

your

project

—

what

possible

flaws

can

you

detect

in

the

project?

If

you

knew

them,

what

actions

did

you

take

to

overcome

them,

and

how

would

you

still

manage

to

retain

consumers

even

after

those

problems?”

I

explained

everything

properly:

how

we

identified

flaws,

the

corrective

steps

we

implemented,

and

the

communication/mitigation

strategies

we

used

to

keep

users

engaged

despite

issues.

Since

I

was

leading

a

team

of

four

on

my

ongoing

project,

I

used

those

experiences

to

answer

the

management

scenarios

—

showing

concrete

examples

of

problem

detection

After

nearly

3

hours

of

waiting ,

results

were

announced

around

9:30–10

PM:

8

students

were

selected

(3

FE,

2

MLE,

3

BA).

journey.prep:
Stay

Positive

and

Believe

in

Yourself

:

The

placement

process

can

be

long

and

stressful.

Losing

hope

or

feeling

demotivated

is

absolutely

normal,

but

always

believe

in

yourself

and

keep

putting

in

consistent

effort.

Better

things

are

on

the

way.

Talking

to

your

friends

and

family

during

tough

times

really

helps

keep

your

mind

calm

and

motivated.

Prepare

Based

on

Company

Patterns

:

Go

through

previous

interview

experiences

for

the

company

you’re

targeting.

Some

companies

grill

your

resume

thoroughly,

some

focus

on

Java

or

DSA,

while

others

might

focus

on

computer

fundamentals.

Knowing

the

pattern

helps

you

prioritize

topics

effectively.

Know

Your

Resume

Inside

Out

:

Be

prepared

for

questions

like

“Why

did

you

build

this

project?”

or

“How

would

you

improve

it

further?”.

Small

bluffs

are

fine,

but

avoid

putting

anything

on

your

resume

that

you

can’t

confidently

explain.

Cover

Both

DSA

and

Fundamentals

:

Don’t

limit

yourself

to

DSA

alone.

Computer

fundamentals

like

OS,

DBMS,

OOPS,

and

Networks

are

equally

important.

For

DSA,

go

through

Striver’s

Sheet

and

give

contests

on

CodeForces

and

LeetCode.

For

computer

fundamentals,

practice

from

Sanfoundry

or

GFG.

These

will

help

you

in

Online

Assessments

as

well

as

interviews.

Stay

Calm

During

Interviews:

Interviews

can

be

nerve-wracking.

I

once

felt

nervous

in

an

interview

and

ended

up

answering

wrongly,

which

got

me

frustrated

and

affected

my

confidence

for

the

remaining

questions.

To

avoid

this,

practice

mock

interviews

with

friends

or

seniors.

They

help

you

get

comfortable

under

pressure.

Trust

the

Process

and

Don’t

Compare

: Trust

God’s

plan

and

your

own

journey.

Failures

are

an

unavoidable

part

of

growth.

Don’t

compare

yourself

with

others—it

only

adds

unnecessary

stress.

Virat

Kohli

waited

18

years

to

win

his

trophy,

Sharma

lifted

one

a

the

league

began

.

Everyone

has

their

own

timeline;

your

journey

without

rushing

through

JUST

TRUST

THE

PROCESS.

ALL

THE

BEST

!!!

journey.howSecured:
The process had 4 rounds. 
1) OA 
2) Technical Interview 1 
3) Technical Interview 2
4) HR Interview
Quantiphi offered 3 roles, FE (Framework Engineer), MLE (Machine Learning Engineer) and BA (Business 
Analyst). We were supposed to order our preference in the Superset Application. 
(To read the ML Interview Experience skip over to page 3)
1.     OA  [ 133 Appeared ]
We had 3 sections
1) Aptitude, Logical & Verbal Reasoning:   40 Questions - 30 Minutes
2) CS Fundamentals:                                    33 Questions - 25 Minutes
3) Coding Problems                                      3 Questions - 30 Minutes
The amount of time was limited, so speed was the key to getting through in this round.
The first section was mostly as expected, but there were quite a few difficult problems on permutations and 
a few other topics. There were also a lot of problems on Area and Volume calculations (What is the profit if 
you sell the material extracted from a pyramid (and a cone) for 10 Rs/cm^3 and you bought the pyramid for 
200). But I had to skip most of these because the time was limited and we didn’t have calcis allowed. My 
advice would be to attempt this section in multiple iterations, solving the easiest questions in the first 
one, then the next and so on. Can’t stress this enough, but time is a huge constraint here so manage it 
well. 
The second section was CS fundamentals (and little dev too). We had general theory based questions 
from OOPs, DBMS and OS. This was pretty standard. There were unexpected questions though that were 
the you know it or you don’t type. 
The final Section had 3 coding problems. An easy one, an easy-medium and a difficult one.
● A thief wants to rob all the houses in a village. There is an array of the number of houses in each 
neighbourhood and the maximum amount of time(hours) he can take. At what minimum speed in 
houses per hour does he need to rob to clean the entire village ?
You just need to take the sum of the houses and divide this number by the total time to get the 
rate of robbing. Round it off to the higher number and return the integer answer. 
● A question very similar to the House Robber Problem from Leetcode. It was a basic include-exclude 
DP problem with one if condition. I didn’t even need to apply DP as the first Recursive code that I 
ran passed all testcases. Link 
● You are given an undirected graph of n islands, each with a loot value, and edges representing travel 
paths between islands with their travel times. A pirate may start from any island, traveling along 
available paths, and can visit each island at most once. The total loot is the sum of the visited islands’ 
values, while the total time is the sum of the travel times along the chosen path. Find the maximum 
loot the pirate can collect.
I was able to solve the first 2 problems but ran out of time attempting the 3rd one. 
2.     FE Interview 1  [ 17(FE) + 17(MLE) + 58(BA - GD followed by interviews)] [ 4:30 PM]
I had mistakenly selected FE as my first preference so I informed my FE Interviewer that I wanted MLE. 
We had been notified of this inward mobility for Roles in the Presentation. I was asked to complete this 
interview after which my request would go on to be processed.
We started with this round with me introducing myself and the interviewer going through my resume. We 
discussed all my projects (2 ML, 2 Dev) one after another and he asked plenty of questions as I was 
explaining. Be thoroughly prepared with your projects and don’t fake anything. You should be prepared to 
answer questions like “Why did you use this service and not the other (Postgres vs Mongo, AWS vs Azure, 
etc)  ?”, “Are there any live applications that provide this service, how does your project compare to 
theirs ?”, “What changes would you make if you wanted to serve 10k users with your project (Scalability is 
a very popular question) and other questions that question the inner mechanics of your project like “What 
purpose does this feature resolve ?”, “Couldn’t you have simplified things this way, your approach is very 
inefficient.”  and so on. Not every interviewer goes in this deep but there are ones that do.. (Baker 😭)
After the resume we started with his questions. He didn’t ask any really difficult questions on DSA or SQL 
that needed time, this was more of an itinerary of easy to medium theory and coding problems. Here are a 
few of those:
● Do you know about normalization ? What is the difference between 1NF and 3NF normalization ?
● What is polymorphism ? How do we implement it ?
● Can you tell me about Indexing ? What are the drawbacks of Indexing ?
● Write an SQL query to remove duplicate entries from a database. (I used row_number() and 
partitioned by PK, after which I removed all entries with a row_num higher than 1)
● Can you do this problem without using windowing functions ? 
There were quite a few questions around this difficulty level and I was able to answer most of them. After 
this round I was asked to appear for Interview 2 where I was informed that I will now be taken to their ML 
Engineer to appear for MLE Interview 1.
3.    MLE Interview 1 & 2 [ 6:30 PM & 7:30 PM]
I would like to start this section with an overview of what I think of ML Interviews. These are just the views 
of a guy that has given 2 ML interviews so read them with a grain of salt. 
There is no defined structure to gauge a candidate’s ability for an ML position at the graduate level. 
So Interviewers are going to ask you a very wide variety of questions and your selection depends on how 
much you can impress them across the duration of the exchange. Here is my personal order of importance 
for the subjects of your interview:
1) Your Projects: Can’t stress this enough, but your projects are your best shot at showcasing your 
skills to the interviewer and showing how deep of an understanding you have in the concepts you’ve 
used in these projects. The interviewer can’t just ask you to explain the architecture of a GNN Model 
to test you because that isn't something you can expect the average candidate to know.
You need to dominate this discussion and tell the interviewer of every sellable skill you’ve 
utilized. Tell him about the nature of the dataset you used, about the challenges you faced in feature 
engineering, about the tools you used to clean/filter the data and augment samples. Tell him about 
why you chose your Model over the alternatives (for me it was why I chose BiLSTM over LSTM 
and GRU) and about the architecture of your model and what understandings you derived while 
working on the model and so on.
2) Fundamentals: The interviewer will then start asking questions to test your fundamentals such as
● What is regression ? How do you differentiate between it and classification ?
● What do you mean by clustering ?
● What will you do if your dataset has a lot of missing values ?
● Why do some models with good training accuracy have bad test accuracy ?
● What is bias vs variance tradeoff ?
● What are false positives and negatives ?
● What are precision and recall and when do they become useful ?
● What metrics did you use to judge your model and explain the significance of each metric ? (I 
answered the confusion matrix, classification report containing accuracy, precision, recall, f1-
score, and the Learning curve comparing training and validation sets)
There will be plenty of questions like this and they can be prepared for in advance.
3) Your Knowledge of ML Models: In the midst of the questions focusing on fundamentals, the 
interviewer also kept asking me questions on popular models. These included
● What is Linear Regression ? Is it related to Logistic regression ?
● Please explain how a Decision Tree works ? Can you draw an example for us ?
● Why do we need Unsupervised Learning ? Can you talk about any popular models 
Unsupervised Learning holds ?
● What is an ensemble model ?
● What will you do when faced with an Image based dataset.
Having a basic understanding of these models is sufficient, you don’t need to be an expert in 
everything.
I think this discussion includes most of the questions asked to me during the interviews. I’ll list the few 
remaining questions here:
● The interviewer asked me if I had deployed any models ? 
● He asked me if I had worked with NLP ? (I started talking about the need to process words and the 
Bag-of-Words Model. I had very surface level knowledge on this matter..)
● He then started to ask more detailed questions related to NLP but I was unable to answer them, from 
his body language it seemed like he expected a little more. In popular ML culture we see everyone 
talking about Deep Learning but NLP spans a whole lot of projects too and is not as much talked 
about. Can read a few things up. 
● He presented to me a situation where I had a dataset of sentences that were classified as good and 
bad and we needed a model that could predict sentences in this manner.
This concludes almost all of what I was asked in MLE Interviews 1 and 2. I haven’t separated the interviews 
into two sections because the flow of the interviews was very similar and it didn’t make sense to separate 
them. The only difference was that the second interview didn’t involve as many fundamental questions as 
the first one and was a little more intense. There was a bit of grilling involved in both the interviews and the 
first one went on for over an hour. The second one was a bit short at 30 minutes.
This was followed by the HR interview. The selection from FE/MLE/BA Interview 1 to Interview 2 
was very brutal. The rate of progression from Interview 1 to Interview 2 at Quantiphi was far lower than the 
average company. 
4.    HR Interview  [ 13 shortlisted, 3 MLE and 10 FE+BA] [ 8:30 PM]
This was a typical “HR Interview”. There weren’t any tough questions, just enquiring things about you. 
Questions included. It lasted a relaxed 15-20 minutes.
After the HR interview we had to wait for almost an hour as all the Interviewers and Execs discussed 
amongst themselves. Finally the shortlist was released around 10 PM and 8 candidates were selected. 
The selectees were 2 from MLE, 3 from FE and 3 from BA.

journey.howSecured:
A total of 3 rounds were conducted - 1 Online Assessment Round, 1 Tech Interview Round & 
Finally 1 HR Round. All were conducted on the same day 5/08/25. The CGPA Criteria for SDE 
was 8.5, later reduced to 8. It was further reduced to 7.5. May not be the case for next year 
if they don’t want more applicants, so it is preferable to maintain a pointer of 8.5 and above. 
(I have included CGPA) 
1. Resume/CGPA Shortlisting: (In this case it was CGPA shortlisting, but still I have provided 
guidance for Resume shortlisting) 
Always tailor your resume to align with the specific job description of the role you're 
applying for . These adjustments don't need to be major — simply swapping a project, 
updating certifications, or modifying the skills section can make a significant difference. 
Ensure that your resume maintains visual and structural consistency. Avoid mixing date 
formats, bullet styles, or using bold/italic formatting inconsistently across sections. A clean, 
well-organized resume gives a strong first impression. 
Once your resume is finalized, evaluate its compatibility with Applicant Tracking Systems 
(ATS). Tools like Resume Worded can help — aim for a score of 65 or above. 
Initially, the CGPA eligibility criteria for this role was set at 8.5, but it was later relaxed to 7.5. 
The shortlist of candidates selected for the Online Assessment and Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) 
was released on 3rd August 2025 at 7:00 PM. 
 
2. Pre-Placement Talk: 
The Pre-Placement Talk was conducted online on 4th August 2025 at 5:00 PM. 
The information shared during Pre-Placement Talks is extremely valuable, so it's important 
to be attentive — not just to the content of the presentation, but also to the names and 
roles of the presenters. I made it a point to take multiple screenshots and jot down the 
specific examples used while the speaker explained some of the company's financial 
services. These details often come in handy during interviews. 
While it's a good idea to ask thoughtful questions at the end of the session, it's even smarter 
to hold back a few insightful ones. Save them for your interview — this gives you an 
opportunity to show continued curiosity and engagement with the company during later 
stages. 
 
3. Online Assessment: (Approx. 160 students appeared, invigilated by the company) 
The online assessment comprised 70 questions to be completed in 90 minutes. It was 
conducted via Google Forms at the college premises. The marking scheme awarded +1 for 
each correct answer and imposed a -0.25 penalty for incorrect ones. The assessment 
covered four major sections: Java, Python, SQL, and Aptitude. 
Java (18 Questions): 
This section focused heavily on fundamental OOP concepts in Java. Topics included the 
Collection Framework (TreeMap, HashMap, LinkedHashMap, ConcurrentHashMap, 
ArrayList), access modifiers, threads and multithreading, keywords like synchronized and 
volatile, compile-time and runtime polymorphism, interfaces, abstract classes, exception 
handling, enums, and functional methods like map, filter, and reduce. 
Most questions were of the “guess the output” type. Although my primary DSA language is 
C++, I had thoroughly studied and revised Java concepts beforehand. A great resource for 
MCQ practice: 
Java Practice - Sanfoundry 
Python (17 Questions): 
Similar to Java, the Python section included “guess the output” questions involving OOP 
concepts, inheritance and MRO (Method Resolution Order), shallow vs deep copies, list 
comprehensions, slicing, dictionaries, sets, stacks, and queues. Many questions required 
careful dry runs and a strong grasp of Python’s internal behavior and edge cases. 
A good practice resource: 
Python Practice - Sanfoundry 
SQL (5 Questions): 
This section tested practical SQL query-writing skills. The difficulty level was moderate, with 
questions based on GROUP BY , JOIN, ORDER BY , UPDATE, DELETE, and various date functions. 
Some tricky questions involved updating joined or aggregated tables. Attempt only if 
confident. 
Highly recommended: 
Top 50 SQL Questions - LeetCode 
Aptitude (30 Questions): 
This was arguably the most challenging section. It covered clock problems, speed and 
distance, trigonometry, upstream-downstream problems, probability, combinatorics, 
statistics, geometry, family relationships, and financial mathematics (including stocks and 
investments). 
Some questions were quite verbose and difficult to interpret, and I couldn’t solve a few. Two 
great resources for aptitude practice are: 
 YouTube Aptitude Series by CareerRide 
 IndiaBix Aptitude Practice 
I performed well in the Java, Python, and SQL sections but found the Aptitude section 
challenging. In total, I attempted around 50–55 out of 70 questions. Fortunately, I was 
among the 44 students shortlisted out of 160. 
Final Tips: 
Keep your technical concepts in Java and Python fresh, practice aptitude regularly to build 
speed, and remain calm under pressure. Time constraints will challenge everyone equally—
focus on accuracy, avoid panic, and read questions carefully. 
 
4. Technical Round 1: [44 student appeared] 2 interviewers in my panel 
As I mentioned earlier, I was unsure of whether I’d be selected for interviews or not. So, I 
was keeping my cool and doing last minute revisions for Java. Around 12:15 pm we received 
the shortlists and I was delighted to see my name at the 17th position. I quickly had a small 
snack before the interviews start so that I am not empty stomach (make sure to eat at least a 
little and not be completely empty stomach due to stress/tension).  
I was very lucky with my interview slot and timings, I was scheduled for 2nd interview in my 
panel. My interview lasted about 30-40 minutes. And there were 2 interviewers in my panel. 
Even if your interview gets scheduled late, don’t worry and do your best. 
I will keep my experience as detailed as possible. 
I entered the cabin and greeted both the panelists, they asked me about my name and 
branch (Didn’t ask me to introduce myself). They asked me why did I choose Data Science 
branch. I was honest and said that during that time I was naïve and wanted to pursue a 
career in data science without much understanding of it, I basically explained how I 
understood and explored other options and found my interest in software development. 
They asked me what backend technologies I had explored, I had done Node.js + Express 
framework and Django in python. He disappointedly asked whether I had not tried Java for 
backend. I answered this question very carefully and told him that I had studied Java for my 
2nd Sem and then I had developed games like Snake and minesweeper using Java, and like 
justified that I know Java. Whereas for backend development my fundamentals are clear 
enough that switching the language won’t be an issue for me. He was happy with my 
response. 
Then he shifted the interview towards Java OOPs, He showed me one of the question from 
Java section in OA.  
 
He started asking whether do I see something wrong in Class Person or a way we can make it 
better. I suggested making string private and having getter and setter method to ensure 
that the name string is not directly accessible from outside of class and only via getter and 
setter method. He asked me which concept was OOPs is this, I answered Encapsulation and 
explained what it meant in this scenario.  
He then asked me about the output of the code, I answered “2 100”. Later they asked me 
how can I make the output to be 1 100. So, I suggested overriding equals and hashcode 
methods provided my HashMap class in Person class to behave such that if the name is 
equal, It will treat it as same object otherwise as different object. He also asked to improve 
the declaration of HashMap object. At first, I couldn’t understand what exactly was needed 
to be done, I suggested having Person class object be immutable as there is a risk of key 
getting corrupted due to change in data within a Person object. Then they asked a follow up 
on what is a immutable class, I explained how to make a class immutable and also 
mentioned about enums. For the earlier question, Later they give me hints and I understood 
and explained that having a ref of parent and object of child class is a better practice in 
Java, as you can change the object to any other child of the parent without having to change 
the ref.  
Map<Person, Integer> mp = new HashMap<>();  

was the answer they were looking for . I needed hints but I caught on to it at the very end. 
They asked me to write a very simple program to remove all the white spaces from a string 
and return the string. I requested whether I could use C++, and I wrote it on piece of paper, I 
started by writing #include<stdio.h> but they said it’s fine and write the logic, so I made a 
function with proper name like removeWhiteSpaces and passed in the string and simply 
iterated over it and checked whether if the character is non space then append it to ans 
string and return ans. The interviewer commented that he liked how I made a function 
instead of writing in Main.  
Then they asked me about a simple SQL query involving a join and order by and limit to get 
the first row. I also said that it’s possible to use max(date) to get the row with latest date.  
The interview questions ended on a brighter note.  
Questions I asked to interviewers: 
1. I asked them to introduce themselves and their role. 
2. How is AI being integrated within ISS and what’s its impact has been for ISS. (I tried 
to enter the convo when they jokingly said that people in the company sometimes 
don’t understand their own code as they use AI and that is why they do code 
reviews. Here I tried to showcase how I personally use AI as more of a tutor for 
learning and deep diving into concepts) 
3. I don’t remember exactly how but they were talking about data scrapping, and I took 
the opportunity and I replied that I have experience with data scrapping as well and 
how I made a script to scrape linkedIn profile data from their user urls using selenium 
and beautiful soup. 
By the end of this, they asked me where do I stay and whether commute will be a problem.  
And just after 10 minutes of leaving the cabin at 2 pm, I was notified that I have been 
shortlisted for next round.  
Why I Think I Got Selected: 
 Timing & Luck: I got an early interview slot, which helped. 
 Confidence & Communication: I stayed composed and articulated my thoughts 
clearly. 
 Honesty: I was transparent about what I knew and didn’t. 
 Engagement: I asked meaningful questions and engaged in a two-way conversation. 
Even if you don’t know something don’t stay completely silent and keep processing your 
thoughts out and don’t panic. Your personality and confidence also matters, try to work on 
soft skills and effective communication. Give as much mock interviews as you can to better 
prepare yourself. 
In total 15 students were shortlisted for HR round including me.  
Tips: 
 Do not lie on your Resume but you can smartly change phrases so that your resume 
looks good. 
 Do not throw the sheets/papers in which you did your OA questions. They can be 
asked in an 
interview. 
 Make sure if you are adding any links then they are clickable in your resume 
 Prepare well around your resume projects & its tech stack. You can ask your friend to 
keep on cross questioning you on them 
 Prepare a couple of scenarios (even if fake) about disagreement in the team, or any 
times that you have shown leadership/ team spirit. These questions are very 
common too. 
 If you don’t know the answer or you are not able to recall it, try to put it across 
politely instead of saying something wrong 
 Think out loud when solving a DSA problem/ SQL query but when saying a theory 
answer try to sort of structure it in your mind first. Make use of technical terms & 
examples where possible 
 
5. HR Round: [15 students Appeared]  2 panelists 
My HR round started at around 3:50 pm, I had prepared in advance for all the common HR 
questions which could be asked. Even if you get caught off guard do not panic and be calm 
and collected, answer it genuinely. My HR round lasted for about 30 minutes. 
I entered the room and greeted the interviewers, their first question was do you know us. I 
had paid attention to PPT so I knew their names and I had mentioned that their cameras 
were not working properly so I didn’t realize it instantly but by listening to their voice. They 
first asked me about my education from 10th, 12th and College CGPA and Cet score. I 
answered the question by making a narrative about how I wasn’t very studious and how I 
got serious about studies and answered each question. They asked me about my family 
background, make sure to answer only what is needed and not more than that. I showcased 
how being a single child, my parents have been supportive and available for me. She also 
asked whether I knew the office location and visited the NESCO IT park, I replied with correct 
answer and was honest that I hadn’t been there. 
She asked me about why did I pursue CSE DS, I again answered genuinely and told her the 
truth. She asked me about my 1st coding project, I mentioned I had gotten into game 
development using Unity and later using Java built snake and minesweeper games. She also 
asked me about masters and would I want to pursue it. I answered no (I genuinely hadn’t 
planned for masters) mentioned that how skills, experience and practical knowledge in 
industry is required to stay relevant and masters is more theoretical and academia focussed. 
So, I would rather up skill myself while working in a job. She pressed on even more about the 
fact that aren’t my parents insisting for me to do masters since I am a single child. Again, I 
thought carefully and answered that it was different during my father’s time where a degree 
was required to grow in pharmaceutical companies. Whereas in tech I don’t need as much 
education, having experience and skills are the most important thing. (Try to justify the 
trade off between masters and job) 
How do I stay relevant about the tech news. I said Youtube, Reddit, Twitter and justified my 
perspective. She started asking me about my perspective about AI, I made sure to answer 
everything positively. I said AI is a tool and won’t completely replace a human, at least not 
until there is a very fundamental change in how AI works. I made sure to cover the positive 
aspects of AI, she said would it have any impact on jobs? And I said that due to this for 
example 10 people doing some work would be reduced to 5-6, but there could be other jobs 
for managing agentic AI systems. She asked me how would I make sure I don’t get replaced 
with AI. I again answered that not staying in the comfort zone for a long time is the key and 
always having continuous growth and learning is essential.  
She also asked me about my hobbies, I answered reading, table tennis, badminton, 
swimming. I made sure to elaborate on how reading was not my strong point and how I 
developed that skill effectively. Sir had only asked me a single question about what is my 
preference regarding application developer and AIML. I made sure to answer diplomatically, 
I said my primary focus is on developing software either for clients or for some internal 
company usage, and within software development I want to keep my options broader and so 
that I am able to figure out my interests, etc. And how I could maybe help others get a new 
perspective in software development processes using my ML and Gen AI knowledge, so no 
knowledge ever goes waste.  
She lastly asked where do I stay and whether commute would be a problem for me. I live in 
thane so I said it won’t be a big issue for me as I have been travelling for SPIT for the past 3 
years. And if I do find it difficult, I would simply shift closer towards the company and ensure 
it doesn’t hamper my work. 
I made sure to ask decent questions: 
1. How is data staleness managed as old data cannot be served to clients 
2. Since ISS is multi-national company serving over 15+ countries, how do they manage 
and maintain regulatory compliance for each country. 
3. How does team and project allotment work for interns and freshers in ISS  
 
HR Interview Tips: 
1. Maintain Eye Contact 
Ensure steady, natural eye contact with the interviewer. It shows confidence and 
helps build a connection, but avoid staring as it may come across as forced. 
2. Be Mindful of What You Share 
Avoid oversharing personal experiences that don’t directly address the question. 
Focus on relevant, concise answers that highlight your suitability for the role. 
3. Use the STAR Method 
Structure your answers to behavioral questions using the STAR method (Situation, 
Task, Action, Result). It provides clarity and demonstrates a problem-solving mindset. 
4. Show Respect in All Responses 
Be polite and professional. Even casual or off-topic comments should be delivered 
respectfully to avoid unintentionally offending the interviewer. 
5. Frame Strengths and Weaknesses as Narratives 
Share your strengths and weaknesses with context. Use short stories or examples 
(real or carefully crafted) that showcase growth and self-awareness. 
6. Avoid Monologues 
Don’t treat your answers like speeches. Keep the conversation balanced, concise, and 
interactive. Know when to stop and where to elaborate. 
7. Display Confidence and Personality 
Strong communication and soft skills often outweigh technical skills in HR rounds. Let 
your personality come through—be confident, composed, and clear . 
8. Always be Positive                                                                                                                                                    
Always answer all questions in a positive manner and I’ll suggest don’t ask for 
feedback in an HR interview, you can in a technical round if you feel that you’ve done 
great. 
9. Always Deny plans for Higher Studies 
Never show interest or accidently hint your passion for academia and research. 
Prepare solid reasons to justify why you’re choosing industry over academia, or it 
may become your reason for rejection. 
 
Lastly, 12 students were selected out of 15, including myself. 2 for Data quality, 2 for 
software testing, 8 for Software Engineering.

journey.howSecured:
A total of 3 rounds were conducted - 1 Online Assessment Round, 1 Tech Interview Round & Finally 1 HR  
Round. All were conducted on the same day. The CGPA Criteria for SDE was 8.5, later reduced to 8. It was 
further reduced to 7.5. It may not be the case for next year if they don’t want more applicants, so it is preferable 
to maintain a pointer of 8.5 and above. 
 
1.   Resume / CGPA Shortlisting: 
Curate your resume to align closely with the company’s job description, emphasising your key strengths. After 
finalising it, evaluate its ATS compatibility using platforms such as Resume Worded, targeting a score of 65 
or higher. The shortlisted candidates for the Online Assessment and Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) were declared 
on 3rd August 2025 at 7:00 PM. 
Pre-Placement Talk 
While the process was originally planned to take place offline, it was later shifted to an online format and 
conducted at 5 PM on 4th August. During the PPT session, make it a point to listen attentively and note down 
the names and roles of the presenters -- this small detail can prove valuable in later interactions.  
 
Preparing in advance is equally important; gather basic information about the company such as its  founding 
year, current CEO, and tagline. These details are not only potential question topics but also help you make a 
positive impression by showing genuine interest. Toward the end of the PPT, consider asking well -thought-
out questions to demonstrate engagement, though it’s not mandatory.  
If you prefer, you can reserve your questions for the post-interview phase, where they may carry even greater 
impact. 
 
2.    Online Assessment: [ Approx. 160 students appeared ] 
The online assessment comprised 70 questions to be completed in 90 minutes. It was conducted via Google  
Forms at the college premises. +1 was given for each correct answer and -0.25 for incorrect ones. We were 
allowed to use the system calculator. It was invigilated by the company executives. 
The assessment covered four major sections: Java  (18), Python (17), SQL (5), and Aptitude (30) – Total 70 
questions.  
The Java and Python sections were largely output -based MCQs, with a strong emphasis on OOPS concepts, 
errors, exceptions, stacks, queues, and all types of sets in Java. Some questions, such as “Determine the total 
number of swaps in the given array using bubble sort”  (with an array provided), were a bit time-consuming. 
It’s advisable to tackle such questions later and prioriti ze quicker ones first . Make sure you are thoroughly 
familiar with Java and Python syntax. Since Python was my secondary programming language, I struggled 
with 2–3 questions due to not knowing the exact syntax. 
For SQL Section, queries were asked for the given table and the required output. The queries covered  topics 
like aggregate functions, date functions, subqueries. The questions were on easy to medium level but all the 
options looked similar at first sight – but had slight differences, making it a bit time-consuming and needing 
a double check. 
I was able to complete the first three sections in 40 minutes, leaving the remaining 50 minutes for the aptitude 
section. 
The Aptitude round consisted of the normal Quantitative Aptitude questions such as Percentages,  Ratios, 
Time-Distance, Boat Upstream-Downstream, Probability, Data Interpretation etc. The questions were on an 
easy level with few medium ones. The key was to identify and solve questions you are most confident and are 
well versed with required formulae or logic. 
 
3.    Technical Round: [ 44 students appeared ] 
I was the last candidate in my panel, and my panelist was the Associate Director at ISS-STOXX. My interview 
lasted for about an hour — the only panel to conduct interviews for that long. It began at 7:30 PM, by which 
time many students had already completed their HR rounds and left. So, if you find yourself waiting outside 
the TPO for hours, don’t panic or stress yourself out. 
 
 
The interview began with her asking my name. She then went through my resume and asked about my 
internship, which I had completed during my diploma. She asked me what skills I had acquired during the 
internship and my overall experience. 
 
Next, she asked what I had prepared for the interview. I mentioned DBMS, OS, SQL, OOPS  and also added 
that I had studied software testing. Be careful whatever you mention will be explored in depth. She then asked 
for a brief explanation of one of my projects, followed by a few questions on its implementation. 
 
Since I had stated Java as my primary programming language, she asked me a few questions about JDK, JRE, 
and JVM, and then about how and why Java is considered platform-independent. Make sure you are clear on 
these basic Java architecture concepts. 
 
The discussion then moved to SQL queries. The first was to find the maximum salary in each department, 
followed by the query to find the top two salaries in each department. I had to write the queries on paper. She 
then added gender and city columns to the same table and asked for the names of female employees with the 
maximum salary in their respective departments. 
 
Next, the discussion moved to OOP concepts in Java. I was asked to briefly explain the four pillars of OOP. 
Then, the interviewer presented a few classes — Shape, Rectangle, Square, and Circle — and asked me to 
apply inheritance to them. Initially, I designed Shape as an interface and implemented hierarchical inheritance, 
where Rectangle, Square, and Circle each implemented the Shape interface. She then encouraged me to think 
of a more convenient approach. That’s when I realized she was expecting multilevel inheritance, such as 
Shape → Rectangle → Square, since every Square is a Rectangle. 
Following that, she introduced a Rhombus class and asked me to integrate it into the inheritance tree. Initially 
unsure, I asked about its properties and understood that, just like every Square is a Rectangle, every Square is 
also a Rhombus . I then attempted to inherit Square from both Rectangle and Rhombus, which led to a 
discussion on the diamond problem in Java, its solutions, and the use of the super keyword. 
 
Then came the DSA questions, the first question was to remove all occurrences of a given key from a linked 
list. I explained my approach in detail before writing the source code. I fumbled slightly while handling the 
pointers but kept thinking aloud and explaining my reasoning. I later wrote the correct code and dry-ran it on 
both the given list and an additional test case to check for edge cases. The second DSA question was 
straightforward — return true if there are three consecutive odd numbers, else return false. 
 
Finally, I was asked a commonly known puzzle: Mislabelled Jars 
 
The interview concluded with me asking the panelist about her own experience at ISS-STOXX — current role 
in the company, and experience in the tech industry. 
 
4.    HR Round: [ 15 students appeared ] 
There were two interviewers in this round — the same ones who had conducted the pre -placement talk. I  
would advise remembering their names, as interviewers sometimes ask if you know them. I was again the last 
candidate for the HR round, which lasted about 30–35 minutes and ended around 10 PM. 
 
 
The conversation began with an introduction about myself and my family background, followed by questions 
about my 10th-grade percentage, diploma percentage, and current CGPA. My diploma caught their attention, 
and they asked why I chose to pursue a diploma  instead of completing 12th grade and attempting JEE/CET. 
I’d advise all DSE students to prepare well for this question, as it is frequently asked in interviews. 
Next, they asked about my interest in technology. I shared that I had been passionate about full stack 
development since my diploma days. This led to a question about my favourite project, for which I described 
one of my ML projects. They probed deeper into it — asking how I came up with the problem statement, the 
overall design, the reason behind my choice of technology, possible alternative technologies, and potential 
edge cases. They also asked about the challenges I faced during development. 
Since my resume listed two ML projects and only one fully dedicated full stack project — and I had chosen 
an ML project as my favourite — they expressed concern about my fit at ISS-STOXX, as the company doesn’t 
work extensively with AI/ML. I clarified that although the projects were ML -based, their core still relied on 
full stack development fundamentals — including a robust backend, scalable database, and interactive 
frontend. When given a hypothetical choice between working on a completely full stack project or a purely 
ML project at ISS, I confidently said I would choose the full stack one, as it has always been my forte and I 
am excited to explore the technologies ISS uses. 
The interviewer knew that the last com pany which came before ISS-STOXX was Nomura, and asked why I 
couldn’t clear its process . This led to questions about how many interviews I had given before, and why I 
thought I couldn’t clear them. My suggestion to others would be to answer such questions honestly, showing 
self-awareness about areas of improvement and demonstrating that you have worked on them. 
The interview concluded with me asking if the company organizes internal hackathons or other competitive 
events for employees. They replied that, at present, they do not, but expressed strong interest and agreed that 
it was indeed a great idea that I gave them. I added that hosting such events could enhance interaction 
among employees, encourage exploration of new technologies, and ultimately benefit the company. 
The final results came at around 11 PM. 
 
 
Finally, 12 students got the offer !!

Russell

Investments

conducted

their

first

internship

drive

in

India

for

our

batch

which

included

many

roles.

informed

us

about

3

roles:

Technology

Intern,

Business

Process

Automation

Intern,

Investment

Research

Intern.

The

rest

of

the

interview

process

was

done

completely

at

their

office

or

through

online

interviews.

The

HRs

informed

us

directly

about

rounds

through

mail

or

calls.

1.

Test

(40

minutes) [30

on

day

1

and

approx.

~25

on

day

2]

●

10

Aptitude

MCQ

●

10

CS

Fundamental

MCQ

3

coding

questions

(Attempt

any

2)

-

Valid

Parenthesis,

Binary

Search

Pseudo

code,

Second

Max

Element

in

array.

test

was

very

easy.

this

was

not

an

elimination

round.

[30

on

day

1

and

approx.

~25

on

day

2]

interview

was

conducted

by

a

Frontend

Developer

and

Devops

Engineer.

interview

focused

mainly

on

my

resume.

discussion

was

regarding

my

internship

and

my

projects.

from

this

I

was

asked

1

leetcode

easy

question

-

find

common

elements

in

2

strings.

few

database

related

questions

were

asked

as

well.

Round

2

[

of

candidates

who

appeared

for

this

round

]

round

was

conducted

by

the

of

Application

Development.

interviewer

focused

on

my

resume.

asked

me

questions

about

my

projects

from

a

business

perspective.

why

would

organizations

choose

my

applications

above

other

companies

or

build

it

in

house.

was

questioned

about

SDLC

and

Testing.

from

that,

I

was

asked

about

my

interests.

The

interview

ended

with

me

asking

him

questions.

here,

the

entire

process

was

conducted

in

1

day

at

their

office.

selected

candidates(6

total

-

4

from

day

1

and

2

from

day

2)

were

allotted

the

role

Intern,

Application

Development.

process

was

over

and

assumed

that

I

had

been

rejected.

But

a

week

later,

I

received

a

call

from

the

HR

that

they

wished

to

conduct

additional

rounds

in

my

case.

that

time,

I

asked

HR

clearly

if

the

rounds

were

for

the

same

role

to

which

she

said

yes.

Later

on,

I

got

to

know

that

the

additional

interviews

were

for

the

Automation

team.

Technical

Interview

3

This

round

was

conducted

by

Application

Development

Manager

in

the

Automation

Team

on

Microsoft

Teams.

I

was

asked

a

leetcode

easy

question

on

arrays

and

a

question

on

joins

in

SQL.

I

was

asked

4

principles

of

OOP

which

I

explained

with

examples.

I

was

asked

to

write

an

efficient

sorting

algorithm

that

sorts

the

array

till

a

particular

index

only.

I

chose

to

write

the

Merge

Sort

Algorithm.

I

was

asked

some

CCN

questions

related

to

HTTP

and

Rest

APIs

which

I

don't

remember

now.

Managerial

Round

This

round

was

taken

by

the

Head

of

Automation

online

a

week

after

the

previous

interview.

She

asked

me

to

introduce

myself

and

share

my

resume.

She

asked

me

the

language

I

was

most

comfortable

in

and

asked

me

to

rate

myself

in

it.

I

rated

myself

7/10

in

C++

and

said

it

was

the

language

I

used

for

DSA

and

CP.

She

googled

C++

and

asked

me

a

very

random

question

related

to

pointers.

I

was

not

able

to

answer

the

question.

I

did

not

know

that

keyword

but

explained

pointers

in

C++

and

why

they

are

important.

This

discussion

went

on

for

15

minutes

where

we

discussed

the

difference

between

C++

and

Java,

use

of

C++

for

building

games,

etc.

As

the

allotted

time

was

over,

I

was

unable

to

ask

any

questions.

A

few

hours

later,

I

received

the

mail

that

I

have

been

selected

for

the

technology

intern

role.

When

I

received

my

offer

letter

it

said

‘Intern,

Data

Automation’.

That

is

when

I

realised

I

was

interviewing

for

a

different

team

in

my

last

2

interviews.

So,

finally

8

technology

interns(of

which

5

were

from

SPIT)

were

selected

with

6

in

App

Dev

and

2

in

Automation.

There

is

not

much

difference

in

the

roles,

I

guess,

as

we

worked

on

the

same

projects

and

technologies.

I

am

writing

this

interview

experience

5

months

after

my

interviews.

So,

I

am

not

able

to

recall

all

the

questions.

But

from

a

preparation

perspective

for

Russell,

you

need

to

have

a

strong

hold

over

CS

Fundamentals

and

know

your

resume

well.

Also,

practice

aptitude

if

necessary.

1.  [Online Assessment]  [ 135+ Students were shortlisted  ] 
 The  OA  had  a  few  sections:  Logical  Aptitude,  Technical  Questions,  and  a  final  DSA  section. 
 Each  section  had  its  own  timer.  It's  all  about  being  choosy  and  smart  enough  to  identify  which 
 questions are the low-hanging fruit for you. 
 Aptitude Section:---> 
 Following  is  just  the  tentative  vague  description  and  not  the  exact  question  (I  really  can’t 
 remember the exact questions , but this description will really help you get a clear idea) 
 1)Coding-Decoding  Analogy:  If  “FADE”  is  “GBWR”  then  follow  the  same  pattern  for  some 
 “xyzw” type of string 
 2)Number  Theory:  how  many  pairs(a,b)  are  there  wherein  division  of  a/b  is  not  an  integer 
 {1,2,3,4…16} something like this. 
 3)Logical  Reasoning  Passage:A  big  3-4  questions  passage  (Some  6  people  ,  given 
 word-equations(ratio  etc)  of  relations  of  their  savings  and  salaries)  and  then  follow  up  questions 
 (easy but time consuming) 
 4)Statistics:  Mean  ,  Variance  ,  Standard  deviation  ,  Coefficient  of  Variation  type  of 
 questions.(Mean  of  10  students  is  3  ,  but  then  some  student  has  mark  correction  and  then  find 
 new mean) 
 5)Basic Probability types question (12 box , 3 has trap , so P(no trap)) 
 6)Question  like  how  many  pair  of  letters  are  there  for  “HERITAGE”  having  as  many  letters  as 
 there in english alphabet series (something like this) 
 7)Profit % types question 
 8)Pipe-work time types question 
 Technical Section:---> 
 1)Proper  Loops  (do-while  etc)  as  a  figure  ,  and  then  interpret  the  figure  and  tell  how  many  times 
 is the code running. 
 2) Some oops (basic) questions 
 3) Standard OS,CCN,DBMS,SQL questions 
 4)Port , Ping , Router , Queues , Quick sort , static keyword numerical , pointers numerical 
 int arr[]= {10,20,30,40,50,60,70} 
 then  something  like  int  *r=arr….  *r1=arr+2  ….  *r2=  arr+5…  and  then  cout<<  something  related 
 with r1, r2 etc 
 5) Binary search tree array ={4,1,2,16,8,33,62,76} something like this , what is left child of root. 
 6)Queue  <int>  of  size  4,  some  position  of  front  ,  rear  pointers  ,  removing  3  elements  ,  and  then 
 MCQ based on the state of the queue. 
 7)2D matrix figure based manipulation question (flowchart based) 
 8)Mysql type question (easy) 
 9) OOPS (conceptual easy question) of inheritance , output based , etc 
 10)One crazy question about OS of CISCO organization for switches 
 11)Basic data structure type question (medium gate level question) : output based 
 12)How many times the flowchart’s loop is running. 
 Coding question:---> 
 1) How many elements are there which are in the correct place and not in the correct place. 
 Correct place means Rightly indexed when seen from a Sorted perspective. (easy isn't it?) 
 ex:         1 3 2 4 
 sorted is 1 2 3 4 
 1 and 4 are in the correct place , whereas 3 and 2 are not in the correct place. 
 2) Given int x, int y and then count special numbers from x and y. 
 Special number means SUM(DIGITS) == 2*(highest digit). Easy?? 
 Points to ponder:---> 
 1)  Be calm 
 2)  Manage time smartly 
 3)  Attack on low-hanging fruits first 
 4)  Attempt questions which you are familiar first 
 5)  Learn to leave lengthy questions 
 6)  Don't get zoned out , every 1 minute has the same value :) 
 2.  [Technical Round 1]  [41 candidates ] (70-90 mins++) {Taken by 2 interviewers} 
 1)  Introduce yourself 
 2)  Was asked question on my projects 
 3)  Specify about Skills , Tech Stack that you have practiced 
 4)  DSA Question (Revolving around Bellman-ford algorithm) 
 5)  What is a cloud? Proxy Server? 
 6)  SQL vs Mongodb , which I have used in the project ? Why? Why not? 
 7)  Real word Application for Abstraction , Stack , Queue and Tree and Graph 
 8)  Port number of Mysql 
 9)  Heavy  discussion  on  my  projects  (AIML  based)  (Maths  behind  Random  Forest  ,  Logistic 
 Regression)  .  Focus  on  Pipelines  and  Flow  of  building  an  ML  Model  (decide  ,  Train  ,  test 
 , tune etc etc) 
 10)  It is impressive if you have published some research paper (or it is in under progress) 
 11)  Indexing in Databases 
 12)  Varchar  in  SQL  ,  why  varchar  ?  How  to  change  the  Varchar  (LENGTH)  once  the  table  is 
 already created. 
 13)  Triggers in SQL 
 14)  Library in Python which I have used (numpy , nltk , pandas , sci-kit ,openCV) 
 15)  Docker ? Kubernetes (I didn't know Kubernetes Technicality) 
 16)  Was  Asked  about  my  approach  to  the  latest  DSA  problem  which  I  had  solved  (it  was 
 about Trie with Bits and finding the Maximum XOR ) 
 17)  Final  question  for  the  interviewer?  :  I  asked  :  how  was  my  interviewer  and  where  am  i 
 lacking  ,  they  said  it  is  important  that  as  a  developer  ,  we  must  have  some  knowledge 
 about  cloud  ,  how  to  deploy  ,  some  advanced  real  life  usage  of  networking(ccn)  ,  code  to 
 be written not just for localhost , but a scalable code for development+deployment etc. 
 Mind it:---> 
 1)  Never give up while giving interview 
 2)  Even  if  you  don't  know,  try  to  struggle  with  the  question  ,  tell  the  interviewers  about  your 
 perspective,  they  are  really  interested  more  on  how  you  think  about  approaching  a 
 problem , if you succeed in this way then this is really impressive 
 3)  Sometimes  you  may  even  get  a  question  that  “hey  AIML  project  is  all  about  templates  etc 
 ”,  that’s  where  you  must  say  that  while  making  a  project  it  is  also  about  proper  lifecycle 
 of  development  and  building  model  ,  which  task?  Which  model?  Why  this?  Why  not  that 
 etc ? 
 4)  Never say anything negative , it may backfire you during the interview. 
 5)  Don't  break  down,if  your  interviewer  is  an  expert  in  a  field  like  (cloud  computing)  and 
 you have zero idea on that field , just be real-self. 
 3.  [Technical Round 2]  [22 candidates ] (90-100 mins++) {Taken by 2 interviewers} 
 1)  Introduce yourself 
 2)  One  DSA  code  to  be  written  on  an  online  compiler.  Mine  was  an  easy  question:  Find 
 peak  element  in  an  (increasing  and  then  decreasing  type)  of  array  (Binary  search)  ,  just 
 ask a clarifying question , what if n==1?==2? and then what if len(decreasing part)==0? 
 3)  Indexing in Database (but advanced level) 
 4)  SQL  query  optimization,  I  was  asked  to  first  tell  Select  *  from  table  with  name  like 
 “T%”  and  then  to  optimize  this  query.  (even  if  you  don't  know  ,  just  try  to  deliver  a  valid 
 logic) 
 5)  Again Applicability for all projects, WHY this ? WHY not that? 
 6)  OOPS:  Compile-time  and  run-time  polymorphism  (overloading  ,  overriding  ,constructor  , 
 public , private , inheritance , Abstraction , encapsulation ) All these in real-life 
 7)  LLD  design  for  Bank  system  ,  make  classes  ,  interfaces  ,  controller(if  you  don't  know  , 
 then  study  it  beforehand)  ,  methods  ,  etc  ,  clean  code  for  RBI  class  (parent  class)  and  then 
 subclasses  like  IDFC  bank  ,  SBI  bank  etc  ,  and  each  having  some  rules,  compliance  rules, 
 seniorcitizen_Age etc , revolving around inheritance etc. 
 8)  What  happens  when  you  type  a  message  in  whatsapp  to  your  friend?  what  happens  when 
 you click on “send message” button. 
 9)  How  do  you  think  messages  travel  from  your  phone  to  your  friends  phone?  Protocols, 
 headers , packets , trivial CCN stuff. 
 10)  What are keys , why keys , normalization , MongoDB familiarity? 
 11)  Code for Trigger (After Insert) , just insert the curTime in logs 
 12)  Was asked about familiarity with Stored Procedures 
 13)  Asked about HSS-Psychology course 
 14)  Was asked about Data analytics and my QGIS findings of land cover change 
 15)  Was asked about my (Airavat,Flipkart grid) Hackathon experience , projects etc 
 16)  Final  question  for  interviewers?  I  asked  :  Is  there  any  way  to  do  “Online  transactions  on 
 mobile  for  metro  between  Ghatkopar  and  Azad  Nagar  without  Internet”  ,  then  we  had  a 
 healthy discussion for about 5+ minutes on this topic. 
 4.  [HR Round]  [9 Candidates] (20 mins++) 
 This  was  a  fairly  relaxed  round,  and  the  HR  representative  was  very  friendly  and  made  me  feel 
 comfortable. The conversation included the following questions: 
 1)  Something  cool  about  me  which  I  have  not  written  on  resume  (I  told  about  my  love  for 
 chess) 
 2)  Why  do  you  want  to  join  IDFC  bank  ?  (Reality:  Along  with  coding  ,  I  could  know  about 
 ITR, finance , economics , equity , IPO , banking sector etc.) 
 3)  Dream company apart from IDFC bank? (I told about my love for space , stars and ISRO) 
 4)  How do you deal with rejections (on-campus 8 times )? 
 5)  What if I wasn't selected today also? (Grind for the best opportunity) 
 6)  Any  creative  Application  ideas  for  HR?  (I  first  bulleted  the  answer  but  she  told  me  to 
 think  again  and  come  up  with  a  brilliant  idea,  so  i  presented  my  idea  for 
 emotion-detection-AI  powered  priority  wise  scheduler  chatbot  /  employee-HR  relation 
 management  site  with  color  coding  feature  ).  She  was  really  impressed  by  this  idea 
 thought  in  a  shorter  timespan.  Like  she  told  me  such  an  application  is  being  used  by  her 
 and that this idea was amazing. 
 7)  Where do I live ? What do I do in my travel time to college? 
 8)  Some behavioral question and that’s it 
 9)  Any  final  question  for  her  :-  I  asked  her  about  the  Location  for  internship  and  then 
 placement,  She  told  that  bootcamp  may  be  in  Banglore  and  then  Joining  for  placement 
 maybe in Mumbai.(most likely) 
 5.  [Business Round]  [9 Candidates ] (20-30 mins++){Taken by 1 interviewer} 
 Okay  so  I  was  pretty  sure  that  yes  I  had  made  it  to  the  end  ,  and  then  we  got  to  know  that  there  is 
 one more Technical Round with the senior engineers or VP or architects of the company. 
 It  was  an  online  round  on  Teams.  I  would  recommend  you  to  give  it  from  college  only  ,  because 
 there  you  will  have  support  from  college  ,  TPO  office  ,  supportive  TPCs  (yes  they  really 
 work  hard  for  our  placement  for  that  entire  day+night)  ,Wifi  ,  HRs  etc.  So  even  if  there  is 
 some  wifi  problem  or  technical  issue  ,  they  are  there  to  handle  it  (SO  GIVE  IT  FROM 
 COLLEGE ONLY !!!) 
 1)  Hey Tushar , Introduce yourself 
 2)  Seen my resume (Screen shared) 
 3)  Talked about my skills 
 4)  Discussed  about  my  projects  (the  one  with  the  most  impact  driven  cause  to  be  discussed 
 along  with  full  flow  ,  architecture  ,  why  this  and  why  not  that  ,  the  mathematics  behind 
 this-that , the impact it is having) 
 5)  My  interviewer  was  a  senior  architect.  He  was  really  very  chill  and  made  me  feel 
 comfortable even after facing some technical issues (wifi problem at 8:05 pm). 
 6)  Final  questions  for  him?  :-  I  told  him  that  I  had  presented  my  views(Technical  round  2) 
 on  “online  transactions  on  mobile  without  internet”  and  what  his  opinion  was  on  this 
 point.  He  praised  this  idea  and  said  some  work  is  going  on  by  RBI  and  all  banks  and  that 
 there is a good scope in this field. 
 After  appearing  for  almost  9  companies,  cracking  OAs  ,  failing  in  some  Round  1,  sometimes 
 Round  2  ,  Sometimes  even  after  HR  round  :(  ,  but  that  day  I  was  confident  that  yes  ,  I  think  I 
 have cracked it. It was around 9pm when we left for our home. 
 Next  Day  ,  at  11:11  AM  :)  We  got  to  know  that  8  students  have  been  selected  for  this  role  ,And 
 finally the hectic game has finally reached its final Destination .

journey.prep:
1. Know your Resume INSIDE OUT: - Make sure you have at least some ideas about each and 
every word written on your resume. Please do  not write anything that you have no idea about, it 
will create a very bad impression 
2. DSA and Fundamental concepts are Important:- It is always good to be prepared  about 
anything and everything. My personal recommendation is that when there is time do problems 
from both Leetcode as well as from CodeForces as it will help you in coming up and implementing 
of solutions. Also keep your knowledge of fundamental subjects clear. 
3. Practice Aptitude:- Use IndiaBix for aptitude. 
4. Build Projects that have some value: - Do not build generic projects, try to see what real -world 
problems can you solve and try to solve that in your projects. It may not be perfect, but is still way 
better than something too generic.  Also try to keep a solid reason ready on why you chose a  
particular xyz technology over something else. 
5. Have a general idea of all projects and your role etc. But practice one project in deep and use 
it everywhere for questioning and cross questioning. 
6. Consistency and Discipline are of paramount importance :- Whatever you do, stay consistent 
with it. I remember, when starting out, I used to get anxious when I couldn’t solve a problem, but 
with time and effort, I did manage to solve those. 
 
7. Communication is unparallelly important! 
8.  There will be times when things will just not work out. 
9. Use an ATS Friendly Overleaf Resume Template. 
10. Lastly, do not lose hope if you are not selected, keep on trying. 
 
Get used to rejections. Do not give up. 
During the entire placement season keep your health up and your overall attitude positive, had severe 
side effects that caused excruciating joint pains, and still had to travel 1 hour daily for online 
assessments and interviews. I faced rejections in interviews from Nomura, and in the HR round of ISS, 
during Wissen’s 2nd round. 
 
Stay connected to your friends. 
They can help more than you can imagine, they conduct mock interviews, help build projects together, prepare 
in groups. It really helps in keeping the momentum and staying motivated. 
 
HR Interview Tips: 
1. Maintain Eye Contact 
Ensure steady, natural eye contact with the interviewer. It shows confidence and  helps build a 
connection, but avoid staring as it may come across as forced. 
2. Be Mindful of What You Share 
Avoid oversharing personal experiences that do  not directly address the question.  Focus on relevant, 
concise answers that highlight your suitability for the role. 
3. Use the STAR Method  
Structure your answers to behavioral questions using the STAR method (Situation,  Task, Action, 
Result). It provides clarity and demonstrates a problem-solving mindset. 
4. Show Respect in All Responses  
Be polite and professional. Even casual or off -topic comments should be delivered  respectfully to 
avoid unintentionally offending the interviewer. 
5. Frame Strengths and Weaknesses as Narratives 
Share your strengths and weaknesses with context. Use short stories or examples  (real or carefully 
crafted) that showcase growth and self-awareness. 
6. Avoid Monologues  
Do not treat your answers like speeches. Keep the conversation balanced, concise, and  interactive. 
Know when to stop and where to elaborate. 
7. Display Confidence and Personality  
Strong communication and soft skills often outweigh technical skills in HR rounds. Let  your 
personality come through—be confident, composed, and clear. 
8. Always be Positive  
Always answer all questions in a positive manner and I will suggest do not ask for feedback in an HR 
interview, you can in a technical round if you feel that you have done great. 
9. Always Deny plans for Higher Studies 
Never show interest or accidently hint your passion for academia and research.  Prepare solid reasons 
to justify why you are choosing industry over academia, or it may become your reason for rejection. 
 
 
Just work hard and you will succeed eventually, it is never over until you give up. 
Rome wasn’t built in a day, it was built gradually so will your career for the day you give up on 
yourself is the day you lose. 
 
Keep your outlook positive and have faith there is some opportunity kept explicitly for you and 
when it comes it will come served on a silver platter for you. 
 
ALL THE BEST!!! 
 
Feel free to contact me on LinkedIn 
In case of any further doubts, you can refer to the past interview experiences shared by TPO.
