1. OA (165 Per Seating arrangement) (11th August from college post PPT):- 
 
Platform:- Microsoft Forms (Proctored) (Do not try to cheat the invigilation was pretty strict). 
Questions:- 30 (MCQs) 
Time:- 30 mins 
Note:- There was no auto submit, so make sure to click the submit button before the time ends. 
Only then your submission will be recorded. 
 
The MCQ’s were based on Java/ Python/ C/ C++/ OS/ CCN /guess-output and few general Aptitude 
questions asked although few participants had questions pertaining DBMS, LLMs, API’s etc too, the 
questions were of moderate difficulty thus doable but do not get stuck on a question, time 
management is key. 
 
A general tip is read the test instructions well enough. 
Keep your basics crystal clear. 
Be efficient at Time management. 
 
Be calm and keep your momentum throughout the day, for me the day of this test was very hectic for 
some like me as we had interviews for Wissen in the morning (at their office at around 9) followed by 
PPT and OA for IDfy and finally ending with PPT and OA of Baker Hughes. If at any point you lose 
your momentum things can go into a spiral.  Keep yourself motivated the placement process can be 
hectic a times even frustrating but it’s up to you to keep yourself going. 
 
2. Digital Interview [45 students appeared] (on the 12th August till 3:30pm):- 
 
Platform:- HireVue 
Type of Questions:- Typical HR and behavioral questions. 
Time per question:- Max 3 mins per question. You can stop the recording once done. 
Preparation time:- 30 seconds before the 3 mins start. 
 
Note:- 
There is no button to pause/retry the recording, you have 3 mins to record the answer 
and a single attempt . You go to the next question after you answer and voluntarily 
procced or timer times out. 
There were a few trials available before starting to answer any of the actual question. 
 
Questions that were asked: 
1. Why did you choose your current degree program? 
2. What do you aim to gain from this internship? 
3. Tell us about a challenging project experience. 
4. How did you manage multiple priorities and time? 
5. Tell us about a time when you realized you have a weakness and how did you try 
to overcome that? 
6. What would you like us to know more about you? 
These questions were the same for everyone. 
 
Some tips for this round: 
1. Please focus on speaking and articulating your thoughts well. Structure your well answer 
in the given 30 seconds. 
2. Do not read any scripts, or use GPT in any form for making these answers, because that 
will definitely look unnatural if you read onto the camera, it can easily be captured. 
3. They do observe the body language and eye contact with the camera  so try to maintain a  
good posture, hand movements and good eye contact with the camera. Keep a decent smile 
(do not overdo) on your face while speaking the answers. 
4.  Visualize as if you are speaking to a real person, if it helps. 
5. Most importantly be confident about what you are speaking, be clear on what you wish 
to convey , be natural and have a positive outlook  do not prolong any answer 
unnecessarily.  
 
 
 
3. Technical Interview [35 students appeared] (on the 14th of August in college):- 
 
We were called at 9:30 am in the morning. The TPCs collected all our resumes before the Interviews 
began and handed each interview panelist a copy before beginning. 
I was the 1st person for my panel; the interview began with me exchanging warm greetings with the 2 
panelists. They asked me to introduce myself while they glan ced at my resume. The y picked up my 
interest for cyber security from my introduction and in continuation to it asked about my cyber security 
project on my resume. They asked me to explain them like they had little to no knowledge of cyber 
security. I explained them keeping their request in mind (I was used to interviewers with no idea asking 
 
me to explain it) but then the tables tu rned one of them started going into depth of it and asked about 
why I choose it and not something different (at this point it dawned on me that this panel is well versed 
in cyber security) we discussed on these lines for about ~40 minutes. After this they asked me a few 
HR questions like did I attend the ppt to which I told them the truth that I wasn’t as I was late and the 
room was full, they asked me the 4 pillars of Baker Hughes to which I answered 2 and tried to think 
but later confessed on not remembering them. They seemed satisfied and said I could leave. At this 
juncture I asked the panelist if he was working in cyber security as no interviewer up to now had an 
idea of what I was speaking to which the grim on his face broadened and answered affirmatively then 
I proceeded to ask him how seriously does Baker Hughes take cyber security after which I asked their 
permission to leave. 
 
 
4. Techo-HR Interview [15 students appeared] (on the 14th of August in college):- 
 
After around 20 mins of finishing my 1st round, I was called for my 2nd round. 
The TPC’s did the same drill collecting a resume copy and handing it to the 2 nd panel, this panel too 
had 2 panelists. The questions in this round were more HR with typical questions like:- 
1. How was your day? 
2. If I walk into a class ad ask your friends, what will they say about you? 
3. What is the thing(s) that all your friends do dislike about you? 
4. Then how did you handle conflict in a group? 
5. One thing that you had to do because none of your teammates were willing to do? 
And so on. Overall it was a 40-45 min endeavor. 
Finally, 9 Students were offered the job me being one of them.

journey.prep:
 Don't take the placement process lightly. 
 Prepare well for placements, especially for the Online Assessment. For DSA, I recommend 
following only one resource instead of mulƟple. For example, if you are following a speciﬁc 
YouTuber, sƟck with them. If you are following a speciﬁc problem sheet like Striver's or 
NeetCode's, pick one and complete it fully. 
 Have at least 1-2 strong projects; it's ﬁne if your other projects are simpler. 
 This was the 6th company I interviewed for. I made several mistakes along the way, and you 
will too, but it's important to believe in yourself. 
 Keep pushing. If you don't get selected, don't worry—just start again. I have seen students 
who cleared their interview on the ﬁrst aƩempt and others who were not selected even aŌer 
interviewing with 10+ companies. But I am sure they will all make it eventually. 
 I started my project work and OA prep only one month before placements. I sƟll succeeded, 
but I missed many opportuniƟes along the way. In the end, it was a happy ending. 
 I believe that if I can do it, you can too. 
 Just believe in the process. When you get the oﬀer, you will deﬁnitely feel that it was all 
worth it. 
 All the very best for your placements! Don't take too much stress. 
 
You can contact me via: 
LinkedIn: hƩps://www.linkedin.com/in/aarya-deshmukh-840b9928a/

journey.howSecured:
Total 3 rounds: Online Assessment, Technical Interview, and HR Interview. 
 
1. Online Assessment [90-100 students appeared] 
The round consisted of four secƟons: Logical ApƟtude, QuanƟtaƟve ApƟtude, Coding, and a Verbal 
SecƟon. Everyone received two diﬀerent coding quesƟons, and the diﬃculty level was quite random. 
Some students received easy quesƟons involving HashSets or HashMaps, while others got diﬃcult 
Dynamic Programming (DP) quesƟons. 
Thankfully, I received very easy quesƟons: 
1. Remove duplicate elements from an array and return the unique elements. 
2. Count the frequency of each character in a string. 
Tips: 
 PracƟcing apƟtude quesƟons from IndiaBix and GeeksforGeeks (GFG) is suﬃcient. Just 
remember the paƩerns and formulas to solve similar types of problems. 
 These paƩerns are repeƟƟve in every Online Assessment, just presented in diﬀerent forms. 
 For Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA), start pracƟcing as soon as possible. I regret 
starƟng only one month before placements. 
 However, if you are starƟng late as I did, you can sƟll succeed. BeƩer late than never, but I 
sƟll recommend starƟng your DSA preparaƟon a minimum of six months in advance. 
 There are students who get beƩer oﬀers without pracƟcing more than 10 DSA quesƟons, but 
this is an excepƟon and relies on luck, so don't depend on it. 
 
2. Technical Interview [32 candidates appeared for this round] 
My technical interview was unique. It's important to know that everything depends on the panel you 
are assigned to. There were three panels, with two panelists in each. The diﬃculty level and types of 
quesƟons were not standardized across all students. You will realize this aŌer a few interviews. My 
panel was very relaxed. 
They didn't ask me for a formal introducƟon. Instead, they asked how my preparaƟon was going, 
how I had prepared for TransUnion, when I started, and if I had spoken with any seniors from my 
college who work at the company. You might think these are easy quesƟons, but your answers, 
where you might menƟon various technologies to impress them, will determine the direcƟon of the 
interview. I didn't menƟon DSA or SQL in my answers because I was not conﬁdent in my skills in 
those areas. 
The interviewer then asked me to explain my projects. This is a quesƟon asked in every interview, so 
you should have 100% knowledge of your projects. Mostly, the interview will focus on the ﬁrst 
project listed on your resume, and someƟmes a second one. AŌer I explained my project, they 
presented some edge cases and asked how I would handle large amounts of data and improve the 
execuƟon Ɵme. 
Then, they asked me how I would handle a Git conﬂict and what prompt I would give to ChatGPT to 
help resolve it. Next, they asked how I would run the project on another system. I answered with 
"Docker," which led them to ask more in-depth quesƟons about cloud compuƟng. However, I 
stopped them and explained that I haven't worked with cloud compuƟng technologies and don't 
have much knowledge about it. It's okay to admit when you don't know the answer to a quesƟon. 
Don't try to give a wrong answer; just be honest. However, you shouldn't say "I don't know" for every 
quesƟon. 
They also asked about a hackathon I parƟcipated in: why my team placed in the top 10 and not ﬁrst, 
what went wrong, and what I learned from the experience. Then, they asked me to explain Docker to 
a layman with no technical knowledge. The interviewer was quite impressed with my analogy. Finally, 
he asked if I had any quesƟons for them. I asked them 3-4 quesƟons. The interview lasted for 27 
minutes. 
Tips: 
 When you enter the room, greet them with a smile and a handshake. 
 Give your introducƟon conﬁdently because the ﬁrst impression is the last impression. 
 You should know the in-depth meaning of every word on your resume. It's not about the 
number of technologies you list, but how well you know them. 
 There are standard quesƟons asked about projects, such as: how you would handle a large 
amount of data, how you would scale the system, why you used a speciﬁc technology, and 
how you would improve performance. 
 You are the driver of the interview, so the conversaƟon will likely follow the direcƟon you set 
with your answers. 
 I wasn't conﬁdent in DSA and puzzles, so I avoided menƟoning them. However, this 
completely depends on the panel. Other companies or panels will deﬁnitely ask more 
technical quesƟons on CS fundamentals like OS, OOPS, DSA, and DBMS. 
 If there are two interviewers, try to maintain eye contact with both. Keep a smile on your 
face to show conﬁdence. 
 They oŌen prioriƟze moƟvaƟon and a posiƟve mindset over just technical experƟse. 
 Ask for their names at the end if they didn't introduce themselves at the beginning.

3. HR Interview [10-12 candidates selected for this round] 
There was one panel with two panelists. Both were very relaxed. They started with small talk, asking 
how my day was going and if I'd had lunch. Then, they asked me to introduce myself, focusing on 
aspects not menƟoned in my resume. 
When asked to explain my project, I didn't get too technical. Instead, I focused on storytelling: how I 
got the idea, my approach, how I collaborated with my team, and the project's future scope. 
They then asked about my family background, if I had any issues with relocaƟon, why they should 
hire me, and if I had plans for a master's degree. Finally, they asked if I had any quesƟons for them. I 
asked a couple of quesƟons and made sure to shake their hands before leaving, as I had forgoƩen to 
do so at the start. 
[8 students received an oﬀer including me] 
Tips: 
 I saw many people with good technical knowledge who were not selected aŌer the HR 
interview. 
 Therefore, try to improve your English ﬂuency. I understand if you don't come from an 
English-medium background (Like me), but at least try to speak conﬁdently, even if you make 
a few grammaƟcal mistakes. 
 Always smile during the interview. 
 I feel that the HR interview is about engaging the interviewers with your communicaƟon 
skills, like telling a story about your projects and your learnings. Don't dive deep into 
technical terms; they are generally not concerned with those details. 
 Try to show them what a good team player you are. 
 Conﬁdence, a smile, and honesty are the keys to succeeding in the HR interview.

journey.howSecured:
The

recruitment

process

had

3

stages;

Online

Assessment,

Technical

Interview

and

HR

Interview.

The

Pre-Placement

talk

was

carried

out

at

SPIT,

in-person

by

the

TransUnion

team,

prior

to

the

Online

Assessment.

1.

[Online

Assessment]

[

87

students

appeared

for

this

round

]

On

the

basis

of

their

resumes,

87

candidates

were

shortlisted

for

the

test

out

of

those

who

applied

for

TransUnion.

The

test

was

conducted

on

4th

September.

It

lasted

for

1

h

30

min,

from

14

00

to

15

30.

The

test

was

conducted

on

SHL

and

calculators

were

allowed.

There

were

4

sections

in

the

test:

Mathematical

Aptitude.

Puzzle

and

Pattern

based

Aptitude.

Coding

section.

English

Vocabulary

and

Grammar

section.

A.

Mathematical

Aptitude

involved

questions

like

ratios,

proportion,

simple

interest,

time,

etc.

Example:

●

If

a

train

travels

120

km

in

2

hours,

how

long

will

it

take

to

travel

300

km

at

the

same

speed?

●

Divide

₹720

among

A,

B,

and

C

in

the

ratio

2:3:4.

B.

Puzzle

and

Pattern-based

Aptitude

involved

questions

like

finding

the

odd

one

out,

guessing

the

next

number,

etc.

Example:

●

Find

the

odd

one

out:

121,

144,

169,

196,

225,

242

●

What

comes

next

in

the

series:

2,

4,

8,

16,

?

C.

The

English

vocabulary

consisted

of

questions

like

finding

the

correct

sentence

or

understanding

the

conveyed

message

from

a

passage.

Example:

●

Choose

the

grammatically

correct

sentence:

A)

He

don't

like

playing

cricket.

B)

He

doesn't

likes

playing

cricket.

C)

He

doesn't

like

playing

cricket.

●

From

the

given

passage,

what

is

the

main

idea

the

author

is

trying

to

convey?

D.

Coding

questions

consisted

of

2

questions

of

varying

difficulty.

I

received

2

fairly

easy

questions.

Q1:

You

are

given

an

array

of

orders.

Find

the

Order

ID

of

every

order

in

the

array.

(There

was

a

lot

more

to

the

question,

I

forgot

the

rest,

sorry

about

that

guys

:P)

Solution:

The

order

ID

is

calculated

by

summing

all

the

digits

of

each

element

in

the

array.

(The

question

was

framed

in

a

confusing

manner,

making

it

seem

more

difficult

than

it

actually

was.

I

got

the

solution

by

analysing

the

results

which

followed

that

format.)

Example:

Input:

[123,

56,

89]

Output:

[6

(1+2+3),

11

(5+6),

17

(8+9)]

Q2:

You

are

given

a

1-indexed

array

of

people

with

labels

1

to

n.

For

the

next

m

turns,

you

have

to

swap

the

people

with

specified

labels

(e.g.,

‘1,

5’

means

swap

1

and

5’s

place).

After

m

swaps,

return

the

person

at

kth

index.

Example:

●

Initial

array:

[1,

2,

3,

4,

5]

●

Swaps:

[(1,

5),

(2,

4)]

After

swaps:

[5,

4,

3,

2,

1]

●

If

k

=

1 ,

return

5 .

Tip:

For

the

Online

Assessments,

I

would

suggest

doing

timed

practice

of

aptitude

questions

and

coding

questions

too.

Be

sure

to

practice

CodeForces

questions

as

their

style

(the

way

they

accept

inputs

and

return

outputs)

can

be

quite

different

from

LeetCode

questions.

2.

[Technical

Interview]

[

32

students

appeared

for

this

round

]

The

interviews

began

the

very

next

day,

on

5th

September,

10

00

onwards.

There

were

3

panels,

with

each

containing

2

people

who

would

interview

you

at

the

same

time.

I

entered

and

greeted

the

panelists.

The

2

panelists

asked

me

to

introduce

myself.

I

stated

my

name,

where

I

was

studying,

and

I

gave

them

a

brief,

yet

comprehensive

overview

of

my

projects.

They

asked

which

programming

language

I

am

most

comfortable

with,

which

framework

I

use

the

most,

which

frameworks

I

have

used

that

contain

my

main

programming

language,

and

‘who

was

the

last

person

you

argued

with?’

About

my

projects,

they

asked

me

what

ML

model

I

used

in

one,

what

is

the

full-form

of

OCR

(since

one

of

my

projects

had

it)

and

some

other

surface-level

questions.

Then

came

a

DSA

question.

It

was

‘ You

have

an

array

containing

elements.

Find

all

of

the

duplicate

elements.

Eg:

Input:

[1,2,3,6,1,1,4,2,2,2,9],

Output:

[1,2] ’.

I

stated

that

we

can

use

a

hashmap,

traverse

the

entire

array,

and

implement

a

frequency

counter

for

each

element.

After

that,

we

use

another

for

loop

on

the

hashmap

to

select

any

element

which

has

a

frequency

over

1.

They

asked

me

the

time

complexity

and

whether

it

could

be

optimised.

They

asked

me

about

Object-Oriented

Programming.

I

stated

that

I

was

more

comfortable

with

OOP

in

Java

than

in

Python.

Then

they

asked

me

to

state

what

pointers

are

and

the

difference

between

Byte

and

byte

in

Java.

Finally,

an

SQL

question.

We

have

a

table,

and

we

want

to

delete

records

containing

email

of

a

certain

value.

We

had

to

write

the

SQL

query

on

paper.

I

was

also

asked

how

SQL

tables

reduce

query

runtimes

in

case

of

extremely

large

tables,

to

which

I

replied

‘indexing’.

They

also

asked

for

the

explanation

of

indexing,

which

I

gave

along

with

a

real-life

analogy.

Lastly,

they

asked

me

whether

I

had

any

questions

for

them.

I

asked

them

what

goes

on

behind-the-scenes

before

TransUnion

decides

to

venture

or

expand

into

a

new

area

or

sector,

how

they

decide

whether

it

is

worth

venturing

into

or

not.

They

liked

the

question

and

gave

a

rough

idea

since

they

didn’t

have

the

answer

to

this,

being

software

developers,

they

weren't

in

charge

of

these

decisions.

Finally,

I

shook

hands

firmly

with

them

as

I

got

up,

thanking

them

for

their

time

and

closing

the

door

behind

me

as

I

left.

The

interview

lasted

only

15-20

minutes.

(Every

other

applicant

was

surprised,

too,

since

interviews

last

for

30-45

minutes

on

average.)

Tips:

Be

confident

and

explain

everything

clearly.

To

explain

your

projects

in

detail

without

going

on

for

too

long,

preferably

use

an

established

method

like

the

STAR

method.

If

you

don’t

know

something,

DO

NOT

go

on

a

long-winded,

vague

explanation

in

hopes

that

it

will

be

correct.

Just

say

you

don’t

know

it,

or

you

have

done

it,

but

forgotten,

and

the

interviewers

will

move

on

to

the

next

question.

(I

did

so

with

the

Byte

vs

byte

question

and

the

optimization

technique

for

the

DSA

question).

The

above

point

also

applies

to

answers

you

are

unsure

about.

Be

confident

and

stick

with

some

answer.

Interviewers

test

your

conviction

and

willpower,

they

don’t

expect

you

to

know

everything

they

ask

anyway.

Know

your

resume

in

and

out.

Explain

your

projects

properly

and

clearly,

without

sounding

too

vague.

Do

not

fake

anything

in

it.

When

explaining

your

DSA

question’s

solution,

state

and

explain

your

thought

process

as

if

it

were

a

tutorial

of

some

sort,

rather

than

going

silent

completely.

Start

with

the

brute

force-approach

and

then

provide

an

optimised

solution

if

prompted.

3.

[HR

Round]

[

Approximately

12

students

appeared

for

this

round

]

I

was

asked

basic

HR

questions.

I

introduced

myself,

and

explained

my

projects

along

too,

hence

they

asked

questions

about

the

projects

on

my

resume.

These

questions

weren’t

about

the

tech

and

more

about

what

I

considered

before

implementing

features

in

them.

They

asked

me

about

general

limitations

that

could

arise

in

my

project

and

how

I

would

deal

with

them.

They

moved

on

to

ask

me

about

my

family,

about

their

occupations,

where

I

stay,

which

location

I

would

like,

and

whether

I

was

open

to

relocation.

Then,

they

proceeded

to

ask

me

why

I

wanted

to

work

at

TransUnion,

what

my

greatest

strength

is,

and

how

I

became

good

at

it.

I

was

also

asked

why

I

chose

AIML

in

engineering.

The

interview

ended

with

me

asking

the

interviewers

the

same

question

I

asked

in

the

first

interview

round

(since

I

got

only

a

rough

answer).

They

answered

it

in

greater

detail

and

I

shook

hands

firmly

with

them

as

I

got

up,

thanking

them

for

their

time

and

closing

the

door

behind

me

as

I

left.

The

interview

lasted

15-20

minutes.

Important

Tip :

Be

attentive

during

the

pre-placement

talk.

Take

notes

if

need

be.

You

MUST

remain

familiar

with

what

the

company

does,

their

values,

and

what

they

expect

from

the

average

applicant,

be

it

technical

skills

or

soft

skills.

Work

on

your

communication

skills.

Even

if

you

have

good

knowledge,

how

you

convey

it

might

make

the

difference.

Take

part

in

mock

interviews

and

mock

speeches

to

reduce

nervousness.

4.

[Final

Round]

[

8

students

appeared

for

this

round

]

Everyone

was

called

outside

the

TPO

and

made

to

sit

in

room

105,

including

the

TPCs.

The

TransUnion

team

entered

and

stated

that

only

2

students

were

selected.

The

remaining

6

had

to

go

home.

Just

kidding.

This

was

a

prank

round.

All

8

people

who

cleared

the

HR

round

were

selected

for

TransUnion.

students

the

job

journey.prep:
• DSA: Easy to medium level is enough for moderate companies. Companies like PhonePe may ask 
graphs, trees, DP, and advanced problems.
• SQL: Asked in almost every interview — know all commands, query execution, differences, and 
internal workings.
◦ In SQL editors, you can test and debug queries, but in interviews, you won’t have that. 
Practice writing queries on pen and paper and predicting outputs carefully.
• Communication: It’s not just about what you know, but how you answer. Maintain eye contact, 
stay conﬁdent, and avoid pauses or stammering.
• OOPs: Prepare in detail with real-life examples and references to your projects/code.
• Core Subjects: Basics of OS, DBMS, and Computer Networks are usually sufﬁcient.
• System Design: Asked only in speciﬁc companies like IDFC, not everywhere.
• Projects:
◦ Know your projects thoroughly — tech stack, challenges faced, standout features, and future 
improvements.
◦ Be ready to explain why you chose the project and why that tech stack.
• HR Questions & Puzzles: Prepare basic HR questions (strengths, weaknesses, goals) and practice 
puzzles from GeeksforGeeks (GFG).
If you have any further questions, feel free to reach out to me on LinkedIn: 
linkedin.com/in/varsha-bojja
In case of any further doubts, you can refer to the past interview experiences shared by TPO.

Ensure your resume is ATS -friendly with standard formatting and clear headings, and maintain a 
CGPA of 7.5 or above, as most companies require this.  
TransUnion criteria: 7 CGPA
journey.prep:
1. Maintain a Good CGPA: Keep your CGPA above 7.5–8, as it helps meet eligibility criteria and 
creates a strong first impression. 
2. Resume Preparation: 
o Use a standard, professional template (e.g., Overleaf Resume Template). 
o Make it ATS-friendly; check your score on Resumeworded (aim for 60+). 
o Be truthful—only include skills, projects, and achievements you can confidently discuss. 
Prepare 4–5 points for each. 
3. Company and Role Research: 
o Understand the company’s work, culture, and role requirements. 
o Prepare relevant questions to ask the interviewer—it shows interest and preparation. 
o Read the job description carefully and incorporate keywords into your answers. 
4. HR Preparation: 
o Prepare for standard HR questions in advance to stay confident. 
o Keep answers authentic and personal; avoid over-reliance on AI for this. 
5. DSA and Problem Solving: 
o Focus on understanding questions thoroughly rather than just solving many. 
o Solve standard problems first; daily practice on platforms like LeetCode or GeeksforGeeks 
helps. 
o Participate in contests to improve time management, an essential skill for coding rounds. 
o Always check constraints; write brute-force solutions first if optimal solutions are not 
obvious. 
6. Core Subjects: 
o Prioritize important subjects like DBMS and CCN—often asked in technical interviews. 
o Choose open electives wisely (e.g., DBMS) to strengthen placement-related knowledge. 
7. Programming Skills: 
o Master your primary language’s basics. 
o Be confident discussing syntax, concepts, and memory management. 
o Practice explaining your approach during coding rounds; interviewers often guide you if 
stuck. 
 
 
8. Team Motivation: 
o Collaborate with peers with similar goals. 
o Motivate each other, take progress follow-ups, and push to stay on track. 
9. Handling Rejections: 
o Treat rejections as learning opportunities. Focus on areas you can improve. 
o Placement success also involves timing and luck, stay confident and persistent. 
10. Additional Skills: 
o Develop puzzle-solving and critical thinking through platforms like GeeksforGeeks. 
o Practice guesstimates to improve analytical reasoning. 
o Participate in mock interviews to enhance confidence, communication, and interview 
stamina 
The placement process can be very hectic, and facing failures along the way is normal. Don’t give up—
keep giving your 100% and continue preparing consistently. In the end, all your hard work and perseverance 
will be worth it..

The selection process consisted of the following rounds: 
1. Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) 
2. Online Assessment 
3. Technical Interview 
4. Techno HR Interview 
1. Pre-Placement Talk (PPT)  
The PPT was conducted offline and began a little late as all the company team members had not yet 
arrived. During this time, the HR ma’am interacted with us informally and invited five volunteers to 
perform a short skit. I was one of the participants in th is activity. I advise actively participating in 
such activities, as they showcase confidence, help during the HR rounds, and leave a positive 
impression on the recruiters. 
Afterward, the company representatives delivered their presentation, providing a detailed 
introduction about the organization, its work culture, and the career opportunities available. I would 
also suggest asking relevant doubts and clarifying queries during the PPT, as it demonstrates genuine 
interest in the company and further strengthens your impression. 
 
2. Online Assessment  [87 students appeared for this round] 
The Test was conducted on 4th September from 14:00 to 15:30 (1 hour 30 minutes). The test was hosted 
on SHL, and calculators were allowed. It consisted of four sections: 
1. Logical Aptitude: Easy to medium-level questions, including puzzles and pattern-based problems 
such as finding the odd one out or guessing the next number. Example questions included: 
o Find the odd one out: 121, 144, 169, 196, 225, 242 
o What comes next in the series: 2, 4, 8, 16, ? 
14 questions were to be solved in 14 minutes. 
 
2. Quantitative Aptitude: Questions on topics like ratios, proportions, simple interest, and time & 
work. Example questions: 
o If a train travels 120 km in 2 hours, how long will it take to travel 300 km at the same speed? 
o Divide ₹720 among A, B, and C in the ratio 2:3:4 
12 questions were to be solved in 12 minutes. 
3. Coding Section: Two coding questions were provided, with difficulty varying randomly among 
candidates. 
o My questions were: 
1. Count the frequency of special characters in a string. 
2. Count the frequency of numbers in a given number. 
50 minutes were allotted for this section. 
4. Verbal/English Section: Questions focused on grammar, vocabulary, and comprehension. Example: 
o Choose the grammatically correct sentence: 
▪ He don't like playing cricket. 
▪ He doesn't likes playing cricket. 
▪ He doesn't like playing cricket. 
o Understand the main idea conveyed in a passage. 
12 questions were to be solved in 14 minutes. 
Note: The coding section difficulty varied significantly for different students. Some received easy questions 
involving HashSets or HashMaps, while others got challenging Dynamic Programming problems. My 
experience was comparatively easier, as my questions focused on counting frequencies, which I could solve 
efficiently within the time limit. 
Tip: Start practicing aptitude questions well before placements, as most companies include them in their 
selection process. Additionally, regularly practice Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) to handle coding 
sections efficiently. 
3.    Technical Round  [32 students appeared for this round] [30-35 mins] 
I. Introduction and Projects 
• The interview began with a general introduction, followed by a discussion of my projects. 
• Projects and Challenges: I was asked to explain all my projects in detail and describe the 
challenges I faced during implementation. 
• Language Preference: The interviewer inquired about my preferred programming languages and 
which ones I was most proficient in. 
II. Java and C++ Deep Dive 
The main technical discussion focused on my Java project. 
• Core Java Questions: 
o Why I chose Java for the project. 
o Key differences between Java and C++. 
o How Java achieves platform independence. 
o Which file is generated upon Java code execution. 
o The role of JVM and JRE in making Java platform-independent. 
• Memory Management in Java (Interview Q&A): 
The interviewer asked about types of memory in Java. I explained that the primary memory areas 
relevant for program execution are Heap and Stack: 
o Heap: Stores all objects and class instances created at runtime. 
o Stack: Stores local variables, method call frames, and references to objects in the heap. 
 
o Example: In public static void main(String[] args), local variables like integers or 
references are stored on the stack, while objects created using new inside main are stored on 
the heap. 
III. Data Structures (Scenario-Based) 
The interviewer presented real-life scenarios and asked which data structure I would use. 
Scenario 1: Stock Market Prices 
 
• Scenario: You are developing an application to track stock market prices throughout the day. You                                                
           need to quickly retrieve the price of a stock at specific integer times, such as 9, 10, 11… 3. 
• Question: Which data structure would you use to efficiently store and retrieve these prices, and 
why? 
Scenario 2: Digital Signature (Undo/Redo) 
• Scenario: 
You have developed an application where, at the final step, the user needs to provide a digital 
signature. If the user creates a signature but is not satisfied, they can clear it and create a new one. 
Later, they realize that the previous signature was better. 
• Question: 
How would you retrieve the previous signature? Which data structure would you use and why? 
IV. Coding and Problem Solving (Palindrome) 
• Problem: Check if a given string is a palindrome. 
My Approach ➔  
• Initial Solution: Brute-force approach using extra space—reverse the string and compare with the 
original. 
• Optimization: Explained time and space complexity of the initial approach, then provided an 
optimized two-pointer solution. 
• Execution: Wrote the optimized code, explained it, and performed a dry run with a test case. 
V. SQL Query  
• Problem: Two tables of sales data were provided. 
• Approach: Asked clarifying questions, explained the thought process, and decided to use Joins and 
GROUP BY to handle multiple entries per customer. 
• Solution: Wrote a correct SQL query incorporating both Joins and aggregation functions. 
VI. Closing 
• The interview concluded with questions about my extracurricular activities. 
• I also asked 1–2 questions regarding the company’s work culture and upcoming projects. 
 
 
 
 
 
4.    Techno HR Round  [10 students appeared for this round] [15-20mins] 
The interview began with my introduction, during which I introduced myself and briefly summarized my 
background. They then asked me about my projects, and I provided a concise overview of each. Following 
this, they inquired about my achievements and participation in hackathons. 
 
They also asked which interview I was currently giving and why I was not selected in previous attempts. 
The discussion then shifted to TransUnion, where I was asked why I chose the company, what kind of work 
TransUnion does, and why I wanted to join. They also asked about my position and responsibilities in various 
committees, including how I mentored juniors and managed my tasks. 
 
Next, the conversation moved to my certifications, including where I completed them and my basic technical 
knowledge. They also asked why I am switching from Electronics to Tech, my weaknesses, my residence, 
family, and how I managed extracurricular activities alongside traveling. I was also asked about my career 
aspirations and where I see myself in the next five years. 
Towards the end, the interviewers gave me the opportunity to ask questions and clarify any doubts regarding 
the company or the role. 
After the process completion 8 students got an offer and I was one of them.

domain

two

:

AI

The placement process can be hectic and stressful, and it’s completely normal to feel overwhelmed. I had 
tests and interviews before this where I didn’t make it, and that’s okay, not everything will go your way.
journey.prep:
•  It’s never too late to start. Whether you’re in first year or already into third, what matters is starting 
today. You’ll thank yourself later. 
• Choose your primary programming language and stick to it. Be it Java, Python, or C++, master one 
language thoroughly. But also have a basic understanding of other popular languages, especially if they 
come up in interviews or MCQs. 
• Start DSA preparation seriously. You can follow: 
o The A2Z DSA Sheet by Striver (great for structured progress). 
o The CSES Problem Set (excellent for logic building and competitive programming). 
• Keep 1–2 strong, impactful, and preferably unique projects in your portfolio. Projects that solve real 
problems, demonstrate initiative, or use newer technologies really help you stand out. 
• Don’t ignore your core Computer Science subjects like DBMS, OS, CN, OOPs, and SQL. These 
come up a lot in interviews—both technical and MCQ rounds. 
• Participate in extracurriculars! Being active in committees, hackathons, and competitions not only 
builds your confidence but also shows that you're a team player and proactive. 
• It’s okay to face rejection. I had tests and interviews where I didn’t make it before this offer. But 
remember: every failure teaches you something, and you only need one "yes." 
• Keep your resume updated and tailor it for each company. Highlight relevant projects, achievements, 
and internships. 
• Mock interviews help. Practice with friends or seniors. The more you simulate the pressure, the better 
you’ll perform. 
• Always stay consistent — even if you can only study or code for an hour a day, it adds up. 
• And finally, never stop believing in yourself. Confidence and self-belief are game changers. 
You've got this! Every small effort counts. The journey might be challenging, but with consistency, smart 
planning, and the right mindset — you’ll get where you’re meant to be. 
Feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn

journey.howSecured:
1. Online Assessment [135 students appeared for this round] 
• The online assessment was conducted on HackerEarth and had a 90-minute time limit. 
• It consisted of 12 technical MCQs, 1 SQL query, and 1 coding question. 
The MCQs were based on CS fundamentals, OOPs, SQL, and code snippet output prediction. 
The SQL question was simple and could be solved using a basic WHERE clause with some AND conditions. It 
required interpreting a table to calculate compensation. 
The coding question was string-based, required generating a lexicographically smallest string based on mapping 
rules from two input strings S1 and S2 (containing only 'T' and 'F'). 
You had to construct an answer string such that: 
o For index i, if S2[i] is 'T', the answer substring starting from i should match S1. 
o If S2[i] is 'F', then at least one character in that range must differ from S1. 
The solution required both brute-force thinking and careful handling of edge cases to ensure the final string was 
valid and lexicographically smallest. 
https://leetcode.com/problems/lexicographically-smallest-generated-string/ 
https://www.thejoboverflow.com/p/p1926/  
 
Note: The test was exactly the same as the one conducted for the Barclays Summer Internship last year, 
including the coding and SQL questions. In fact, Barclays has been repeating the same test pattern and 
questions for the past two years, so going through previous year test experiences can give you a strong edge. 
 
2. Technical Round [37 students shortlisted] 
The interviews began around 10:30 AM, but I was called only after the lunch break at 3:00 PM. So, if your slot 
is later in the day, there’s no need to worry, delays are normal. 
My interview began with a brief introduction round. The interviewer asked me to introduce myself, followed by 
questions about my family background, CGPA, and whether I was satisfied with my college and academic 
performance so far. 
Next, he asked me about my primary programming language, to which I responded Java. He then asked a 
simple DSA question on finding duplicates in an array. 
He handed over his laptop and asked me to code the solution in as many ways as I could. 
• I first implemented the solution using a HashSet. 
• After that, he asked me to make a few variations in the code, which I successfully implemented. 
Following that, the discussion moved to Java concepts and Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs). 
The interviewer then focused deeply on Exception Handling in Java. He: 
• Asked several questions, ranging from basic to advanced level. 
• Requested me to code examples using try-catch-finally blocks directly on his laptop. 
• Asked about different types of exceptions, their behavior, and expected outputs. 
• Also made me predict the output of the code I had written, then verify it by running the program. 
While coding and answering, I made a few minor mistakes, but nothing major. The interviewer seemed okay 
with them, so don’t stress too much over small slips. 
Lastly, we discussed one of my projects, where I gave an overview and explained the problem statement, tech 
stack used, and key features. 
At the end of the interview, he asked if I had any questions. I asked him about his role at Barclays and the 
technologies he works with. 
That concluded my first technical round. 
 
3. HR Round [21 students shortlisted] 
Just 10 minutes after my technical round, I was called in for the HR interview. 
The HR round began with the interviewer asking me to introduce myself, followed by questions about the 
hackathons I had participated in and won. 
He then asked me about the company values that were shared during the pre-placement talk (PPT session). He 
wanted to know: 
• What those values meant to me personally 
• And how I had implemented any of those values in my daily life 
We then had a detailed conversation about the committees I was a part of, and this part of the discussion went 
on for quite some time. 
Towards the end, he asked if I had any questions for him. I took the opportunity to ask about: 
• The team he leads at Barclays 
• And what kind of work his team is involved in 
This brought the HR round to a close. 
In total, 16 students, were selected.

Overview

The

placement

process

at

Barclays

involved

three

rounds,

starting

with

an

online

assessment

and

progressing

to

two

interview

stages.

On

July

26th

there

was

an

online

assessment,

followed

by

interviews

on

July

29th.

Out

of

133

participants

who

appeared

for

the

online

assessment,

37

were

shortlisted

for

the

first

technical

interview.

Subsequently,

21

individuals

advanced

to

the

final

Tech

+

HR

round,

Round

1:

Online

Assessment

(90

minutes)

The

Barclays

online

assessment

was

a

three-part

test

consisting

of

MCQs,

a

SQL

query,

and

a

coding

problem.

The

MCQs

were

the

key

differentiator

for

shortlisting.

1.

Multiple

Choice

Questions

(MCQs)

These

questions

tested

foundational

knowledge

across

various

programming

languages

and

concepts.

●

Core

Language

Concepts:

Questions

involved

predicting

the

output

of

short

code

snippets

in

languages

like

C++

and

Java .

Topics

included

pointers,

bitwise

operators,

control

flow

( continue ),

and

variable

scope.

●

Object-Oriented

Programming

(OOP):

This

section

focused

on

OOP

principles,

such

as

the

difference

between

abstract

classes

vs.

interfaces

and

method

overriding

vs.

overloading .

It

also

covered

topics

like

the

impossibility

of

overriding

private

and

static

methods

and

the

order

of

class

initialization.

●

Exception

Handling

(Java):

Questions

evaluated

an

understanding

of

try-catch-finally

blocks.

A

key

point

was

knowing

that

a

return

statement

in

a

finally

block

overrides

any

return

from

try

or

catch ,

and

that

System.exit()

prevents

the

finally

block

from

executing.

2.

SQL

Questions

This

section

included

both

a

query

and

theoretical

MCQs.

●

Queries:

The

questions

required

you

to

apply

your

SQL

knowledge

to

real-world

scenarios.

This

involved

using

multi-table

joins

to

combine

data,

filtering

data

by

date

using

functions

like

EXTRACT(MONTH

FROM

date) ,

and

translating

complex

business

rules

into

a

single

SELECT

query.

●

SQL

Theory:

MCQs

tested

your

knowledge

of

commands

like

DROP

vs.

TRUNCATE

vs.

DELETE .

A

crucial

distinction

was

the

difference

between

an

equi

join

(which

uses

only

= )

and

an

inner

join

(a

broader

category

of

joins).

3.

Coding

Problem

The

coding

problem

was

a

single,

complex

challenge

that

required

careful

logical

thinking.

●

"String

Generation":

The

task

was

to

create

the

lexicographically

smallest

string

S

based

on

a

pattern

string

( S1 )

and

a

rule

string

( S2 )

of

'T'

(true)

and

'F'

(false)

constraints.

●

Solution

Logic:

The

recommended

approach

was

to

first

satisfy

all

'T'

constraints.

Then,

fill

the

remaining

positions

with

the

smallest

possible

character,

'A'.

Finally,

iterate

through

all

'F'

constraints

and

minimally

modify

the

string

(e.g.,

change

the

rightmost

'A'

to

a

'B' )

to

break

any

invalid

matches

while

preserving

the

lexicographical

order.

This

problem

went

beyond

a

simple

build-and-check

method,

demanding

a

more

nuanced

strategy

to

correct

violations.

Round

2:

Technical

Round

1

Following

the

online

assessment,

37

participants

were

shortlisted

for

the

interview

rounds.

There

were

five

interview

panels,

and

I

happened

to

be

assigned

to

one

of

the

more

challenging

ones.

My

interviewer

was

highly

experienced

and

went

into

very

detailed

questions

on

every

topic.

This

round

lasted

for

approximately

an

hour.

The

interview

began

with

a

standard

introduction,

after

which

I

was

asked

to

brief

him

about

my

projects.

He

then

inquired

about

the

programming

languages

I

was

comfortable

with.

Following

this,

he

asked

me

to

explain

the

concept

of

method

overloading

and

to

write

a

Java

program

demonstrating

a

real-world

example,

encouraging

me

to

think

beyond

common

examples

like

'Area'

or

'Vehicle'.

He

then

moved

on

to

an

in-depth

discussion

about

my

projects.

Noticing

my

significant

frontend

projects,

he

transitioned

into

detailed

questions

about

React

and

HTML.

He

gave

a

scenario

about

creating

a

dropdown

within

another

dropdown

using

React

and

asked

about

the

distinction

between

a

textbox

and

a

textarea.

Further

questions

included

how

to

limit

the

number

of

words

in

an

input

field

and

how

to

display

the

count

of

letters

already

entered.

While

I

couldn't

recall

every

specific

detail,

I

explained

my

approach

clearly.

He

then

asked

detailed

HTML

questions,

presenting

a

scenario

where

he

needed

to

input

seven

addresses

in

a

form.

He

asked

how

I

would

extract

the

second

address,

impose

a

limit

on

the

number

of

addresses,

and

manage

IDs

if

they

were

assigned

sequentially

(e.g.,

1

for

the

first

address,

2

for

the

second).

Specifically,

he

asked

what

would

happen

to

ID

1

if

the

first

address

was

deleted—would

it

be

reassigned,

or

would

a

new

one

be

created?

He

also

wanted

to

know

how

I

would

track

the

total

number

of

addresses.

After

assessing

my

Java

knowledge,

he

shifted

to

SQL.

He

asked

if

I

knew

about

Procedures

and

Triggers,

to

which

I

confirmed.

He

then

asked

for

an

explanation

and

relevant

queries.

At

this

point,

I

honestly

confessed

that

I

hadn't

practiced

writing

queries

for

procedures

and

triggers,

but

I

explained

the

underlying

concepts.

I

remained

calm

and

continued

to

answer

all

his

questions.

He

then

inquired

about

the

partitioning

concept

in

DBMS

and

what

partitioned

tables

are,

asking

me

to

write

a

query

for

it.

Finally,

he

asked

about

different

types

of

indexes

in

DBMS.

The

interview

concluded

with

a

question

about

the

risks

a

bank

might

face

and

potential

solutions.

I

left

this

round

feeling

devastated

and

demotivated,

convinced

it

had

gone

terribly

wrong

and

almost

on

the

verge

of

tears.

Round

3:

Tech

+

HR

Round

To

my

surprise,

I

was

called

for

this

final

round,

which

shortlisted

21

candidates.

This

round

lasted

for

about

half

an

hour.

The

interviewer

started

by

sharing

the

positive

feedback

he

had

received

from

my

first

interviewer,

which

was

a

huge

relief

and

a

pleasant

surprise

given

how

I

felt

after

the

first

technical

round.

He

then

asked

me

to

describe

my

internship

experience

and

elaborate

on

my

projects,

cross-questioning

me

further

to

see

my

understanding

and

contributions.

Following

this,

he

moved

on

to

the

HR-specific

questions.

He

asked

classic

questions

like

"Why

do

you

want

to

join

Barclays?"

and

a

challenging

scenario:

"If

another

company

offered

you

double

the

salary,

would

you

switch?"

He

also

presented

situations

involving

workplace

ethics

and

problem-solving,

such

as:

"If

your

manager

gives

you

a

task

with

an

unrealistic

deadline,

how

would

you

approach

it?"

and

"You've

completed

your

work

for

a

strict

weekend

deadline

and

left

for

vacation,

but

midway,

you

realize

you

forgot

to

push

an

important

update

to

GitHub.

How

would

you

resolve

this?"

Another

thought-provoking

question

was:

"If

you

were

stuck

on

a

project

you

built

from

scratch,

and

a

friend

helped

you

resolve

a

small

error

that

had

a

big

impact,

and

then

you

were

nominated

for

an

award

for

that

project,

would

you

accept

the

award

or

tell

your

team

members

about

your

friend's

contribution?

Discuss

the

pros

and

cons

of

each

decision."

He

asked

many

more

similar

situational

questions.

I

ensured

to

be

confident

and

true

to

myself

in

my

responses,

which

seemed

to

satisfy

the

interviewer.

At

the

end,

I

took

the

opportunity

to

ask

him

about

his

role

and

what

Barclays

expects

from

interns,

specifically

if

prior

knowledge

of

finance

is

required.

With

these

questions,

the

interview

concluded.

Areas

for

Improvement,

Preparation,

and

General

Tips

My

selection

was

largely

due

to

my

ability

to

stay

calm

under

pressure,

even

when

faced

with

questions

I

couldn't

fully

answer.

My

honesty

about

my

limitations,

coupled

with

explaining

my

approach

or

conceptual

understanding,

showed

integrity.

My

detailed

preparation

in

OOPS,

Java,

HTML,

React,

SQL,

and

DBMS

fundamentals

was

crucial,

especially

since

MCQs

were

a

deciding

factor

in

the

initial

round.

In

the

HR

round,

being

confident,

truthful,

and

demonstrating

problem-solving

skills

with

practical

reasoning

helped

immensely.

Engaging

the

interviewer

and

asking

relevant

questions

also

showed

genuine

interest

and

initiative.

Areas

for

Improvement:

My

biggest

learning

from

this

experience

was

the

need

for

thorough

practical

application

of

concepts,

especially

in

areas

like

SQL

procedures

and

triggers,

beyond

just

theoretical

understanding.

It's

crucial

to

not

only

know

what

a

concept

is

but

also

how

to

implement

it

with

code

or

queries.

journey.howSecured:
The process had 3 rounds.First round OA,then the shortlisted candidates from the OA round had to attend the 
PPT ,followed by 2 interview rounds and one prank round 3 days after the OA round.  
Clearing OA is very tough as major filtering happens in this round. So being well versed with various aptitude, 
CS fundamentals’ mcqs and coding questions is really important.Hence start practising for the same from the 
beginning. 
1.     Online Assessment Round [133 candidates appeared for this round] 
This round was conducted in college on the Hackerearth platform. It had multiple mcqs based on java 
fundamentals mostly OOPS and some code snippets from which we had to guess the output.The mcqs were 
quite tricky.There was 1 coding question exactly same as this: 
https://leetcode.com/problems/lexicographically-smallest-generated-string/description/?envType=problem-
list-v2&envId=string 
And there one an easy SQL query,where we were to find the name of candidates who had made purchases in 
the month of October.I used MONTH() to solve it. 
2.     Technical Round [ 37 candidates appeared for this round] 
Before this round there was PPT where we were told about company’s values(RISES) and its work culture. 
It is very important to be attentive during the PPT as it helps a lot while answering in the interview rounds. 
So my Technical round was mostly theoretical ,testing my understanding of each and every concept. It lasted 
for about 45 minutes.Firstly I was asked to give my introduction, which should be given very thoughtfully as 
everything from there is based on what you have said.After that I was asked about the projects so I gave a 
brief about all the 4 projects I had mentioned and then he specifically asked me to explain the 4th project 
which was the major project.Know your projects inside out.After that he gave me an SQL query to write which 
was something like there are 2 tables department and employee and I had to find the names of departments 
where number of employees were more than 10.From this i said multiple words like joins, group by and all so 
he started asking what did each of them do and how will i use what kind of join in various cases.Satisfied from 
my answers he asked me the next question,which was based on OOPS design.Given a colony of ants,some 
ants were soldiers,some were workers and there was one quee n ant.Workers could act as soldiers during 
dangerous times.I had to represent this in class diagrams. It is very important that you keep talking to the 
 
interviewer while solving such things as they want to know how you are thinking. Then he asked me where 
would certain functions lie ,in which class so like walk is general so it will lie in the main ant class then i was 
asked, how will you make sure that there is only 1 queen ant to which i answered using singleton class.Then 
I was asked how to empty an input field in react, where does js gets loaded browser side or server side and 
then I was asked the difference between C++ and Java then he gave me a scena rio where i had to design 
windows 12 how would i do it with these 2 languages.Then I was asked basics about mongoDB and MySQLI 
wasn’t asked any DSA question but many of my friends were asked DSA so be prepared for it.The interview 
ended with me asking him a few questions. Do learn LLD concepts as they were very important this year. 
3.    HR Round  [ 21 candidates appeared for this round ] 
This was a pure HR round for me but some others had a mix of technical + HR. So the Round started with 
where do I live ,then since the interviewer was an alumni of SPIT he told me how he used to travel to 
college.Then I was asked about my Minors degree from SPJIMR,what did i learn there and why i chose it.After 
that he told me to explain situations where I had used the RISES. This went well for about 15-20 minutes and 
then it was some general talk ,me asking him a few questions and telling him why i chose c omputer science 
as a career, telling my weaknesses. It is very important to speak confidently in this round as you are mostly 
judged on your speaking skills and what type of answers you give.  
 
After this there was a prank round where 16 candidates were called and finally we were told that we have been 
selected for the program.

which

I

answered

with

relevant

examples

like

in

maps

for

determining

shortest

paths.

He

proceeded

to

ask

a

DSA

question,

which

was

a

variation

of

Dijkstra’s

algorithm.

I

was

asked

to

code

the

solution

on

paper.

I

wrote

the

code

and

explained

the

entire

logic.

During

the

explanation,

he

asked

several

detailed

questions

about

each

part

of

my

code—why

I

used

heaps,

how

I

handled

initialization,

and

the

overall

structure

of

the

solution.

He

then

asked

me

to

think

through

potential

edge

cases

and

confirm

whether

my

code

handled

them.

After

that,

he

asked

me

to

do

a

dry

run

of

the

code.

I

walked

him

through

the

step-by-step

execution,

and

he

was

satisfied

with

my

explanation

and

approach.

After

the

DSA

question,

the

interviewer

briefly

moved

on

to

my

resume.

He

asked

about

my

participation

in

hackathons

and

what

I

had

implemented

in

one

of

them.

He

then

asked

about

the

projects

listed

in

my

resume,

including

their

purpose

and

technical

implementation.

Since

I

had

mentioned

LangChain

in

my

resume,

he

asked

several

questions

related

to

it.

These

included:

what

is

LangChain,

why

is

it

used,

what

is

LangGraph,

why

not

build

directly

without

LangChain,

and

what

advantages

it

offers.

I

answered

these

questions

based

on

my

project

experience.

Next,

he

asked

me

to

explain

another

project

I

had

worked

on,

including

the

technologies

I

used.

He

then

shifted

focus

to

OOP

concepts

and

asked

questions

about

the

static

keyword,

implementation

of

singleton

classes,

encapsulation,

and

interfaces.

After

that,

he

asked

me

two

SQL

questions.

He

initially

provided

two

tables:

student

and

subject,

and

asked

a

medium-level

SQL

query

involving

joins,

which

I

solved

successfully.

Then

he

added

a

third

table

called

department

and

asked

a

follow-up

query.

I

was

able

to

solve

all

three

queries

completely,

and

the

interviewer

seemed

satisfied.

Then

he

asked

a

few

questions

related

to

React

like

to

explain

the

component

structure,

then

explain

the

two

hooks

usestate

and

useffect.

Then

he

asked

about

Virtual

DOM

and

working

of

virtual

DOM

and

how

it

improved

efficiency.

Then

he

asked

some

general

topics

like

MongoDB

and

databases.

He

asked

me

to

explain

the

differences

between

SQL

and

NoSQL

databases,

and

in

what

scenarios

I

would

choose

one

over

the

other.

He

also

asked

me

to

give

two

real-world

examples

where

I

would

use

both

types,

which

I

was

able

to

answer.

Finally,

he

asked

me

about

different

types

of

NoSQL

databases

beyond

key-value

stores.

I

admitted

I

wasn’t

aware

of

all

the

types.

He

then

asked

about

indexing

in

DBMS

and

whether

indexing

can

be

done

in

NoSQL

databases

as

well.

The

interview

concluded

after

this

discussion

and

I

asked

about

how

AI

is

leveraged

in

finance.

He

answered

briefly

and

the

interview

concluded.

4.

HR

Round

[

8

candidates

were

shortlisted

for

this

round.

]

The

HR

round

was

very

relaxed

and

conversational.

The

interviewer

was

warm

and

made

me

feel

comfortable

from

the

beginning.

It

felt

more

like

a

discussion

than

a

formal

interview

and

lasted

around

15

minutes.

For

studies,

I

that

I

believe

gaining

hands-on

industry

experience

is

path

for

me.

At

the

end

of

the

interview,

she

asked

if

I

had

any

questions

for

her.

I

asked

about

MSCI’s

commitment

to

ESG

and

climate

initiatives,

and

how

those

values

are

integrated

into

the

company’s

work

culture.

She

appreciated

the

question

and

gave

a

thoughtful

response

before

concluding

the

interview.

5

students

were

offered

the

job

1.

Resume

Shortlisting

2.

Pre-Placement

Talk

3.

Technical

Interview

4.

HR

Interview

1.

Resume

Shortlisting

[

Everybody

above

6

CGPA

applied

]

Applications

opened

on

Superset

on

1st

September

with

a

minimum

eligibility

criteria

of

6

CGPA.

However,

during

the

shortlisting

stage,

only

students

with

7.5

CGPA

and

above

were

considered.

Resume

shortlisting

was

done

based

on

keywords

in

the

resume,

required

skills,

or

possibly

relevant

internships

and

projects.

After

this

round,

13

students

were

shortlisted,

and

the

list

was

announced

on

8th

September.

Pre-Placement

Talk

-

The

PPT

was

conducted

just

before

the

interviews

on

10th

September

by

TransBnk’s

CTO

and

HR.

They

explained

about

the

company—how

they

started,

what

motivated

them,

their

current

situation,

and

the

type

of

candidates

they

were

looking

for.

They

also

gave

us

an

overview

of

the

company’s

complete

workflow.

I

am

specifically

mentioning

this

round

because

attending

PPTs

and

interacting

with

the

presenters

can

really

help

during

interviews.

This

worked

for

me

too—I

asked

a

few

questions

during

the

PPT

based

on

the

homework

I

had

done

about

the

company

beforehand.

This

showed

my

genuine

interest,

and

they

answered

my

questions

in

detail.

Then

we

were

introduced

to

the

two

panelists

who

would

conduct

the

technical

interviews—both

were

senior

developers

at

the

company.

2.

Technical

Interview

[

13

students

appeared

]

The

first

panelist

started

the

interview

by

asking

me

for

my

introduction.

He

then

went

into

detail

about

my

internships

and

asked

me

to

explain

my

projects.

I

explained

all

my

projects

thoroughly.

After

that,

he

went

through

the

skills

section

of

my

resume

and

asked

whether

I

had

learned

those

skills

through

my

college

curriculum.

I

clarified

that

I

had

self-studied

most

of

them.

He

then

noticed

the

extracurricular

skills

mentioned

in

my

resume

and

seemed

curious,

so

we

had

a

short

discussion

about

them

for

about

a

minute.

After

this,

he

began

asking

technical

questions

based

on

my

resume

and

projects.

He

asked

me

about

JWT ,

its

working,

and

format,

which

I

explained

in

detail.

He

also

asked

the

difference

between

JWT

and

Session ,

along

with

some

follow-up

questions.

Later,

he

moved

on

to

questions

about

Java ,

including

multithreading,

its

types,

and

working .

Since

one

of

my

projects

involved

AWS,

he

asked

me

to

explain

AWS,

its

services,

use

cases,

and

overall

working .

Finally,

he

said,

“That’s

all

from

my

side,”

and

handed

it

over

to

the

second

panelist.

The

second

panelist

gave

me

a

problem

on

paper:

Missing

and

Repeating

Number

I

directly

explained

my

optimal

approach

based

on

equations

and

then

wrote

pseudo

code

on

paper.

He

was

satisfied

with

my

explanation.

Next,

he

gave

me

a

slightly

tricky

problem:

“How

would

you

sort

a

file

containing

numbers

of

size

8GB

when

you

only

have

6GB

RAM?”

He

asked

me

to

sit

in

another

cabin

and

solve

it

while

he

interviewed

the

next

candidate.

I

wrote

down

multiple

approaches

(not

code,

just

logic)

and

then

went

back

to

explain

them.

My

approaches

included

swap

memory,

virtual

memory,

and

an

external

merge

sort–based

approach.

They

seemed

satisfied

with

my

answers.

This

round

lasted

for

about

25–30

minutes.

3.

HR

Interview

[

6

students

appeared

]

After

almost

2

hours

of

waiting

and

the

lunch

break,

I

was

called

for

the

HR

interview.

There

was

one

panelist,

the

same

person

who

had

presented

the

PPT

and

was

the

HR

representative

of

the

company.

The

interview

began

with

my

introduction,

followed

by

an

overview

of

my

projects

and

internships.

He

then

asked

about

my

internships

in

detail.

The

discussion

moved

on

to

my

interests,

future

goals,

5-year

and

10-year

plans,

and

whether

I

had

any

plans

for

pursuing

a

master’s

degree.

I

explained

my

reasons

clearly.

He

then

grilled

me

for

a

while

on

one

question:

“Would

you

start

your

own

venture

if

you

had

the

right

resources

and

people?”

After

that,

he

asked

why

I

chose

engineering

and

why

I

pursued

a

diploma

instead

of

HSC.

He

also

asked

me

to

share

something

that

wasn’t

mentioned

on

my

resume.

Towards

the

end,

he

said,

“That’s

all

from

my

side,”

and

asked

if

I

had

any

questions.

I

asked

him

a

couple

of

questions

about

the

company,

which

he

answered

in

detail.

I

also

gave

some

inputs

in

between,

showing

that

I

had

done

my

homework

about

the

company.

He

even

recalled

the

question

I

had

asked

during

the

PPT.

The

interview

concluded

after

about

20

minutes.

The

results

were

announced

after

all

interviews

were

completed.

They

played

a

small

prank

on

us

by

calling

four

of

us

into

a

cabin

and

saying

they

had

only

three

vacancies,

asking

who

would

back

off.

After

a

tense

moment,

they

revealed

they

were

just

kidding

and

offered

jobs

to

all

four

of

us.

🎊

journey.prep:
1. Prepare for Quantitative Analysis and Aptitude: 
For companies like KPMG, aptitude and quantitative analysis play an important role. Practice 
regularly on platforms like GeeksforGeeks, IndiaBix, or other competitive aptitude sites. Time 
management is crucial, so focus on both accuracy and speed. 
2. Resume: 
o Use a clean and professional format, such as a LaTeX template. 
o Keep your resume ATS-friendly to increase the chances of being shortlisted. 
o Be precise and impactful: describe your projects in 2–3 points each, and quantify your 
achievements wherever possible. Numbers and results stand out. 
o Prepare your resume thoroughly from start to finish: Make sure you are familiar with 
every detail, description, and word mentioned in it, so you can confidently discuss any aspect 
during the interview. Being well-versed with your own resume shows professionalism and 
helps you answer questions accurately and convincingly. 
Parnika Das Resume 
 
3. Internship and Work Experience: 
From my observation, candidates with some form of internship experience tend to have an advantage, 
especially in technical rounds. Even part-time internships or summer projects provide real-world 
exposure and talking points for interviews. This is not a strict rule, but it definitely helps strengthen 
your profile. (It helped me a lot to stand out) 
 
4. Strengthen CS Fundamentals and DSA: 
Prepare both the theory and coding aspects of computer science. This includes: 
o Data Structures & Algorithms (DSA) 
o Computer Science fundamentals like Operating Systems, DBMS, Networking, etc. 
o Solve as many coding questions as you can. Do the questions on your own, and if you are not 
able to do it, learn it from any explanation video and do it by yourself. Follow the Strivers' 
sheet or Leetcode Top Interview 150. And for SQL, you can solve LeetCode SQL 50. 
o Practising coding problems regularly will build confidence for technical interviews. 
 
5. Communication is Key: 
Your ability to communicate effectively is often the first impression you make. Clear and confident 
communication can give you a significant edge over other candidates. Practice introducing yourself, 
explaining your projects, and discussing your experiences concisely and engagingly. 
 
6. Maintain Confidence and Positivity: 
o Keep a smile on your face during interviews. 
o Show confidence without arrogance. (Most Important) 
o Put in the effort to make a strong impression on the interviewer. 
 
7. Academic Performance Helps: 
A good academic record (preferably 7.5 GPA or above) adds weight to your profile. However, 
academics alone are not enough - balance it with projects, internships, and skills. 
 
8. Early and Consistent Preparation: 
o Start placement preparation as early as possible. 
o Maintain a healthy balance between studies, skill-building, and personal life. 
o Consistent effort beats last-minute cramming. 
o  
9. Resilience and Patience: 
Placement journeys are rarely smooth: 
o At first, you may struggle with clearing online assessments. 
o Even after clearing OA rounds, you might get rejected in interviews. 
o Sometimes, rejection happens even after the HR round, which can be heartbreaking. 
Key: Don’t lose hope. Hard days are part of the journey, and persistence is what separates success from 
failure. Give your 100% in every attempt, but also accept that luck plays a great role. 
 
10. Believe in Yourself: 
o Put in your best effort. 
o Keep improving, learning, and refining your skills. 
o Stay motivated, even when facing setbacks. 
 
My Overall Placement Experience 
 
I started my journey by attempting several Online Assessments (OA), which were initially challenging. 
Gradually, as I improved my speed and accuracy, I began clearing OAs after 5 tests or something, but 
then faced rejections in interview rounds. In one process, I was even rejected after the HR round, which 
was very disheartening. 
During my interviews, I focused on presenting my projects, internships, and experiences clearly, 
highlighting the technologies I worked with, challenges I faced, and how I resolved them. I made sure to 
stay confident, smile, and communicate effectively, which helped me leave a positive impression. 
I practised quantitative aptitude, DSA, and CS fundamentals rigorously and maintained a decent 
academic record alongside internships and projects. I also asked thoughtful questions about the role and 
career growth, which left a strong impression on the interviewers. 
Despite the ups and downs, I learned to stay persistent, balance preparation with personal life, and give 
my best in every attempt. Receiving the Letter of Intent from KPMG was the culmination of all the hard 
work, and the experience was truly unique compared to my peers. I believe the key takeaways were 
patience, consistency, preparation, and belief in oneself. 
 
All the Best!!!

Parnika Das 
        BE CSE AIML
 
The selection process for the Analyst - Tech Enablement Role (KPMG 2nd Role) was officially announced on 
3rd September 2025. Initially, it was mentioned that the process would include an Online Assessment (OA), 
followed by a Group Discussion, two Technical Rounds, and one HR Round. However, the Group 
Discussion round was later cancelled, and the process moved directly to the Technical Interviews after the 
Pre-Placement Talk. Our process took place online from college.  
 
1. [Online Assessment Test] [ About 20 candidates for second role only] 
 
The Online Assessment (OA) was held on 8th September 2025 and was of easy to medium difficulty. It 
mainly focused on Quantitative Analysis, along with other aptitude -based questions. It consisted of 55 
questions with 3 sections being Aptitude, Quantitative Analysis and Verbal Ability . The test was for 40 
minutes only. It was proctored with camera access and full -screen mode enabled, ensuring a monitored and 
fair evaluation environment.  Each question required proper calculations, logical thinking, and step -by-step 
solving; there were no simple one -word or direct MCQ -type questions. It required quick problem -solving 
skills as the time limit was quite tight. Both speed and accuracy played a crucial role in performing well in 
the assessment.  
It was conveyed that those who applied for  the first role and cleared the test of the first role were allowed to 
sit for the second round directly if they applied. 
2. [Technical round 1] [ 14 candidates] 
 
After the announcement, the process began with a brief online Pre -Placement Talk (PPT) conducted jointly 
with SPCE students (their offer and role were different). The session was quite informative, covering details 
about KPMG as an organisation, what the firm does, its service lines, work culture, and the type of work we 
would be involved in. They also explained that the role would include client interactions, analytical work, 
and frequent travelling as part of on-site engagements. 
Following the PPT, the Group Discussion round was skipped, and the process moved directly to the 
Technical Interviews. A total of 14 candidates were shortlisted and divided into two panels, with 7 
candidates in each. The interviews were conducted online through Microsoft Teams, with each slot spaced 
approximately 20 minutes apart. The overall process was well-organised and smooth, giving candidates 
ample time to prepare between rounds. 
I was the first candidate to be interviewed in my panel. The interviewer began the conversation in a friendly 
manner by asking how I was doing, which helped ease the initial nervousness. He then asked me to introduce 
myself, following which he requested me to give a brief overview of my work experiences. 
Since I had three prior work experiences, including one at Amazon India, he showed particular interest in 
understanding the kind of projects I had worked on. He went in-depth about my responsibilities, the 
technologies I was introduced to, and how I managed and contributed to each project. We discussed the 
challenges I faced, the problem-solving approaches I used, and the overall learning outcomes from each role. 
My interview didn’t follow the typical question -answer format ; instead, it felt more like an engaging 
discussion about my experiences and professional journey. The interviewer seemed genuinely interested in 
understanding how I applied my knowledge in real -world scenarios, which made the interaction quite 
comfortable. 
 
After discussing my work experiences, the interviewer moved on to ask about my academic background. He 
asked me what subjects I had learned during my computer engineering course and what I was currently 
exploring. I mentioned that I was learning about emerging technologies like Cloud Computing  and 
Blockchain, which naturally led to a deeper conversation about new advancements in technology. He seemed 
interested and asked me which of the latest technologies fascinated me the most and why, along with a few 
related follow-up questions. 
After that, he shifted the focus toward Computer Science fundamentals . He asked me about the different 
sorting algorithms I had explored and specifically questioned me on the difference between Bubble Sort and 
Merge Sort, discussing their time complexities and use cases.  He also asked me to tell him the pseudo-code 
of the merge sort algorithm briefly. 
He then moved to Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) , asking me to explain the fundamentals , such as 
stacks and queues, along with their real-life applications. For instance, he gave examples like the undo-redo 
functionality in applications and how it relates to stack operations. He also asked me some OOPs 
fundamentals as well  but not so much in depth . The discussion was quite interactive, as he appreciated the 
logical reasoning behind my answers and encouraged me to explain concepts in my own words. 
 
Towards the end of the interview, he asked me if I had any questions for him. I took the opportunity to ask 
about the key responsibilities I would have as an Analyst at KPMG and also inquired about the career 
growth opportunities within the organization. He seemed particularly impressed by the second question, 
appreciating my curiosity about long -term development. He then explained both aspects in great detail , 
describing the nature of the work, the kind of projects analysts are involved in, and the structured growth 
path within KPMG. It was an insightful conclusion to the interview and gave me a clearer understanding of 
the role and the organization’s work culture. He then ended the interview. The interview  was around 45 
minutes, so he didn’t get to ask much about my other skills. He did n’t ask about my projects and all. Other 
candidates were asked some other basic CS fundamental questions, hobbies, projects and basic DSA.  
3. [Technical round 2] [ 6 candidates] 
 
6 candidates were divided into 2 panels again. 
 
In the second round, the interviewer in my panel focused primarily on my projects rather than my internship 
experiences. He began by asking me to introduce myself, and then I briefly mentioned my internships. After 
that, he delved deeper into my latest projects, asking me about how I implemented them, the tech stacks I 
used, the challenges I faced, and how I resolved them. 
I had four projects in total, and he specifically asked about my final year project  as well as my first two 
projects — one based on Kubernetes and the other on Machine Learning. He was keen to understand which 
projects were group projects and which were individual, and for the group projects, he wanted to know my 
specific contributions and how I coordinated with my team. 
The interview was relatively brief, lasting around 25 minutes, but it went well. Towards the end, he again 
asked if I had any questions. I asked about the kind of work an Analyst does  and the typical career 
progression from Analyst to Associate Consultant, which he explained in detail. 
Unlike some other candidates, I was not asked about location preferences. Everything was going smoothly, 
and the interaction felt positive and engaging. Unfortunately, despite a good technical discussion, I did not 
get selected for the HR round. 
 
4. [HR round]  
 
The HR round was a brief 10-minute online meet that mainly covered basic HR questions. I was asked about 
my hobbies, strengths and weaknesses, and why they should hire me. The conversation felt largely formal in 
nature, serving more as a procedural step rather than a detailed interview. 
Shortly after this call, I received my Letter of Intent from KPMG . Overall, this experience was quite 
different from what my peers and friends went through , making it a unique and memorable process.  
 
Out of these 4 candidates from the HR round, 3 were sent a Letter of Intent and  1 candidate from the 
technical round 2 (that was me) was also sent a letter of intent.
